PREFACE 

Thirty years have passed since the excellent treatise on the Ohio Lien Laws, by Treadway and Marlatt, was first published. 

This fine work satisfied a long felt need and for many years remained the only authoritative text book in Ohio upon the subject. 

With the adoption of the Constitutional Amendment of 1912, however, under the authority of which the present Mechanics Lien Law was enacted in 1913, the whole theory of the law relating to mechanics liens underwent a radical change. In place of the old attested account, by which mechanics and materialmen could intercept funds only which were due the contractor from the owner, the new law now grants each a direct lien upon the real property of the owner. 

On account of the sharp conflict between the rights and remedies afforded by these two theories of the lien, the bench and bar of Ohio have experienced no little difficulty in construing the new act in the light of the decisions on the former law. 

Many cases have been decided which involve the interpretation and application of the later act, and yet many of its perplexing provisions have not yet been passed upon by the courts. 

No text book or treatise has been offered as yet to the bench and bar of Ohio which attempts, in more than a casual way, to discuss all of these reported cases or those provisions of the statute that have not yet been the subject of adjudication. This book represents the sincere effort of its author to perform this office. 

It is believed that all reported decisions have been cited and, in some instances, fully discussed or questioned. Where certain provisions of the law have not been judicially passed upon, or where the author has felt that the decisions of the courts of other states might be helpful in illuminating or amplifying the principles and rules laid down by the Ohio courts, frequent reference has been made to those decisions. 

This book has been in preparation over a period of five years in the midst of a somewhat busy practice. I would be remiss in the obligation I owe my many fellow lawyers who so often and in so many ways have aided me in the preparation of this work, should I fail here to acknowledge their helpfulness. Especially do I wish to express my very grateful appreciation for the assistance which Professor William W. Dawson of the Western

Reserve Law School rendered in the writing of the chapter, "Proceedings to Enforce the Lien," and of Clarence H. Royon, of the Cleveland Bar, in the writing of the chapter, "Attested 

Accounts". To Herbert A. Rosenthal, of the Cleveland Bar,

I also wish to express my cordial thanks for his inestimable help and untiring patience in reading the entire manuscript, in sug-

gesting changes, and in verifying citations. My thanks are also due to Roger I. Wykes and Ralph B. Wilkinson for their generous permission to refer frequently to their respective text books on the Michigan Mechanics Lien Law; also to The Ohio Legal 

Blank Company and The Columbus Blank Book Manufacturing 

Company for their valuable aid in the preparation of forms. 

If this book shall prove to be of assistance to the members of the bench and bar of Ohio in the construction or application of this important subject of legislation, the author will feel amply repaid for the labor he has spent upon its preparation. 

CLINTON DEWITT. 

March 15, 1931.

Constitutionality of the Mechanics Lien Law Sec. 6. The Constitutional Amendment of 1912 Sec. 7. The Law Today Sec. 1. At Common Law. 

By the common law, a laborer, contractor, or one who performed labor in any form, or one who furnished materials, in or for the construction, repair, alteration, demolition or removal of a building, structure, or other improvement, had no lien upon the real estate upon which the building, structure, or other improvement was located, for the value of his labor, service, or materials. His lien, if allowed at all, was one that attached to personalty only.¹ It was obtained only by his detention of the chattel upon which his labor had been performed or in which his materials had been used. "Possession by the lienor of chattels on which the lien was claimed was indispensable

Tiffany on Real Property, 2nd

Edition, Vol. 3, Par. 659. 

A mechanics lien on real property was unknown to the common law.

All he could do was to hold the property until the owner came for it and retain possession. until he was paid for his labor or materials. By issuing an attachment, however, he could furnish a method by means of which the property could be sold and he could realize his money from the proceeds of the sale.4

Sec. 3. The Statutory Lien. 

(A) Definition 

A mechanics lien is a species of lien created by statute in most of the states, which exists in favor of persons who have performed work or furnished materials in and for the erection, demolition, alteration or removal of a building. In a narrow and restricted sense, a mechanics lien is a lien for labor, as distinguished from a materialman's lien, but in a broad sense it means a lien for material as well as for labor, and it is frequently used as a general term to designate liens of contractors, subcontractors, laborers and materialmen.9

Historical Review "The Mechanics Lien Law * * * establishes a right in rem and not a right in personam. * * * This means that the proceeding is brought to determine the status of the thing itself, the particular thing in the case (the real estate), and is confined to the subject matter in specie."10 

By the great weight of authority, statutes that relate to liens of mechanics and materialmen are remedial; instead of creating new and substantive rights, they simply afford new and cumulative remedies to enforce obligations previously recognized.11 "Of itself, when the statutory requisitions to its creation are observed, it (the lien) has not the force and effect of a judgment, and is not self-enforcing or selfexecuting. Until a judgment is obtained, in the mode pointed out in the statute, it is inchoate; and it is as dependent, for operation and effect, upon the rendition of judgment, as the statute directs, as is the lien created by the levy of an attachment upon the rendition of judgment "It may be defined to be a claim created by law for the purpose of securing a priority of payment of the price and value of work performed and materials furnished in erecting or repairing a building or other structure, and as such it attaches to the land as well as the buildings erected thereon." 

Van Stone VS Stillwell &

The remedy is cumulative, and may or may not be employed in connection with the ordinary action for the collection of the debt." Caulfield vs Polk, 17 Ind.

It does not create, even after being judicially established by judgment or decree, any privity of estate, or right of entry thereunder, but is in the nature of a legal charge, running with the land, encumbering it in every change of ownership, and preventing subsequent alienations or encumbrances only by making them subordinate to the rights of the lien holder."12 

While it is generally said that mechanics liens are purely a creature of statute, the term "statute" is often employed in that broad and comprehensive sense which includes alike the organic law (the Constitution of a state) and the statutes enacted under it. In some states the Constitution creates the lien and the Legislature is left to provide only for its enforcement.13 In the majority of jurisdictions, however, it is conceded that the Legislature has the power to enact laws creating the lien as well as enforcing it, without specific constitutional authority. In a few jurisdictions, as in Ohio, the Constitution, while it does not itself create the lien, empowers the Legislature to enact appropriate legislation to do so and to provide remedies for its enforcement.

In construing this section it was held that though the legislature could provide by statute for liens in addition to those provided for by the Constitution, it could not impair or detract from the rights to liens which the quoted provision of the Constitution confers. Huttig Sash &

(B) Purpose

While there is no analogy in form, the purpose or object of the laws creating mechanics liens is to secure to laborers and materialmen the same protection, (by way of a lien on the building and the land upon which it is erected, or from which it is removed) as was secured by the common law to artisans upon chattels manufactured or repaired in their workshops. 

The labor of the workman and the material of the materialman having contributed to the erection or removal of the structure; having, indeed, created, in part, or enhanced the value of, the very property on which the lien is sought to be attached, the purpose of the law is to give to such parties the right, where the contractor refuses to pay, to be paid for their labor and material out of the fund which has been earned under the contract, and out of the structure, and the land upon which it stands.14

It was to secure to the laborer his hire or reward for the construction or repair which he had made. The means devised was, to permit him who had, by labor, skill, or material, contributed to constitute a permanent object of value, to hold proprietorship pro tanto therein, until paid the price thereof according to contract, if under contract, or otherwise according to the just value of such contribution. 15

It is not the contract for erecting or repairing the building which creates the lien, but it is the use of the materials furnished and labor expended by the contrac- 

14. Bullock vs Horn, 44 Oh. 

St. 420. 

15. Thomas vs Huesman, 10 

Oh. St. 153.

Sec.  tor, whereby the building becomes a part of the freehold, that gives the materialman and laborer his lien under the statute.16

It was never intended that the mechanics lien laws should protect persons who become possessed of claims in tort against the contractor, or who occupy the position of ordinary contract creditors, no matter how meritorious the claims of the latter may be, and no matter how much they may have contributed to the improvement. These must look only to the personal responsibility of their debtor for payment. They have no right to a lien.17 

Upon this principle, one, who furnishes money to a contractor to pay the workmen employed by him, has only a personal claim against the contractor. He is not any sense a subcontractor and is therefore not entitled to a lien.18 in 

(C) Origin 

Although the legislature of the state of Pennsylvania had in 1784 passed a law for the protection of persons engaged in building or repairing vessels, the state of Maryland is said to have been the first to enact a law granting mechanics and materialmen a lien on the land and the buildings erected thereon as security for the payment of their claims for labor performed and material used in connection with the construction of the buildings. 

It is related that in 1791, Thomas Jefferson, James Madiand others addressed the legislature of Maryland as follows:

Sec. Historical Review 

"Your memorialists conceive it would encourage master builders to contract for the erection and furnishing of houses for certain prices agreed upon if a lien was created by law for their just claims on the house erected and on the lot of land on which it stood."

In response to this suggestion the legislature of Maryland on December 9, 1791, passed an act creating such a lien. It was undoubtedly the purpose of these gentlemen to promote and encourage the building of dwellings in the new city of Washington, to which the seat of government of the United States was soon to be removed. 

The next lien law to be enacted was passed by the legislature of Pennsylvania in 1803. "These statutes, while they contained the germ of all subsequent legislation on the subject, are imperfect and meagre in comparison with the state of the law at the present time. The whole subject has been one of gradual growth, extending from imperfect and limited enactments, embarrassed by adverse decisions, to be the settled policy of all the States, and of unquestioned importance. The experiment was at first confined to towns and cities, but has by degrees, as its necessity and justice became apparent, extended itself in a majority of the States to the agricultural districts. The lien was designed in its inception, for the most part, to secure only the principal contractor, until the frauds perpetrated upon subcontractors and workmen gave rise to amendments for their proper protection. It attached in some of the States only when the party making the contract was the owner of the legal title in fee simple. It is now generally provided, that, however small may be the interest of the contracting

Sec. 

10 

 party, the lien fastens itself to that extent, and whether the title be legal or equitable. Formerly it applied by some statutes only to cases of original construction. It is now almost universally applicable to repairs. It was con. fined in some localities to the building of dwelling houses. 

At present, where the pursuits or industries of the particular section of the country render it of sufficient importance, it attaches to bridges, canals, flumes, machinery, fixtures, etc. Distinctions were sometimes made between labor performed and materials furnished. They are now universally deemed equally meritorious. And where statutes failed by express terms to subject the land to the lien, as well as the building, the courts have by judicial interpretation remedied the defect. In the matter of remedy there have been no less valuable improvements."19 

As it is not the purpose of this book to discuss the lien laws in other states than Ohio, enough has been said to point out the gradual growth and expansion of the earlier laws into the modern mechanics lien laws of today.

Sec. 4. History of the Mechanics Lien Laws of 

Ohio.

I. The first mechanics lien law in Ohio became effective January 21, 1823. (21 Ohio Laws, 8).

The first section thereof provided: "That on any house, boat, vessel, or other water craft, building or buildings, erected or constructed after the taking effect of this act, within the limits of the corporation of the city of Cincinnati, the mechanics, laborers and furnishers, for the value of their labor, 19. Phillips on Mechanics Liens, Sec. 7.

Sec. 4

Historical Review skill, and materials, jointly or severally, therefor, on contract with the owner or owners, of any of the before named buildings, done, furnished, or pro- Ivided shall have and hold a lien." 

It will be noted that this act was a local law only, as it was limited in its operation to the city of Cincinnati alone. It apparently was intended to relate to original construction only, as it made no reference to labor performed or materials furnished for the alteration or repair of a house, vessel or other building or water craft. Nor did it specifically create a lien upon the land on which the building stood.

In order to obtain the lien, the claimant was required to make a statement in writing, under oath, containing a description of the property and the items and value of labor and material. This statement had to be filed with the recorder of Hamilton County, within two months after the labor was done or the material furnished. 

This operated "as a lien on the several descriptions of buildings, in the first section of this act above named," for the period of two years from the commencement of the labor or the furnishing of materials. It further provided that the lien holder might proceed to obtain a judgment for the amount due and that the lien would continue until such suit was finally determined and the judgment satisfied. If, for any reason, the owner should suspend the progress or completion of the work, the laborers or materialmen could, at their own expense, inclose the building to prevent waste, provided they adhered to the same plan intended by the owners. If the owner did not have the legal title to the premises, provision was made for renting the property until the net proceeds derived

Sec. 

12 

 from such income would discharge the liens thereon. 

II. By an act, effective February 5, 1833, (31 Ohio

Laws, 88) the provisions of the act of 1823 were extended so as to include the township of Fulton in Hamilton County. By another act, effective March 12, 1840, (38 Ohio Laws, 115) the law of 1823 was again amended so as to include the counties of Washington, Montgomery, Scioto, Muskingum and Knox. It was further amended so as to include work done or materials furnished "for all repairs, additions or improvements" on the buildings, vessels or water craft mentioned in Section I of the act of 1823. The time for filing the lien was extended from two to four months. 

III. On March 11, 1843, the first general mechanics lien law was passed. (41 Ohio Laws, 66). In place of the former local laws, which were by this act repealed, a new and revised law was passed which embraced in its operation the entire state. Although the act was loosely drawn20 and incomplete in many respects, it was nevertheless the first real effort to embody in one act all the rights and remedies, which, in the combined experience of other states having mechanics lien laws, seemed most practical and effective in securing the mechanic and the materialman the payment of their just claims. 

As such, then, it is deserving of more than passing notice.

The first section provided: 

"That any person who shall perform labor, or furnish 

20. "The act is so loosely drawn as to be open to constructions very different, or, indeed, quite opposite."

Choteau et al vs Thompson and Campbell, 2 Oh. St. 114.

Sec. 4

Historical Review materials, or machinery, for constructing, altering, or repairing any boat, vessel, or other water craft, or for erecting or repairing any house, mill, manufactory, or other building, or appurtenance, by virtue of a contract or agreement with the owner thereof, shall have a lien, to secure the payment of the same, upon such boat, vessel, or other water craft, and upon such house, mill, manufactory, or other building, or appurtenance, and the lot of land upon which the same shall stand."

It will be noted that the type of construction upon which a lien might be obtained was extended so as to include "mill, manufactory, or other building or appurtenance" and also that for the first time the statute specifically creates the lien upon "the lot of land upon which the same shall stand."

The second section of the act creates for the first time the "attested account." Provision is made so that a laborer, subcontractor or materialman furnishing work or materials to the principal contractor may, by filing an attested account with the owner, tie up in his hands the remaining funds due the contractor. The marginal notes to the act call such subcontractors "middlemen."

IV. By an act passed March 25, 1851 (49 Ohio 

Laws, 108), a person holding a lien was given, in addition to the remedy of an action at law, provided for in the act of 1843, the right to proceed in chancery against the owner "as in other cases of liens." Thus was the remedy of foreclosure established.

V. By the act of March 12, 1853 (51 Ohio Laws, 

417) the amendment of section seven of the act of 1843 consisted in the change of the words "items," "materials"

Sec. 14 

 and "descriptions," as used in the original section, into the words "item," "material," and "description." The limitation for the continuation of the lien was also changed from two years after the "commencement" of the labor or furnishing of materials to two years after the "completion" of such labor or the furnishing of materials. There was evidently some doubt as to the exact amount of details required in making up the account by reason of the use of the plural in the words "items," "materials," and "descriptions." To remove this doubt the singular was substituted. It was therefore held that, where a mechanic undertakes and completes a building as an entire job and for an entire price, he need not in the account filed with the recorder, make a detailed statement of his labor and materials, but that he might express the same in a single item.21 

VI. By the act of May 1, 1871, (68 Ohio Laws, 107), section two of the act of 1843 was considerably altered. This was the section which provided for the filing of an attested account by the "middleman" with the owner. By the amendment of 1871, the right of the "middleman" was extended so as to apply to many other types of construction or improvements than those upon which the original contractor might have a lien. It included "any house, mill, distillery, bridge, manufactory, fixture, road, turnpike, street, sewer, ditch, railroad or other structure," and protected the "middleman" whether such work was done "as journeyman, laborer, carman, subcontractor or otherwise." The act further provided that if the owner, after the receipt by him of the me- 

21. Thomas vs Huesman, 10 Oh. St. 153.

Sec. 4

Historical Review chanic's attested account, made any payments to the contractor without reserving enough to pay the mechanic, the latter would have a lien, as of the date of the filing of the attested account for the amount of his labor or material, not exceeding the amount of such payments, upon the structure and the lot of land upon which it stood. 

Public property was expressly excluded. The lien of the principal contractor was postponed to that of the "middleman." Any assignment by the contractor of his contract or of the claims arising thereunder was subject to the rights of the "middleman." In the event more than one attested account was filed, and the funds applicable thereto were not sufficient to pay all in full, the lien claimants shared pro rata. The words "lot of land" were defined "to mean the estate of such owner therein," and the word "materials" was held to include "any material, apparatus and machinery."

VII. By the act of March 30, 1875, (72 Ohio Laws, 

166) Section I of the act of 1843 was amended so as to extend the right of a lien to include work done or materials furnished "for constructing, altering, or repairing any boat, vessel or other water craft, or for erecting, repairing, removing, raising or lowering any house, mill, manufactory, or other building or appurtenance, or any portion thereof." It covered not only the land on which the structure stood but also that to which it might be removed. By the same act, section I of the amendatory act of 1871 was likewise changed with reference to the character of work done in connection with the types of structure or improvements enumerated therein. 

VIII. On May 4, 1877 (74 Ohio Laws, 168) an act

Sec. 

16 

 entitled, "For the better security of head contractors, subcontractors and materialmen," was passed. The purpose of this act was to completely revise and recodify the entire law relating to mechanics liens and attested accounts. 

By virtue of the fact that the legislature had on March 31, 1874, (71 Ohio Laws, 51) passed an act "to secure pay to persons performing labor or furnishing materials in constructing railroads," the act of 1877 omitted any reference to that class of construction. Henceforth liens upon railroads were created by special legislation upon that subject. Reference to this type of lien will be made in a subsequent chapter.22 As the law of 1877 was intended to take the place of all previous legislation upon the subject of mechanics liens, with the exception as to railroads, the act of 1843 and the amendatory acts of 1871 and 1875 were expressly repealed. While subsequent amendments changed in many ways the act of 1877, nevertheless that act became the nucleus of the law as it exists today. 

IX. On March 13, 1878, (75 Ohio Laws, 48) Sec tion II of the act of 1877 was amended so as to extend the lien from one to two years after the filing of the attested account. No homestead or other exemption as against any lien under the provisions of this law was permitted. 

X. On May 11, 1878, (75 Ohio Laws, 514) section X of the act of 1877 was amended, so as to permit the owner to request the lien claimant to file suit thereon, in default of which, after sixty days, the lien became void. 

22. See "Mechanics Liens upon Railroads", Part IV.

Sec. 4

Historical Review 

XI. By the act of March 22, 1881, (78 Ohio Laws, 78) the additional remedy, the right to proceed in chancery, was extended so as to apply to the lot of land on which the building stood "or to which it may be removed." 

XII. On April 18, 1883, (80 Ohio Laws, 183) an act was passed creating a lien in favor of laborers, employees, and operatives upon the the real property of their employers. As this is a different type of lien than that of the mechanic and materialman, special reference to it will be made in a subsequent chapter.23 

XIII. By the act of January 26, 1887, (84 Ohio

Laws, 6) the type of construction upon which a mechanic or materialman might have a lien was extended so as to include "the digging, drilling, or boring of any gas well, oil well, or any other well." 

XIV. On March 5, 1887 (84 Ohio Laws, 46) a general revision of the law of 1877 was made. Fourteen sections were amended. The lien of the contractor was extended from one year to two years after the date of the filing of the affidavit for a lien. The claimant was obliged to describe in his affidavit for a lien "any promissory note or notes given for such labor, machinery, or material, or any part thereof, with all credits or offsets thereon." The provisions relating to attested accounts were considerably amplified. 

XV. By the act of March 27, 1889 (86 Ohio Laws, 

143) section I of the law of 1877, as amended by the law of January 26, 1887, was supplemented by the addi-

 tion of a new section. By this act a lien was created in favor of persons performing manual labor in mining coal or removing it from the mines or other work connected therewith. The lien covered all real and personal property of the owner thereof. 

XVI. On April 15, 1889 (86 Ohio Laws, 372) Sec tion I of the law of 1877, as amended by the act of January 26, 1887, was again amended so as to include "any furnace or furnace material" among the types of construction upon which a lien might be had. It was also extended to machinery furnished. Supplementary sections were also added. A penal statute was included for the purpose of punishing a contractor or subcontractor who misrepresented the purpose for which materials, purchased by him on credit, were to be used. A method of perfecting a lien on contiguous lots was provided. The lien was extended from two to six years. The word "owner" was amplified.

XVII. By the act of April 18, 1892 (89 Ohio Laws, 

373) the lien was made to apply to "the interest, leasehold or otherwise, of the owner" XVIII. Up to this time the right to a direct lien upon the interest of the owner was created only in favor of those persons who had performed labor or furnished materials under or by virtue of a contract with the owner or his authorized agent. By the act of April 13, 1894, (91 

Ohio Laws, 135) an attempt was made, for the first time, to create a lien in favor of any person, who had performed labor or furnished materials in the construction of an improvement upon the land of the owner, whether he had a contract with the owner or not. By the

Sec. 4

Historical Review amendment of 1894, a lien was created in favor of any person who had performed labor or furnished materials upon the land of the owner "by virtue of a contract with, or at the instance of the owner thereof or his agent, trustee, contractor or subcontractor." This was a great departure in principle from the previous laws and gave immediate rise to questions involving its constitutionality.24

XIX. After the Supreme Court of Ohio, in the case of Palmer and Crawford vs. Tingle, 55 Oh. St. 423, had decided on December 8, 1896, that the act of April 13, 1894, was unconstitutional and void in so far as it created a lien in favor of mechanics, materialmen and subcontractors having no contract with the owner or his authorized agent, the bench and bar of the state were in a quandary as to just how much of the previous law had been made void by this decision.

XX. An attempt was made therefore to remove the confusion. On April 18, 1902, (95 Ohio Laws, 209) an act was passed which provided for a new and different method by which the subcontractor could obtain a lien. 

The law was loosely drawn and failed utterly in its purpose. Like its predecessor it, too, was declared unconstitutional,25

XXI. By the act of October 17, 1902 (96 Ohio 

Laws, 7) the section of the act of April 18, 1902, relating to the statement filed with the recorder for the purpose of notifying fellow subcontractors, mechanics and others, was amended.

Sec. 20 

XXII. On account of the confusion caused by the acts of 1894 and 1902, all thought of creating a lien in favor of persons, not under contract with the owner, was abandoned, except in the form of the attested account. 

Accordingly, therefore, an act was passed on April 20, 1904, (97 Ohio Laws, 499) repealing some and amending others of the objectionable features of these two acts. 

In a general way, the lien law was reenacted substantially in the form it had existed prior to these acts. 

XXIII. On May 10, 1910, (101 Ohio Laws, 229) the section relating to the furnishing of a sworn statement by the mechanic or materialman to the owner of the amount of labor performed or to be performed and material furnished or to be furnished was amended. Proof that such statement was mailed by registered letter was to be taken as prima facie evidence of the filing thereof. 

XXIV. Such then is the history of the mechanics lien laws in Ohio, from their inception in the first local law in 1823 down to the amendment to the Constitution of Ohio, adopted September 12, 1912. Following this amendment the whole law was again revised and many new provisions were enacted. These will be discussed in a subsequent chapter.

Sec. 5. Constitutionality of the Mechanics Lien 

Law.

It has been seen from the brief history of mechanics lien legislation in Ohio up to the year 1912 that the lien was entirely a creature of statute. Neither the Ordinance of 1787, the Constitution of 1802, nor the Constitution of 1851, contained any provisions specifically authorizing

Sec. 5

Historical Review such legislation. It was generally conceded, both in Ohio and elsewhere, that laws creating liens in favor of mechanics and materialmen did not violate any of the rights or privileges guaranteed by the Constitution. Indeed, until the law of 1894 was passed, no question was ever raised in any court in Ohio, regarding the constitutionality of such legislation. 

Prior to the law of 1894, only those persons, who performed labor or furnished material under or by vir tue of a contract with the owner or his authorized agent, were entitled to a lien upon the real property of the owner upon which the improvement stood. By the act of 

1894, the right to the lien was extended so as to include all persons, who performed labor or furnished materials by virtue of a contract with or at the instance of the owner or his agent, trustee, contractor, or subcontractor. 

Instead of subrogating the lien, for labor and material furnished the contractor, to the contractor's rights under his contract with the owner and the state of account existing under it, the act of 1894 gave a direct lien upon the real estate of the owner as an incident to the power of the contractor or subcontractor, as the owner's agent, to bind him.

Immediately, the constitutionality of this act of 1894 was questioned. It was urged that the act undertook to appropriate property of the owner for the benefit of a person with whom he had made no contract; that the owner may have had no notice of the claim until after he had paid the original contractor in full, with the result that he might have to pay again what he had already paid; that it discriminated in favor of a special class of creditors; that it placed upon the owner of real estate a

Sec. 22 

 burden that was not borne by the owner of any other class of property; and that it violated section I of the 

Bill of Rights which guaranteed the right to freedom of contract and protection of property.

On the other hand it was urged that since the owner was presumed to know the law, he should be considered as having entered into his contract with full knowledge of his obligations to those performing labor or furnishing materials at the instance of his contractor or of any subcontractor; that the owner had ample means of protecting himself, either by taking an indemnity bond from the contractor, or by paying the subcontractors, laborers, and materialmen himself; that he might stipulate with the contractor to defer payment until the time was passed for the filing of liens. 

With the opinions of the bench and bar so hopelessly divided it was inevitable that the question would soon be presented to the courts. In January, 1895, the case of 

The Van Cleve Glass Co. vs. Wamelink 26 was decided by the court of Common Pleas of Cuyahoga County. It was argued that the law of 1894 violated the clause of the Constitution of the United States prohibiting the taking of private property without due process of law. The court held that, "however obnoxious the law may be to the rights of property owners, its operation cannot be defeated under the claim of constitutional power to pass it." The next case was that of Palmer and Crawford vs. 

Tingle,27 decided by the Circuit Court of Putnam County. 

It was there held that the law violated Section I of Arti cle I and Section II of Article I of the Bill of Rights and 

26. 1 Nisi Prius 203. 

27. 9 C. C. 708.

Sec. 5

Historical Review was therefore unconstitutional and void. In the following year, the question was again presented this time to the Circuit Court of Cuyahoga County.28 It was argued, as in the Putnam County case, that the law violated the Bill of Rights; that it deprived the owner of the right to own, possess, enjoy and contract in regard to his property as guaranteed to him by the highest law of the state. Without so much as mentioning the Putnam County case the court arrived at the opposite conclusion. It declared the law constitutional. "Where the owner knows all these things, and knows that there is a wise and remedial purpose in the statute, he cannot lawfully claim the same is unconstitutional, because it works to him nothing more serious than inconvenience, unless he has failed to protect himself as he may do by law."

Such was the status of the question in the lower courts. On December 8, 1896, the case of Palmer & 

Crawford vs. Tingle29 was reviewed and decided by the

Supreme Court. In the language of the fourth syllabus of the case, it was held that, "the act of April 13, 1894, in so far as it gives a lien on the property of the owner to subcontractors, laborers, and those who furnished machinery, material or tile to the contractor, is unconstitutional and void." A similar conclusion had already been reached by the Courts of Michigan,30 and of Pennsylvania.31

But the controversy was far from settled by this adjudication. Immediately the question arose as to the ef

Sec. 6. The Constitutional Amendment of 1912. 

"Laws may be passed to secure to mechanics, artisans, laborers, subcontractors and materialmen, their just dues by direct lien upon the property, upon which they have bestowed labor or for which they have furnished material. No other provision of the constitution shall impair or limit the power.' 99 The above amendment to the Ohio Constitution of

The language of the amendment is, of course, broad enough to include improvements to personal property. 

However, if such an application be given that amendment, it is perfectly apparent that it can have no operation upon the issues of the present controversy, because the amendment is not self-executing and by its terms provides only that "laws may be passed". In the absence of any legislation pursuant to that amendment the situation remains exactly as it was before the amendment. If any force and effect were to be given that amendment, in the absence of legislation pursuant thereto, it would be more reasonable to say that mechanics, artisans, and other laborers could have no lien upon personal property until legislation were enacted. The obvious purpose of this amendment was to remove all possibility of doubt as to the power of the Legislature to enact laws providing for the protection of mechanics and materialmen. For the first time, in the history of mechanics lien legislation in Ohio, express permission is granted by the Constitution to the Legislature to pass such laws as in its judgment will most effectively obtain the results desired. Henceforth the Legislature has unlimited power to legislate upon the subject of mechanics liens. "It may pass any kind of bill that it chooses and the same will not be unconstitutional. There is no room for it to be unconstitutional. Courts have only to ascertain what the enactment says and the same becomes clear at once."41

So long as such laws do not violate any of the provisions of the Constitution of the United States, the right of the Legislature to enact laws relating to the subject of mechanics liens as absolute.

42. "In undertaking to give to a subcontractor a lien for his labor, two different theories or systems have been adopted in the statutes of the different states. By one system, sometimes known as the 'New York' system, a subcontractor is given a lien by way of 'subrogation', as it is expressed, to the rights of the contractor, that is, he stands in the place of the contractor, and cannot claim a lien for a sum greater than that due to the contractor at such time as the subcontractor may give notice of his claim to the owner, who is thus enabled to withhold from the principal contractor sufficient to satisfy the claim of the subcontractor. 

Under the other system, sometimes termed the 'Pennsylvania' system, the subcontractor is given a direct lien, without reference to the rights of the contractor, and consequently the owner ordinarily acts at his peril if he makes any payments to the contractor, unless he has first satisfied himself that the subcontractor's claims are paid. 

So, while under the New York system the subcontractor has no lien if the contractor's default in his contract leaves nothing owing the latter, such default does not, under the Pennsylvania system, affect the subcontractor's lien for the full amount of his claim. But even where the latter system prevails, the subcontractor's right to a lien arises from the original contract between the owner and the contractor, and he cannot claim for work not authorized by such contract, nor demand payment in a mode other than that named therein."

Sec. 12. Extra-territorial Effect As a broad proposition it may be stated that the general rules of statutory construction are applicable to the statutes upon the subject of mechanics liens. For the purpose of ascertaining their meaning and application, courts will not only consider their language and arrangement, but also the intention of the legislature, the object or purpose of the laws,1 the circumstances surrounding their passage, and to a certain extent the construction put upon similar laws by the courts of other jurisdictions. 

But construction and interpretation have no place or office where the language of a statute is unambiguous and its meaning clear.2 

1. "The mischief which the statute was designed to remedy is an important guide in ascertaining its meaning."

National Fire Proofing Co. vs 

Town of Huntington, 81 Conn. 632. 

2. "It is only when the terms of the statute are ambiguous and their significance is uncertain that the rule of liberal construction has any function. * * * 

They (the courts) may not assume or presume purposes and

Sec. 

32 

All statutes are presumed to be enacted by the legislature with full knowledge of the existing conditions of the law, and with reference to it. Where two statutes are in apparent conflict, they should be so construed, if reasonably possible, as to allow both to stand and to give force and effect to each.2a If it is not possible to reconcile inconsistent statutes, the dates of their enactment will intentions that the terms of the statute do not indicate, and then enact or expunge provisions to accomplish these supposed in tentions. ✶✶✶ There is a con clusive presumption that the legislative body intended what it declared; the statute must be held to mean what it clearly expresses, and no room is left for construction." 

Brun vs Mann, 151 Fed. 145. 

In Ohio Savings & Trust Company vs Schneider, 25 Oh. App. 

259, 262, the court said: "A careful reading of the governing statute, just referred to, enumerates and sets forth the particular items or things upon which a mechanics lien may be predicated; and rental of machinery, or anything of that nature or kind, does not appear, and is not contained therein. It occurs to us that, if the Legislature had intended that such rental as is here sought was to be made the subject of a lien, it would have so stated in the law. Courts must not read into a statute that which does not appear therein. It is presumed that the lawmakers placed in the statute all that was intended. If not, the remedy is lodged in the Legislature to change by amendment or otherwise. It is not within the province of our courts to change or modify. "It is the duty of courts in their interpretation and construction of statutes to give effect to the intent of the lawmaking power, and to seek for that intent in every legitimate way. If the words and sentences used are free from ambiguity and doubt, and express the clear purpose and intent of the framers of the law, there is no occasion to resort to other means of interpretation.

Sec. 9. Liberal and Strict Construction. 

In an early case in Ohio, the Supreme Court said: "Looking thus at the object of the statute, and perceiving it to be one of an equitable character and beneficent tendency, section seven (of the act of 1843 as amended 1853) being directory of the mode of securing the object of the statute, the same ought to be liberally construed, for the furtherance and attainment of such object."6

In a later case, the court, in denying the owner the right of set-off, as against a mechanics lien properly acquired, a claim against the contractor not growing out of the contract, said: "The statute is highly remedial in its character, and should receive such liberal construction as will pose that the Ohio Legislature, in adopting such provision of the Michigan act, did so in view of the construction which had been put upon it, and with the intention that it should receive the same construction as had been given it by the Michigan Courts."

But with the increase of judicial decisions in many states on the subject of the construction of lien laws, there was developed a new principle. Some courts felt that a distinction should be drawn between the construction of the law as it affected the creation of the lien and its construction insofar as it affected the enforcement of the lien. It was held by some that, since these laws are in derogation of the common law and derive their sole existence from the statute, the provisions of the law which relate to the creation of the lien should be strictly construed, while at the same time they held that, once a lien

 Sec. 10. The Statutory Rule of Construction. 

With such confusion on the part of the courts, with reference to the rules of statutory construction as applied to the mechanics lien laws, it was but natural that the legislature would undertake, by statutory enactment, to declare a rule of construction, which would be binding on all the courts. If for no other reason than in the interests of uniformity of judicial construction, it was a wise measure. Accordingly in the law of 1913, provision was made to this effect: "This act is hereby declared to be a remedial statute and to be construed liberally to secure the beneficial results, intents, and purposes thereof; and a substantial compliance with its several provisions shall be sufficient for the validity of the lien or liens hereinbefore provided for and to give jurisdiction to the court to enforce the same."14

It will be readily seen that the former and somewhat the courts as remedial in their nature, and are liberally construed, and the rule is that if anything is named by the statute as a condition precedent to the obtaining of the lien, such as furnishing the material under the contract and with the owner, that that must be complied with; but that, in taking the steps to perfect the lien upon the record, no error will be regarded as defeating the lien, unless it is such as is prejudicial to the owner. If such a mistake should be made and innocent parties should obtain an interest in the property, or a lien upon the same, without actual knowledge, questions of a different nature would arise, which it is not necessary to consider in this action." Lapham vs Spink, 24 C.C. (N.S.) 348.

Code. 

A similar statute in Michigan has been considered as applicable only to the provisions of the law with respect to the remedies and pleadings and not to the question as to whether a lien may be acquired at all.

157 Mich. 544.

Construction of the Law doubtful distinction between the rule as applied to the creation of the lien and the rule as applied to its enforcement has to a certain degree, been done away with. 

Henceforth, the courts must construe with equal fairness and liberality the provisions of the act which relate to the creation or acquisition of the lien, as well as the rights and remedies that are derived thereunder.15 

It must be borne in mind, however, that courts can only declare the law; they cannot make it; and therefore under the guise of "liberal construction" they cannot extend the statute to meet cases for which the statute itself does not provide,16 though these may be of equal merit with those provided for.17 On the other hand it is equally true that courts should not by technical adherence to the letter of the law emasculate the statutes by a narrow restricted construction of their beneficent provisions.18

Sec. 11. Effect of Amendment or Repeal of Law. 

Section 25 of the General Code of Ohio provides: 

The statute provides the procedure to be followed in order to come within the provisions of the law, and if one of that class furnishes material which is actually used in the construction of a building, and subsequently complies with the provisions of the law relative to the procedure necessary to establish a lien, he should not be devested of his right by reason of his failure to state with precision the party to whom the material was furnished. This is particulary true where it is not made to appear that the party against whose property the lien is claimed has been injured by reason of any such technical defect. The essential fact to be set out in the lien statement is that certain materials were furnished which were actually used in the construction of the building on certain described premises. The purpose of naming the contractor in such statement is apparently to apprise the owner under what authority the material was furnished, and thereby afford him protection as to payments to be made to the contractor; and unless the owner has been misled to his injury by reason of the erroneous designation of the parties by whom the materials were furnished, such a defect is not fatal." 

Eberle vs Drennan, 40 Okla. 

59, 51 L.R.A. (N.S.) 68. 

23. Guest vs Shamburger 120 

Okla. 164.

Sec. 11 Construction of the Law 

"Whenever a law is repealed which repealed a former law, the former law shall not thereby be revived."

Section 26 of the General Code of Ohio provides: 

“Whenever a statute is repealed or amended, such repeal or amendment shall in no manner affect pending actions, prosecutions, or proceedings, civil or criminal, and when the repeal or amendment relates to the remedy, it shall not affect pending actions, prosecution, or proceedings, unless so expressed, nor shall any repeal or amendment affect causes of such action, prosecution, or proceeding, existing at the time of such amendment or repeal, unless otherwise expressly provided in the amending or repealing act.' "24

In so far as the provisions of the Mechanics Lien Law of 1913 are concerned there is no room for doubt as to its effect upon contracts or proceedings entered into before its enactment, as it is expressly provided by Section 8323-10 of said law that: "This act shall not be construed to apply to contracts made or entered into at any time before this act shall take effect.” 

In view of the fact, however, that subsequent amendments to the lien law may give rise to some questions relating to the effect of amendments or repeals, a brief review of the general principles involved may not be amiss. By Article II, Section 28, of the Constitution of 

Ohio, "The general assembly shall have no power to pass retroactive laws, or laws impairing the obligations of contracts" ***. It becomes necessary at the outset, therefore, to determine whether the Mechanics Lien Law 

24. See also G. C. 13766 and 13767.

On this point the Supreme Court of Ohio has said: "By the great weight of authority statutes that relate to liens of mechanics and materialmen are remedial; instead of creating new and substantive rights, they simply afford new and cumulative remedies to enforce obligations previously recognized."25

While it is true that the legislature cannot create a liability for acts as to which there was no liability when they were committed 26 or destroy, by amendment or repeal of the statute by which it was obtained, a mechanics lien once vested,27 it is perfectly clear that if a liability exists, the form of the remedy may be changed or the

Construction of the Law existing provisions supplemented by other legislative enactments. "The rule is well settled by repeated adjudications that no one has a vested interest in any particular remedy for the enforcement of a right. The remedies which one legislature may have prescribed a subsequent legislature may modify provided a substantial and adequate remedy is left."28 In enforcing the rights under 

28. State vs Barlow, 70 Oh.

This is upon the ground that remedies which are available for the enforcement of the contract at the time and place where it is made are a part of its obligation, and that to allow the remedy to be taken away, or materially restricted, would, to that extent, impair the obligation of the contract. Whatever belongs merely to the remedy may be altered accordingly to the will of the statute, provided the alteration does not impair the obligation of the contract. Laws changing remedies for the enforcement of legal contracts, or abolishing one remedy where two or more existed, may be perfectly valid, even though the new and remaining remedy be less convenient than that which was abolished, or less prompt and speedy. It follows, therefore, that in so far as a right to a mechanics lien in a given case is concerned, we must look only to the statute in force when the material or machinery is furnished or the labor is done; and also that, in so far as there may be an attempt by legislation to take away or materially impair the remedy for the enforcement of such lien, neither leaving nor substituting an efficient remedy we must look to the same source. 

Subject to this exception, the rule has been laid down, we think, correctly, that the rights of parties under mechanics lien laws are to be ascertained and fixed by the law in force when the contract is made; but such rights are to be established and enforced by the law existing at the bringing of the suit." 

Goodbub vs Hornung's Estate, 127 Ind. 181.

Construction of the Law 

Statutes of limitations pertaining to the remedy and not to the essence of the contract, and enactments prescribing the time for filing statements or notices, provided they be not so unreasonable as to amount to a deprivation of the right within which a lien shall be enforced, are proper subjects for amendment and will be enforced at the time the remedy is asserted notwithstanding they may have not been in existence at the time the right to the lien arose.30

In the case of Smith vs The 

New York Central Rd. Company, 122 Oh. St. 45, the court said: "Except where constitutional provisions expressly forbid, the

Legislature has power to make, amend, and repeal laws relating to the remedy, and make the same applicable, not only to existing causes of action, in which suits have not been instituted, but even in pending suits. 

Section 28 of Article II of the 

Ohio Constitution denies to the 

General Assembly the power to pass retroactive laws. It has, however, been decided in numerous cases that retroactive laws refer to those which create and define substantive rights, and which either give rise to, or take away, the right to sue or to defend actions at law. It has been further declared at numerous times that a statute which is remedial in its operation on rights, obligations, duties, and interests already existing is not within the mischiefs against which that clause of the Constitution was intended to safeguard, and the remedial statutes do not even come within a just construction of its terms. Rairden vs Holden, Admr., 15 Ohio 

St., 207; Templeton vs Kraner, 24 Ohio St., 554. Under these well-settled rules of interpretation, there is no constitutional inhibition in the State of Ohio against the enactment of laws relating to the remedy and against making them applicable to pending actions and existing causes of action.'

The answer is that the mere enlargement of the time in which to commence the action, at least in a case where the time had not yet arrived in which to file any statement of the plaintiff's claim for a lien, does not affect any right or remedy provided for in the old act. The remedy consisted of the taking of certain proceedings by which this sale was to be accomplished.

Sec. 12. Extra-Territorial Effect. 

It is fundamental that the laws of Ohio have, ipso proprio vigore, no extra-territorial force. So far as their effect is concerned, every other state must be regarded as a separate sovereignty to the same extent as though it is not repealed by implication by the Mechanics Lien Law of 1913, Sections 8310 et seq. of the 

G. C. 

32. 36 Cyc. "Statutes", 1151. 

This principal may be most suitably applied in construing conflicts between mechanics lien laws and the so called "Torrens 

Law", particularly with reference to the manner of obtaining a lien. In the case of Mizner vs 

Paul, 29 O. C. A. 33, where registered land was involved, a mechanic having a valid claim under the mechanics lien law, had complied with such law in all respects, but had failed to file a caveat or notice of his right to claim a lien or to have a memorial of same inscribed on the certificate of title, as required by the "Torrens Law". In denying the validity of the lien on the registered land, the court decided, that the mechanics lien law and the "Torrens Law" are not incompatible; but the privilege granted by the former of acquiring liens is restricted in its exercise by the law. The "Torrens

Law" was therefore given effect

Construction of the Law were a foreign nation. The laws of Ohio can bind only its own subjects, and others who may be within its jurisdictional limits. The rights and privileges accorded to mechanics and materialmen under the laws of Ohio cannot be imposed upon the property or persons of others beyond its borders. 

On the other hand one who, in another state, sells and delivers to a principal contractor, materials to be transported by the latter to this state and used by him here in constructing a public improvement, is entitled to the same rights under the mechanics lien laws of Ohio, that one may assert who sells and delivers, within this state, materials to be thus used. To apply to such a transaction the mechanics lien laws of Ohio, is not giving to them an extra-territorial operation. "Remedial laws *** do not operate extra-territorially, on account of being applied by the courts of the state in which they are in force, to actions pending in such courts on contracts made and to be performed in another state or country. Remedies will be administered according to the law of the place where the action is instituted, without regard to the law of the place where the right arose."33 as an exception to the mechanics lien law.

Sec. 15

Sec. 14. The Statute Abridged. 

Reduced to its lowest terms, the statute provides that every person who does work or furnishes machinery, material, or fuel, for constructing or altering certain structures or improvements, by virtue of a contract, express or implied, with the owner of any interest in real estate, or his authorized agent, and every subcontractor, laborer, or materialman furnishing labor or material or fuel, to each original contractor or any subcontractor, in carrying forward such contract, shall have a lien. 

Sec. 15. In General. 

Generally speaking, whoever is competent to make the contract, which is the basis of the lien, has capacity to acquire the lien.¹ But inasmuch as the right to acquire a lien is limited only to those who come within the class or classes of persons which the statute expressly designates as entitled to the benefits thereof, the statutory designations, coupled with the judicial interpretations of such designations, must, at the outset, be consulted to determine what persons may acquire a lien thereunder.1a 

1. 40 C. J. "Mechanics Liens" 

-17. la. "It is well settled, however, that while this statute is to be liberally construed in reference to the property to which the lien attaches, only those persons enumerated and embraced in the statute are to be held entitled to the lien, and that no persons are to be included under its provisions unless they make it clearly appear that they are so entitled, without a strained construction of the statute." 

In re American Lime Co., 201 

Fed. 433.

Sec. 56 

An examination of the mechanics lien law of Ohio discloses that there are four main classes of persons entitled to a lien under the proper proceedings, namely, the contractor, the sub-contractor, the materialman, and the laborer. It becomes important, therefore, for an intelligent understanding of the law, and of its effect upon these classes of persons, to define these terms. 

Sec. 16. "Person" defined. "The word 'person' includes a corporation or partnership or two or more persons having a joint or common interest." G. C. 8323-9 

Sec. 17. "Laborer" defined. "The word 'laborer' shall be construed to include any mechanic, workman, artisan, or laborer employed in or about any such work, as hereinbefore specified." G. C. 8323-9 

It will be readily seen that the definition above is not complete in itself. It does not pretend to specify all persons who might fall within the meaning of the term "laborer", nor does it exclude others as not being within the meaning of the term. The door is left open, to a limited extent, for judicial construction as to what various persons may fall within this class of persons known as "laborer". In the popular acceptation of the term, "a laborer is one who labors with his physical powers, in the service of and under the direction of another, for fixed wages." He is associated with the idea of manual labor and toil as opposed to mental labor and skill. 

But it is plain that the statute does not intend to draw a distinction between skilled and unskilled labor. The

Sec. 17

 use of the terms "workman” and “artisan" in the statute clearly indicates an intention to include skilled labor as well as unskilled labor within the scope of the mechanics lien law. "Workman" is a general term. "It frequently applies to one who does relatively skilled work, as contrasted with a 'laborer', whose work demands strength or exertion rather than skill; an artisan is one who is employed in an industrial or mechanical art or trade; 'mechanic', once synonymous with 'artisan', is now commonly restricted to a workman who is skilled in constructing, repairing or using machinery."2 It is significant however that the statute does not include the term "employee". 

While no definition is possible which will express with meticulous exactness the meaning of this term, there is, nevertheless, a generally accepted impression of the type of person it includes. He is generally hired with the prospect of a definite term of employment; he is paid a salary rather than a daily wage; his work is more mental than physical; it has generally to do with correspondence, dictation, books of account, records, filing of papers, auditing, preparation of reports, supervision of others, selling and buying, and in the main, clerical work within the office of his employer. He is the "shirtsleeves” worker as distinguished from the "overalls" laborer.

It is quite clear that an "employee", in the sense used above does not come within the meaning of the term "laborer" used in the statute. It was never intended that he should come within the scope of the mechanics lien law. The whole history of the development of mechanics lien legislation excludes him. The "laborer" referred to 

2. Webster's New Int. Dictionary.

Sec. 58 

 in the statute is he, whose work is a physical part of the construction of the improvement.2a The man who carries his shovel to the job and plunges it in the earth; the carpenter, who packs his box of tools, and goes to the job to do his work; the plumber, who by the light of his candle, installs with his own hands the pipes and fixtures; the man, who, by the sweat of his brow, becomes a part and parcel of the building constructed; these are the types of "laborers" whom the statute was designed to protect. The "employee" in the office is not one of these. 

By the same construction, a contractor or subcontractor who causes labor to be performed by persons employed by him is not a "laborer" within the meaning of the statute.3 So, too, a contractor, who does manual labor in the erection of a building, is not entitled to a lien as a laborer. His relation to the property owner is that of a contractor and this relation is not altered by his personal labor in performing his contract.4 

2a. See discussion in Lohman vs Pioneer Products Co., 26 N. P. (N.S.) 24. 

3. "It is clear, we think, that by the term 'laborers', the legislature did not contemplate or intend to extend the legislation so as to include a class of persons known as 'contractors', who usually perform or carry into effect the work which they have undertaken, not by their own labor, but by means of the services of employees, from whose labor they expect to, and generally do, make or secure a profit."

Sec. 18

Sec. 18. "Contractor" defined.

The statute (G. C. 8323-9) does not define the word "contractor". The term is too well understood to need a statutory definition. The "contractor" is sometimes referred to as the "principal contractor" or the "original contractor". Whichever term is used, it may be said that "he is a person who contracts directly with the owner of property, or his agent, to erect or construct a building or other structure or improvement, or any main division or part thereof."5 There may be more than one "contractor", "original contractor", or "principal contractor". Not infrequently, in the erection of structures of large proportion, such as a modern “skyscraper”, a union depot, or a hospital, the work is subdivided into certain main divisions, such as the steel construction, the stone or concrete work, the heating and ventilating systems, and the electrical work. Each of these divisions may be covered in several distinct contracts between the respective "contractors" and the owner. That the law contemplates such situations may be seen from the language used in the statute.6 The fact that a contract, instead of being for a stipulated sum, is what is known as a "cost plus" contract, does not convert the person contracting with the owner, for compensation on that basis, into an agent, nor

As has already been said, the statute does not define the term "contractor". It becomes, therefore, a question of judicial construction. While G. C. 8310, unquestionably, creates the right to a lien in favor of one who sells materials under a direct contract with the owner, as well as in favor of one who sells to a contractor or subcontractor, the law does not specifically state in which capacity (as a contractor or materialman) he shall perfect his lien, if he contracts directly with the owner. 

G. C. 8323-9, in defining the words "materialman”, says that these words "shall be construed to include all persons by whom any machinery, materials, or fuel are furnished." ** *** It will be seen that the statute does not control, limit, modify, or restrict the term “materialman" by any reference to the fact that he may have contracted with an owner, contractor or subcontractor. His status as such is not fixed by the person with whom he contracts, but by the fact alone that he furnishes "machinery, materials or fuel in or for any construction" *** regardless whom he may have contracted with for its purchase.

It may reasonably be inferred, I think, that by the term "contractor" is meant one who engages to construct, to erect, to alter the thing. It presupposes one who will furnish skill and labor, although he may furnish materials too, as opposed to one who furnishes materials alone and does not labor or furnish any skill in making them into and a part of the structure.

Sec. 

62 

Any other construction would impose upon the materialman the necessity of complying with G. C. 8312.

He would have to furnish a statement of the names of all his employees in his shop and of all his creditors for material; a requirement that no other materialman is obliged to do and a proceeding utterly futile and uncalled for in so far as the rights of the owner are concerned. 

By the use of the maxim "Expressio unius est exclusio alterius", one who furnishes materials is a materialman whether he contracts directly with the owner or not.7a 

Sec. 19. "Subcontractor" defined. "The word 'subcontractor' shall be construed to include any person, firm or corporation who undertakes to construct, alter, erect, improve, repair, remove, dig or drill any part of the structures or improvements mentioned herein under a contract with any person other than the owner." G. C. 8323-9

It was formerly held that a sub-contractor of a subcontractor was not entitled to a lien, but under the provisions of G. C. 8310 there is now no question but that a subcontractor of a subcontractor, or as he is sometimes called, a "subcontractor in the second degree", is entitled to a lien.

The statute makes and preserves throughout a distinction between materialmen and subcontractors. It accords a lien to both, but upon conditions essentially different. 

The distinction between these two classes of lien claimants must therefore be definitely drawn and fixed; otherwise, the owner would never know how to protect himself, and the materialman and subcontractor would not know what procedure would be necessary to perfect their respective rights to a lien.8

Sec. 66 

 Sec. 22. Other Persons Who Have or Have Not Rights to Liens. 

As has already been pointed out in this chapter, the statute does not pretend to include, by express designation, all of the persons who may be entitled to the benefits thereof, nor does it expressly exclude others. Four main classes of persons are specifically mentioned by the statute as being entitled to liens thereunder, but it is left, to a certain extent, to judicial construction to determine what particular persons may fall within any one or more of these four general classes. It may be well, therefore, to discuss certain types of persons who have been held by the courts as being within or without these classifications. 

Sec. 23. Architect.

Is an architect, who prepares the plans and specifications for an improvement or structure and who supervises its construction on the very site of its erection, entitled to a mechanics lien for his services? While the decisions upon this question are by no means harmonious, the weight of authority seems to support the view that the right to such a lien exists, where the language of the statute is general. It will be noted that the language of the statute creating the right to the lien, is, as a rule, of materials on the building site to constitute the structure, and not to the manufacure of such materials, which later may be somewhere combined with others to make a building.” 

See also, Curtis-Dayton Co. vs. 

Timken Roller Bearing Co., 22 

O. L. R. 277.

Another test is to determine the relative value of materials and labor supplied. If the value of labor is small in comparison with that of materials furnished the claimant is a materialman. 

Ferger vs. Gearhart, 44 Cal. 

App. 245, 186 Pac. 376.

Sec. 23  general and comprehensive in its terms.13 It may reasonably be inferred, that had the Legislature not intended that an architect be included in the general classification of "mechanic, workman, artisan, or laborer employed in or about any such work," it would doubtless have made use of more restrictive terms. 

There seems to be no valid reason for excluding him. 

The labor and skill of an architect and his supervision of the work upon the building are a necessary part of the expense of erecting the building, and, not infrequently, an indispensable and highly valuable part. As an item of such expense, he enters into and helps to form the value of the structure. In the very nature of things, there seems to be no sound reason why the person, who performs such labor and furnishes such skill, should not receive the same protection as that accorded the mason, the carpenter, the plumber, or the materialman. Without the services of the former there is often no opportunity for employment of the latter.13a

It may be stated as a general rule that where the services of the architect include not only those spent in the preparation of plans and specifications, but also in supervision of the construction of the improvement, he will be entitled to a lien therefore under the provisions of the mechanics lien law.14 But where the architect

Sec. 25. Lawyer.

It was certainly never the intention of the legislature to include in the class of persons furnishing "labor”, within the meaning of the lien laws, a lawyer.24 The very lack of adjudications upon the question is convincing evidence that the profession itself does not consider its services a lienable item.

Sec. 27. Partnership.

As in the case of a corporation, so, too, a "partnership or two or more persons having a joint or common interest," by virtue of the statutory definition, comes within the meaning of the word "person".26 It has been held that where, after work was commenced by a partnership, one of the partners dropped out and the remaining partner carried forward the work to its completion, the latter was entitled to take out the lien in his own name.27 

Sec. 28. Guarantor or Surety.

A person who is not a party to the contract, but merely guarantees that the contractor will comply with his contract,28 or a person who merely guarantees payment of materials purchased by another,29 is not entitled to a lien.

Where a surety on the bond of a contractor, given to secure the faithful performance of his contract for the erection of a building, in which it is stipulated that the contractor shall furnish and pay for all materials used therein, is also one of the materialmen who furnish materials therefor, he will be precluded by his relation to the contract for the building from enforcing a lien for such materials upon the failure of the contractor to pay laborers. It must file as a contractor.

Sec. 29. One Advancing Money. 

Where a person advances money to a principal contractor to pay the wages of different workmen employed by him in carrying out his contract, he has only a claim against the contractor therefor, and cannot be considered as a subcontractor. The same is true as to one who furnishes money for the payment of materials.31 

Sec. 30. Non-Resident.

By the terms of the statute, "any person" may have a lien who shall have furnished any materials which have been used in the erection of any building or the constructing of any improvement within the state. There is no express limitation or restriction in the statute upon non-residents who may seek to enforce the remedies, provided therein, in the courts of this state. It has accordingly been held, therefore, that one, who in another state, sells and delivers to a principal contractor, materials to be transported by the latter to this state and used by him here in constructing a public improvement, is entitled to the same rights under the mechanics lien laws of this

 state, that one may assert who sells and delivers, within this state, materials to be thus used.32 

Sec. 31. The Owner. 

An owner cannot acquire a mechanics lien upon his own property.33 At law, the lien of the owner, if he were to have one, would merge in the superior title of his ownership, since the greater title would include the lesser; in equity, it would be manifestly unjust to permit an owner to enforce a lien on his own property at the expense of third persons, who hold similar liens on it for debts contracted by the owner, or his contractor, to such third persons. Upon the same principle, one who joins in a voluntary association of citizens to promote a new industry in their city, and subscribes for stock or bonds of the company to be incorporated, cannot, altho he furnishes his own materials for the construction of the plant, take out a lien for his unpaid claim, to the prejudice of his associates in the common. enterprise.34 

Sec. 32. Infant.

The only limitation, if there is any, upon the right of an infant to acquire a lien, would seem to arise by
