But, as the disability of a minor is a personal privilege, his contracts being voidable and not void, the minority of the claimant cannot be available as a defense to his lien, where one has received the benefit of his services or materials.35 

The rules of law generally applicable to the rights and obligations of a minor will obtain in the enforcement of a lien in his behalf.

Sec. 33. Married Woman. 

By virtue of the enabling acts, a married woman may contract to the same extent and in the same manner as if she were unmarried, and she may sue and be sued as if she were unmarried.36 To all intents and purposes, therefore, she has the same rights and will be subject to the same obligations as any other person, who comes within the provisions of the mechanics lien law. 

Sec. 34. Materialman of a "Materialman.” 

It sometimes happens that a materialman, who has taken a contract from the original contractor or a subcontractor, to furnish materials for the erection of a structure, finds himself unable to complete the order from his own stock on hand or by his own manufacture. Should he purchase a portion of the order from another materialman and then use this material in the job in order to fulfill his contract, the question immediately arises as to 

35. Van Bramer vs. Cooper, 2 Johns 279 (N. Y.) 

Whitemarsh vs. Hall, 3 Den. 

375 (N. Y.) 

36. G. C. 7999 and G. C. 11245.

Sec. 76 

 whether the selling materialman will have a right to a lien, upon the building of the owner, for the materials sold and delivered to the purchasing materialman and used by him in the job. The question must be divided into two cases: (a) Where the selling materialman did not know the purpose for which the material was to be used. (b) Where the selling materialman knew the purpose for which it was to be used. (a) The whole history of the lien law shows a continuing intent on the part of the legislature to protect only those persons who render service or labor, or furnish materials with the purpose and intent of aiding in the construction of a particular improvement. In an early case, the Supreme Court said: "Should a man's domestic patch a window or mend a lock in his employer's house, or a farmer's hired man make or repair a door of his barn, no one would say that a lien attached in either case. So if a materialman sell his wares with no understanding, express or implied, as to their application, he can assert no lien upon the building or vessels in which they may be placed. He trusts to the responsibility of the buyer alone and takes no security. He sells, not for the special purpose named in the statute of "constructing, altering, or repairing," but for any purpose that may seem best to the buyer. But it is only where the materials are furnished for a purpose named in the act that a lien is acquired."37

Following the rule of this case, the Superior Court of Cincinnati held that, where iron was furnished by A to B, 37. Choteau vs. Thompson & Campbell, 2 Oh. St. 114.

Sec. 34

 who manufactured the same into stair cases, railings, etc., which he used in the construction of a building for 

C, A had no right to a lien. He must look to his vendee for pay. The court said: "In the case before us, it is evident the iron sold to the contractor Horton, was not delivered on the credit of Carlisle (the owner) or on the faith that it would in some form or other be placed in his building. The vendee was under no obligation thus to use it. He might have appropriated it for any other purpose demanded by his business; and it cannot be said if he had manufactured it into grates, or railing, or any commodity in his line of business, and sold the same, a lien would accompany each article; such a proposition could not be maintained” * * *38 In a later case the Supreme Court restricted the rule still further. In construing the law of 1875, it was held that a materialman, who sold materials to a subcontractor, could not file an attested account with the owner for his claim, under section 2 of the act which provided that "any person who shall furnish materials for the construction of any such building *** may deliver to or file with the owner *** an attested account *** of the value of the materials furnished *** and unpaid.

The court said: "The terms of the section, 'any person who shall furnish materials', are comprehensive enough to include the creditor of any subcontractor, as well as the creditor of 'the contractor'; but upon examination of the whole statute, it is quite clear that the legislature did not intend to provide a remedy for materialmen who 

38. Horton vs. Carlisle, 2 Disney 184.

Sec. 78 

 credit any person other than the owner or the original contractor."39

From these cases it may be readily perceived that the whole trend of decision is to disallow the lien where the materials are simply sold in the general course of trade without any specific intention that they are to be used in a particular building. While it is probably true that the rule of the last above quoted case does not apply today, in view of the express authority for a lien in favor of a materialman who furnishes materials to a subcontractor,40 nevertheless, even in such case, (the sale by a materialman to a subcontractor) it is undoubtedly the law, that the rule of Choteau vs. Thompson and Campbell41 still applies and that the materials sold to such subcontractor must have been sold by the materialman for the purpose of being used in a particular construction. The words "in carrying forward, performing, or completing any such contract" unquestionably means "for the purpose" of carrying forward such contract.42

But, to return to the sale by a materialman to another materialman; it will be seen from the quotation from the statute40 that while a lien is specifically granted to a materialman who furnishes materials to each contractor or any subcontractor, there is no similar specific authority granting a lien to a materialman who furnishes material

Nor can it be said that, since the lien is granted if the materials are sold to a "subcontractor", the purchasing materialman may be considered as a subcontractor. If the decision is placed upon this ground alone, i. e., the bond confers greater rights than does the law relating to mechanics liens in such cases,50 no real criticism can be made thereof, although no good reason has been assigned why persons furnishing labor and material upon or for a public improvement should have any better right to be paid or be granted broader remedies than those who furnish their labor and material upon or for a private job. In either case the justification for their special relief is the same, i. e., their labor and material has been merged and its identity lost in the improvement. Sec. 35. Vendor of Machinery Retaining Title. 

The retention, by contract, of title to machinery furnished in or for the structure by the lien claimant, as security for the purchase price, is not inconsistent with, and will not estop the vendor from enforcing, his statutory mechanics lien. The retention of title creates a lien only upon the machinery; the mechanics lien covers that and also the real estate upon which it stands. The former

Sec. 36. Vendee in Possession Under Contract of Purchase. 

A vendee in possession under a contract of purchase cannot by improving the real estate with a building or other structure acquire a mechanics lien thereon for his labor and materials, as against the unpaid vendor, and those claiming under him. In constructing such a building on land, the title to which he intends to acquire for himself, he is working for himself. As to the vendor, he is merely a volunteer in making the improvements.55

Sec. 39. Contract with the Owner.

The foundation of the right to a mechanics lien is a valid contract with the owner of some interest in the real estate to be improved.1 Before one who furnishes labor or material may have a lien to secure the payment therefor, it must appear as a condition precedent that the same was furnished by virtue of a contract, express or implied, with the owner, or his authorized agent; or, that one has, as subcontractor, laborer, or material man, furnished such labor or material to an original contractor of the owner

"Before a mechanics lien can attach there must exist the relation of creditor and debtor; a debt must be created before there can be a lien."3 It is not essential, however, that the owner be personally indebted to all such persons who assert and are entitled to a lien under the statute.4 

In the case of the subcontractor, materialman, or laborer, the owner is usually not bound by any contract with them and is consequently not, as a rule, personally liable to them. 4a

Sec. 41.

Nature of the Contract. 

The statute does not prescribe the form or requisites of the contract other than to say it may be express or implied. Plainly, then, it need not be in writing. But since, by the term "contract", is meant something more than a mere agreement to do work or sell goods, it would seem necessary that it indicate the particular purpose for which such labor and material is to be furnished. "It is only where the materials are furnished for a purpose named in the act that a lien is acquired. That they are so furnished, may be proved by evidence of an express agreement, or by proof of circumstances from which the purpose may be inferred. A tacit understanding may be as good as an express one."9 It is not necessary that the contract should stipulate for such a lien, or, even, that the labor or material should be furnished with an existing intention to perfect a lien upon the property.10

To meet this situation, and to remove one of the most flagrant sources of injustice to the workman and materialman, the amendment to the Constitution in 1912 was passed.36 By this express authority, "laws may be passed to secure to *** subcontractors and materialmen their just dues by direct lien upon the property" for the improvement of which they have furnished their labor and materials. In the exercise of this authority, the Mechanics 

Lien Law of 1913 was enacted. Sections 8310 and 8311 

of this act create an absolute and direct lien upon the property of the owner in favor of persons furnishing labor or materials for the construction, alteration, repair, removal or demolition of any building, structure or other improvement upon such property. This is an entirely new and distinct type of lien-wholly unrelated to the derivative type that existed in Ohio before the amendment of 1912. Under the earlier type of lien, the laborer, materialman and subcontractor had only the right to intercept funds due the contractor from the owner. No right to a specific lien upon the real estate of the owner existed. 

But this is no longer true. Now, by virtue of the 

Mechanics Lien Law of 1913, a right to a direct lien the contract permitted the owner to pay the contractor by giving him land, stock, or by rendering personal service, or by some other compensation than money, if the owner defaulted there was a breach of his contract and the contractor became immediately entitled to his damages in money. Mechanics, subcontractors, and materialmen could therefore insist upon payment of their claims in money also.

The contract between the owner and the contractor is no longer the source of the lien. The statute creates the lien and neither the owner nor the contractor can bargain it away insofar as the rights of laborers, materialmen or subcontractors are concerned. The statute seems to give importance to the contract only as giving consent of the owner that the improvement be made on his land, and, if a contract price is stated therein, to limit the liability of the owner as to the liens that may be acquired upon his property growing out of the construction of the improvement under the authority of such contract. 

Therefor, if an owner undertakes to erect a building and to pay the stated contract price therefor by conveying other real estate of the owner to the contractor, or in some consideration other than money, that agreement, while it may bind such owner and his principal contractor, will not defeat the statutory right of all lien claimants to acquire direct liens for their claims upon the property of the owner and the improvement thereon which their labor and materials have produced. In such a situation, the laborers, materialmen and subcontractors cannot be required to rely on and proceed against the other real estate of the owner which the contractor agreed to accept as his compensation for making the improvement; not being bound by the provisions of the principal contract in respect to the manner of payment of the contract price, of which it is immaterial whether they had notice or not, such lien claimants are not only entitled to acquire liens upon but also to enforce payment thereof out of the

Sec. 47

The Contract structure or improvement, and the land upon which it is situated, for which their labor and materials were furnished.37

The provision of G. C. 8313 in the expression, "shall not be liable to the subcontractors, materialmen or laborers for any greater amount than he contracted to pay the original contractor" does not alter the effect of the principle just stated. This provision "merely places a limitation on the owner's liability."38 So in the case last referred to, where the aggregate of the liens filed did not exceed the contract price named in the principal contract, it was properly held that such liens could be enforced against the particular property for which the labor and materials were furnished. In such case the owner is paying no more for his improvement than he contracted to pay. True, he is paying it in a manner different from that in which he intended to pay but he must be held to have contracted with full knowledge of the statute giving persons furnishing labor and materials a direct lien upon his property which he is about to improve. This statutory right exists independent of his contract and he, therefore, can neither abrogate nor curtail it insofar as the rights of persons other than himself and his principal contractor are involved.

From the preceding chapter it appears that the lien of the contractor, subcontractor, materialman, or laborer, though created by statute, is dependent upon and exists only by virtue of a contract between the owner and another, who has agreed to. construct, alter or repair some structure or other improvement upon the real estate of the owner.

A valid contract, such as is contemplated by the statute, having been entered into, it remains to be seen how far it is incumbent upon the person asserting a right to a lien to show performance of or compliance with the obligations and conditions of such contract. In general, it

Sec. 106 

 may be said that, as far as the obligations of the principal contractor are concerned, or of the subcontractor as to the performance of his own subcontract, the general principles governing the enforcement of contracts under similar circumstances apply, and the extent of their right to a lien is controlled entirely by the results of their own efforts or ability to comply with the terms of their respective contracts. On the other hand, quite a different question arises as to how far the failure of performance by the principal contractor of his contract with the owner may affect the right to, or the extent of, the lien of a subcontractor, materialman, or laborer, who has fully performed the conditions of his own contract or employment. 

For this reason the questions will be discussed separately. 

(A) As Between Contractor and Owner Sec. 49. Necessity of Substantial Performance. 

As a general proposition, it may be said that to entitle a contractor to assert and maintain a lien for the contract price of the improvement he has constructed, repaired or altered, he must, as a condition precedent, affirmatively show that he has complied with the terms of his contract with the owner. Every person has a right to construct a house, building or other improvement according to the design and of such materials as in his own judgment best suit his notions of utility or style. If the owner himself, or with the aid of an architect or engineer, designs a building, in keeping with the local building ordinances, of a certain size and design and prescribes the kind of materials and equipment to be used in the construction thereof, and a contractor undertakes to erect such building according to the plans and specifications,

Sec. 49

Performance of the Contract he cannot recover payment of or a lien for the labor and materials used or employed by him in carrying out such contract unless he can show that he has performed and completed such contract in accordance with such plans and specifications. He has no right to change the plans or substitute his own judgment for that of the owner as to materials or equipment to be used therein. Having engaged to erect a building of a certain type, unless performance thereof has been waived by the owner, he cannot recover for the construction of a building of another type. In the same manner he cannot recover for a partial performance only. The contract is express and entire. 

He cannot of his own choice create an implied obligation on the part of the owner to pay for what he has only partly performed. "Where the undertaking is to do work and furnish materials under the terms of a special contract, and the work is abandoned after part performance, and left unfinished by the fault of the workman, in the absence of all evidence showing the assent of the employer, or his acceptance of the work part finished, there can be no recovery pro tanto upon any established principle known to the law."1 But it is not essential that the con-

Sec. 50

Performance of the Contract Sec. 50. What Is Substantial Performance. 

To justify a recovery upon a contract as substantially performed the omissions, deviations or errors must be the result of mistake or inadvertence, and not deliberate departures, much less fraudulent; and they must have been trivial and unimportant, or susceptible of replacement or reconstruction, so that an allowance would give the owner substantially what his contract entitled him to have.5 "There is no substantial performance when no attempt is made to comply with certain express requirements of the specifications and no excuse or explanation is given for the failure. A contract is not substantially performed by substituting for that which is expressly required materials, methods, or workmanship which, in the opinion of the contractor and his experts, are 'just as good', unless the substitution relates to a matter of minor importance, is made in good faith, and for sufficient reasons, and there is an adequate allowance for the difference. The owner has a right to what the contractor agreed to give him, and unless he has it, or, when the failure is neither willful or substantial, is fully compensated for the omission, there is no substantial performance, and there can be no recovery. This right to insist upon substantial performance is personal to the owner. It cannot be availed of by other lienors or encumbrancers see Nolt VS. 

Crow, 22 Pa. Sup. Ct. 113 where the court said: 

“*** The measure of performance is a matter that concerns only the parties to the contract. The owner may waive any feature of it which is designed merely for his benefit. 

He may, for instance, waive delay in performing, failure to complete, or defects in the quality of the work or materials. It is sufficient if the claimant has done to the satisfaction of the owner anything for which the law gives a lien. He is not bound to perform his contract, nor is the owner required to hold him to it, merely to serve the purpose of those who are not parties to it. If other incumbrancers may impeach his lien on the ground of incompetent performance, they may with equal right impeach it for failure to perform within the stipulated time, or for defects in the work or materials. The owner may stand on the letter of the contract, and hold the claimant to its terms, if he so chooses, but strangers to the contract have no such right." Sec. 51.

Satisfaction of Owner and Approval of Architect.

The doctrine, that if a person substantially performs a building contract, he may recover the contract price subject to recoupment for damages as to the particulars in which the contract has not been literally performed, has no application to a contract which provides that the contract shall be done to the satisfaction of the owner or a third person. In such case the contractor cannot recover if the owner or the third person is in good faith dissatisfied with the performance of the contract, even though the court or jury might think they ought to have been satisfied. And this is so, even though, from the nature of the contract, the owner is obliged to keep the thing upon which the work has been performed, and, hence, to retain some benefit from the labor which the contractor has performed. And where it was agreed that a furnace for a dwelling should be placed in a house and should be satisfactory to the owner and if he was not satisfied with it he need not pay for it and reject it, it was held to be error to charge, "that if the furnace was built in a workprovision of the specifications, the owner by insisting on compliance with the specifications waives the guaranty.

Sec. 52. 

Waiver of Performance.

A verbal agreement between an owner and a contractor, to be effectual as a waiver, variation, or change in the stipulations of a prior written contract between the parties, must rest upon some new and distinct legal consideration. It cannot be supported on the supposition that it is founded on the continuation or extension of the consideration of the prior or written contract. An agreement by one person to discharge another from the obligations of a written contract, as a matter ex gratia and in the nature of a donation, would be of no binding validity as a mere executory agreement, and to be effectual, must be fully executed by an actual release, or surrender of the contract in writing.18 There is a class of cases, however, where a written contract may be altered or modified by a mere verbal agreement of the parties, which, at its inception, or as a mere executory agreement, would have no binding effect, yet by being acted upon by the parties until it would work a fraud or injury to refuse to carry it out, becomes binding and effectual as a contract.19 A party to a contract containing a provision that it shall not be altered, modified or changed, except by a written

Sec. 53

Performance of the Contract Sec. 53. Measure of Damages. 

Breach by Owner

In an action by a contractor against an owner for damages for having prevented such contractor from performing or completing his contract, the contractor is entitled to recover the difference between the contract price and what it would have actually cost him to have completed the contract. In other words, if his contract price was in excess of what it would be worth to complete the work, that would be the measure of damages. On the other hand, if the contractor took the contract at a price at which there was no profit in it, he lost nothing by the action of the owner in abandoning the contract, and he can recover nothing.25 While this may be the rule in an action for damages brought by the contractor against the owner, yet, since the statute creates the right to a mechanics lien only for labor and material furnished, he can acquire no lien for damages arising out of the failure or refusal of the owner to permit him to complete his contract. His right to a lien extends to only that part of the work which has been done and not paid for.26 In deter-

(B) As Between Owner and Subcontractor 

Séc. 54. In General.

In order to entitle a subcontractor, materialman, or laborer, to a lien it would seem but reasonable that, as a condition precedent thereto, he shall have substantially performed the conditions of his own subcontract. If, by his own willful departure from the terms of his contract, or by his furnishing of defective material, or by his own unskillful workmanship, he has failed to substantially comply with the provisions of his contract he ought not to be permitted to enforce a lien. By his contract he has undertaken to perform a part, at least, of the original contract. To that extent he has made the performance of the original contractor his own performance and since, as it has been seen, the original contractor can have no lien unless he has substantially performed his contract, value of the building to the owner in its defective condition, and its value perfectly constructed, if it is neither fair nor reasonably practicable to remedy the defects, or by the reasonable cost of remedying the defects where that is practicable."

Sec. 60. Destruction of Building. 

In the case where a contract for the erection of a building has not been performed by reason of the destruction of the building by fire, storm or some other cause beyond the control of the parties, the rule governing the respective rights and obligations as between the owner and the contractor, where the contract is for the entire building, is well defined. If one contracts to furnish lumber and materials to erect a building on the land of another, he will not ordinarily be excused from the performance of his contract by the destruction of the building without his fault before the time fixed for the delivery of it. The contractor in such case continues to be the owner of the building until completed and turned over to the party for whom it was constructed. If destroyed before the completion of the contract, he must restore it and complete his contract before he can recover any consideration for the work and material furnished. 

There can be no recovery pro tanto for the work done before its destruction.51 Of course, where the destruction 

50. Bergin vs. Braun, 15 0. D. 383. 

51. Bailey vs. Brown, 9 C. C. 455.

In the latter case there is an implied condition of the contract that the building shall continue in existence, and its destruction without fault of either of the parties, will excuse performance of the contract, and the contractor may recover payment pro tanto for the work done.53

In the case of a subcontractor, one who has but a portion of the work to do, the remainder being done by the owner or principal contractor, there is a legal excuse for the non-performance of the contract on the part of the subcontractor. The destruction of the property upon which the work is done, without the fault of the subcontractor, furnishes such excuse, and the subcontractor may recover upon his contract pro tanto, because of the fact that he is excused from its full performance, having been prevented from doing so without his fault.54

Sec. 62

 Sec. 62. In General. 

The theory of the mechanics lien law is that the party furnishing labor or material for the erection, alteration, or repair of a building has done that which enhances the value of the building in which his labor or material is employed, and that he has parted with his rights in such labor and material when it has been merged into and become an integral part of the building.¹ But since the right to a lien is purely a creature of statute, the party claiming its protection must show affirmatively that he has performed such labor or furnished such materials as are described in the law authorizing the lien. 

In the early history of the law it was usually necessary to show that the labor performed or materials furnished had gone into something that became a part of the realty and that it had enhanced its value by reason thereof. But this doctrine has been somewhat relaxed in the later decisions. Attachment to the realty is no longer an absolute requirement for the validity of a lien and questions of benefit to the owner or of enhanced or increased value are now considered immaterial. 

There are four main classes of lienable items mentioned in the statute. These are: labor, machinery, material, and fuel. But since the right to a lien for these various items depends, to a certain extent, upon the nature of the building, structure or improvement upon which the labor is performed or for which the material is furnished, it may be well to classify the several types of construction on which the lien may be acquired. 

1. Treadway & Marlatt "Ohio Mechanics Lien Laws", Par. 34.

Sec. 134

Sec. 64. Public Property. 

It must be borne in mind, however, that the construction referred to in the previous section is that which is done on privately owned property only. It is an almost universal rule of law that there can be no direct lien, in favor of a laborer or materialman, acquired or enforced against or upon the public property of a state or any political subdivision thereof.2 Unless expressly so provided, public buildings owned or being constructed by public authority out of public funds are not within the purview of mechanics lien laws.3 

Sec. 65. Work and Labor. 

Wherever a lien is given to secure the payment "of work done" in the erection of a building, it includes all the labor which is ordinarily employed in the erection of the building contemplated by the contract. The law makes no distinction between the values of the various kinds of work, but places those contributing artistic labor, used

 Sec. 67. Loss of Profits or Commissions. 

The statute expressly limits the right to a lien to labor performed or materials furnished. Accordingly it has been held that the lien can be obtained only for work actually performed, although it may not have been as fully performed as the lienors, wrongfully discharged, were entitled to perform it.10 So, loss of profits or damages for breach of contract in refusing to allow a contractor to do the work is not lienable.11 A contractor's commissions which are to be earned on a cost plus contract are not lienable as to that part which might have been earned if the owner had not discontinued the work.1 12 A bonus for speeding up the work is not a lienable item.13

Sec. 69. Transportation and Freight Charges. 

be Upon the very narrow and restricted doctrine that only such labor and material that is performed upon or enters into the construction of the improvement may the subject of a lien, it was held in an early Massachusetts case15 that a teamster, who, under a subcontract with the contractor, carted lumber and sand to be used in the erection of a building, was not entitled to a lien for his labor in hauling such material to the job. The court said: "The petitioner does not allege that he performed any labor upon material which became a part of the structure, so as to change its shape or character in order to adapt it to the building. He did nothing with the sand to make it fit and proper to enter into the construction of any part of the house, nor did he perform any labor by which the lumber was fitted or adapted to any section of the house. *** It is difficult to distinguish the claim of the petitioner for lien from that of the railroad for transporting the lumber, or from that of the teamster who carted it to the railroad, or from the claim of the wood-cutters who felled the trees, provided they stood, in other respects, towards the respondent as does this petitioner."

Sec. 74. Work Done Away from the Premises. 

In early days the work of the laborer was done upon the site of the building being erected. The stone was cut and fashioned; the windows, doors, and sashes, were sawed, planed and assembled; the iron ornamentation was forged upon the anvil. All this was visibly apparent on the job. But times have changed. In these days a large proportion of the material furnished for the construction of buildings, such as cut stone, ironwork, inside finishing, etc., is prepared at the yard or in the shop of the contractor or manufacturer, in accordance with the plans and specifications of the particular structure being erected.

It is generally held, therefore, that a lien may be acquired for labor performed on materials which the la-

 Sec. 75. Work Incident or Appurtenant to Principal Structure. 

A lien may be acquired for work and labor performed or for materials furnished in connection with the construction, alteration or repair of a principal structure although not an integral part thereof, and even though it be not performed directly upon the premises upon which the principal structure is being erected or the lien is sought. Where it appeared, while a building was in the course of erection, that buildings on the adjacent land, not belonging to the constructing owner, were in jeopardy, and the architect ordered the contractor to shore up the building on the adjoining lot, it was held that the work done by the contractor, outside the limits of the lot imthough doubtless that was contemplated. They engaged to furnish the cut stone. They would have satisfied their contract had they purchased the stone, all fitted, and then delivered it to the owner of the building. 

The distinction is clear. Where one engages to erect a building, or to do certain things in the erection of the building, as, for example, the carpenter work, or the painting, or the plumbing, or the granite work, his employees have liens for their labor in doing these things. And if, in connection with doing these things, he agrees to furnish, and does furnish, the materials, the result is the same. It is not necessary that all of the labor should actually be done on the structure itself. To illustrate: 

The doors and windows may be made at the shop, the boards may be sawed and planed at the mill, or the iron work done at the blacksmith shop. These processes are all a part of the erection of the building. The work so done, in the contemplation of the statute, is done 'in the erection of a building'. Webster vs. 

Real Estate Improv. Co., 140 

Mass. 526, 6. N. E. 71.

But where one contracts to furnish completed articles for a building, and is to have no part in the erection of the building, his employees have no lien for their labor in preparing and completing the articles. Their labor is in no proper sense performed 'in the erection of the building"."

And where cement walks, a pergola, driveways and garages are all appurtenant to the building being erected and are included in one plan or scheme of development, liens in favor of the persons who perform labor thereon or furnish materials therefor will attach to the buildings and land upon which they stand.40 In the same manner a reservoir constructed for an electric light plant, for the purpose of storing water sufficient to supply the steam engines operating such plant, is a part of the main structure of such plant and is therefore an "appurtenance" thereto; and work and labor performed therein is lienable.41 A pipe connecting a house with a sewer built in the street, necessary to the use of the house, and included in the contract for building it, is a part of the house and a lien may be had for work and labor in laying it.42 So too, a laborer, who hauls dirt from and hauls sand to a trench dug in a street for a steam pipe connecting a plant

 will be noted that the mechanics lien statutes do not expressly define the kind of material entering into the construction, alteration, or repair of any structure which will be protected by their provisions. The word "material" has been defined as, "a term importing the substance matter of which anything is made or may be made; everything of which anything is made; matter which is intended to be used in the creation of a mechanical structure. The term "material" is commonly used to designate any article employed in the erection and completion of buildings; something that goes into and forms part of the finished structure.45 

Sec. 78. "Materials", "Appliances", "Equipment" Distinguished.

To distinguish between materials and equipment is comparatively easy, since the term "materials" includes such articles only as enter into and form a part of the finished structure, or, it may be, such articles as are capable of being so used and are furnished for that purpose, while "equipment" is, what the word imports, the outfit necessary to enable the contractor to perform the agreed service, the tools, implements, and appliances which might have been previously used, or might be subsequently used by the contractor in carrying on other work of like character.46 According to the lexicographical

So it does not include machinery that may be used for the manufacture of the materials themselves.47 There is a wide distinction between "material" and "appliance".

The term "appliance" refers to machinery and all the instruments used in operating it.48

Sec. 79. No Lien for Tools, Appliances, or Re pairs Thereon.

The general rule is that articles furnished for use merely as tools and appliances in carrying on the work of construction are not "materials" for which a mechanics lien may be claimed.49 It is presumed that a contractor is prepared with machinery and necessary appliances to do his work, and that such items are furnished upon his own credit and as a part of his working equipment and business and are not furnished upon the implied credit of the land upon which they are being temporarily used

Sec. 82. "Furnishing". In General.

While the mechanics lien statutes do not as a rule use the term "delivered" or "delivered at the building," as applied to machinery, material, or fuel for which a lien is claimed, it is generally held that the term “furnish” (in any of its tenses) connotes an actual or constructive delivery of such materials to the owner, contractor, subcontractor, or some other person authorized to receive or accept them. Nor do these statutes expressly designate the place where such delivery shall be made. 

It is not always possible to deliver the materials upon the actual building site. The modern skyscraper is usually built in congested business districts and generally occupies every square foot of land upon the site. There is therefore no room for the delivery and storage of materials that will be needed in the construction, and it would

Sec. 83.

Distinction Between Material "Fur nished" and Material "Used."

There is said to be a conflict of opinion on the question as to whether there may be a lien for material "furnished" but not actually "used" in or incorporated into the structure or improvement. That there is such a conflict of opinion is admitted. But an examination of the decisions on one or the other side of this controversy, discloses an apparent failure on the part of some courts to discriminate between materials which are, from their very nature and available use, the proper subject of a lien, and those, which, though in their nature lienable but technically not furnished for the purpose of being actually incorporated in the structure, are claimed to be the proper subject of a lien by reason of their actual use in facilitating the work of construction; as, for instance, lumber for scaffolding or for concrete forms. For the purpose of clarity these two types of so called "materials" will be discussed separately. 

(A) Lienable Material Furnished But Not Used 

At the outset of this discussion a distinction must be recognized between those mechanics lien statutes which provide a lien for materials "furnished" for the construction of an improvement and those which provide a lien for materials "used" or "to be used" in the construction of an improvement. In the case of the former there is admittedly a conflict of opinion as to whether materials, 67a. King, Gilbert & Warner vs. Ship Building Co., 50 Oh. St. 320.

Sec. 83

 which are by their very nature lienable, may be the subject of a lien when they are not actually incorporated into the structure. In the latter case the explicit language of the statute leaves no room for doubt upon the question.68 On the other hand some statutes expressly provide that where lienable materials are actually delivered to the owner of the structure or to the site where the structure is being erected the lien will not be lost because such materials may not have been actually used in the construction of the building.69

Confining this discussion, however, only to those statutes which admit of judicial construction, by reason of the use of the term "furnish" therein, we find a hopeless conflict of opinion. On the one hand it is said: "It is well settled, both in this state and elsewhere, that a materialman claiming a lien must ordinarily show that his materials were furnished for and were actually used in the erection, alteration, or repair of the building against which the lien is asserted. *** The provisions of the statute respecting the furnishing of machinery are not substantially different from those with regard to building materials. The machinery furnished must be so attached

On the other hand, there is an equally imposing line of authority to the effect that actual use of the materials furnished for the construction of a building is not essential to the validity of a materialmans lien.71 There seems to be a growing tendency however, to break away from the somewhat harsh rule that actual use of the materials is essential to the lien. One of the recognized exceptions to the old rule is in the case where the material is prepared especially for the building, and is of little or no value for any other purpose. "Under such circumstances that is, where the materialman contracts directly with the owner, and where the material is manufactured and especially designed for the building the material is furnished in contemplation of law as soon as prepared and ready for delivery, and the owner should not be permitted to defeat the lien by a wrongful refusal to receive or accept the material."72 And where materials have been specially designed for a certain building and have been furnished to the contractor therefor, a lien may be had for the whole amount so furnished altho only a portion has been used in the building on account of the contractor having suspended work on the building.73

For the Building

The last twenty years have witnessed a great transformation in the building industry. The frame or brick building of two or three stories has given way to the many storied building of steel, stone, and concrete. To facilitate the work of construction, to provide for the safety of workmen, and to reduce the cost of construction by speeding up the work, great quantities of material are used in and about the building altho not actually incorporated therein. To this end lumber is used to enclose the premises during the progress of the work; or for scaffolding to assist the bricklayer, the stone mason, the painter and other trades; or for making forms into which the concrete may be run; or for shoring up adjacent buildings; or for building temporary shelter for men, tools, or teams. In the same manner explosives are used to prepare the way for excavations and lubricants and soapstone are used in the operation of building machinery and equipment.

A great deal of this material is utterly consumed or destroyed by its use for these purposes, and much of it, though salvaged, is greatly depreciated in value. While it is true that none of this material can be said to go into the actual construction of the building and become a physical part thereof, it is equally true that much, if not 

78. DeBolt vs. Farmer's Exchange Bank, 51 Okla. 12.

Sec. 162 

 all, of its life and substance has in effect gone into the structure and its value lost, to the same extent as if it had been physically incorporated therein. 

The question may well arise, therefore, as to whether such material may be truly said to have been "furnished for the erection, alteration, or repair" of a building or improvement so as to entitle the seller thereof to a lien for its purchase price, if consumed, or depreciated value, if salvaged. For a long time the courts consistently declined to allow a lien for such material which, though entirely consumed or partially destroyed in the work of construction, became no actual or physical part of the structure.

These cases held fast to the old rule of strict construction that the lien laws were intended to protect only those materialmen whose materials were actually incorporated in the building and became a part thereof. 

Such items of material, as were used only for the purpose of facilitating the work of construction, were regarded merely as a necessary part of the contractor's equipment, in the same manner as his tools, machinery and other appliances. Upon this theory the lien was denied.79

The rule seems now well settled, however, that the lienability of the material does not depend upon its suitableness in its crude condition for use in the construction of a building, or on its identity being maintained, but whether it was furnished especially for the manufacture of something to be used in such structure. The whole question depends upon the purpose for which the raw material was furnished. If it appears that it was furnished by the seller for the purpose of enabling the contractor to manufacture or fabricate it into some form to be used in the erection of a particular building it is lienable. If on the other hand the raw material was sold for the purpose of manufacturing a generally marketable article, without reference to its use in any particular structure, it would not, of course, be lienable as against the building it might later be found to have been used in.92

Sec. 93. Fixtures. 

In the construction, alteration, or repair of a building there is generally a certain amount of distinctly chattel property furnished the owner or contractor for the purpose of being used to fit up the building for its more convenient use. Lighting fixtures, window shades, radiators, stoves, ice boxes, and store counters, are suggested as only a few of the many articles of a personal nature which are furnished for this purpose. Whether such articles may be made the subject of a lien in favor of the seller who furnished them, or of the laborer who installed them, is a question upon which there is a hopeless conflict of authority.

Among the earlier decisions the question turned upon the inquiry as to whether such articles, by reason of their annexation to the realty, became "fixtures" in the technical sense in which that term was used. A "fixture" was said to be an article which was a chattel, but which, by being affixed to the realty, became accessory to it, and parcel of it.103 If the article furnished became a fixture

Home Stove Co., 121 N. E. 293, 70 Ind. App. 226.

Some cases laid great stress upon the method or manner of annexation; others upon its adaptability or appropriateness to the use or purpose for which it was furnished, while many cases considered the intention of the party making the annexation as a controlling factor. It was always a mixed question of law and fact, and the question was further complicated by the fact that the rule was often varied when applied to certain classes of persons, such as mortgagor and mortgagee, vendor and vendee, landlord and tenant, and heir and personal representative. 

A majority of the earlier cases laid much stress upon the method or manner of annexation. If the articles were so attached that any effort to remove them would substantially damage the building, they were deemed "fixtures" and were lienable. If, on the other hand, they were easily removable, and without damage to the building, they were held to have retained their chattel nature, were not "fixtures", and therefore not lienable.

But with the great transformation of methods, designs, and general equipment used in the construction of the modern building, the old rule requiring physical annexation has been somewhat relaxed. It is now very generally

Another test now often applied is to inquire whether the articles so furnished were intended by the owner to be such a part of his building that they would pass as a part and parcel of the building in the event he would sell the building to some purchaser. And so, by the application of these general principles of construction, the courts are rapidly breaking away from the old test of lienability by the rule of "fixtures". A few examples may suffice to indicate this change. Sec. 117. Dower

The fundamental purpose of all mechanics lien laws was to secure to the mechanic the payment of his claim for labor and materials furnished for a building, by subjecting to a lien the identical structure he had helped to construct, alter or repair. But as the building was a permanent or fixed improvement on the owner's lot, the lien, to more effectually carry out the purpose of the law, was generally extended, though not always in the earlier legislation, to the lot of land on which the building stood. 

An examination of the statutes of the various states on the question as to what buildings and land are affected

Sec. 182 

 by the lien discloses an irreconcilable conflict of legislative opinion. It would serve no useful purpose to discuss these various statutes in detail.

Some limit the lien only to the building for which the labor and material were furnished and the lot upon which it stands; others, by judicial construction, permit it to extend to other buildings which may stand upon the lot improved. Some limit the lien upon the land to a certain definite area, such as one acre, or one town lot; others permit the lien to cover only so much of the land as is proper and necessary to the convenient use and enjoyment of the building upon which the work has been performed. In a few states the statute has been construed to mean that the lien extends not only to the lot improved but to parcels nearby, though not necessarily contiguous thereto, if these parcels are necessary to or are in fact used as a component part of the operation or enjoyment of the parcel upon which the building, which has been constructed, altered or repaired, stands.1 

Sec. 95. Early Ohio Statutes. 

It seems appropriate to review briefly the historical development of the Ohio statutes upon this question. 

By the first lien law of Ohio, the local law of 1823, the lien was said to "operate as a lien on the several descriptions of buildings." The law did not specifically extend the lien to the land upon which such building or buildings stood. With the passage of the first general lien law of Ohio in 1843, however, the lien was granted not only upon the building for which the labor and mate- 

1. See cases cited in 26 L. R. A. (N.S.) 831.

Sec. 95

 rials were furnished, but also "the lot upon which the same shall stand." In construing this law, the Supreme 

Court said: "The word 'owner' is not limited in its meaning to an owner of the fee, but includes also an owner of the leasehold estate. If the ownership is in fee, the lien is upon the fee; if it is of a less estate, the lien is upon such smaller estate. To hold that an owner in fee only is meant, would be directly subversive of the policy of the act, and in a great degree render it useless."2 The legislature accepted this construction of the law, and in 1871 an act was passed in which it was provided that "the words 'lot of land' used in this act shall be held and considered to mean the estate of such owner *** therein." By the amendment of 1875, the lien covered the building "and the lot of land on which the same shall stand, or be removed to." With the general revision of the whole lien law by the act of 1877, the lien was granted upon "the interest of said owner *** in the lot of land on which the same shall stand or be removed to." 

In 1887, this clause was again amended so that the lien attached to "the interest of the owner in the lot of land on which the same may stand, or be located, or to which it may be removed." The words "or be located" were stricken out in the law of 1889, and have never since reappeared in any subsequent amendment. By this law, it was also provided that "every person, including cestui que trusts, for whose immediate use, enjoyment, or bene-

184 

 fit any building, erection, or improvement shall be made shall, under this act, be included in the words owner or proprietor." With the law of 1892, the lien, for the first time, was granted not only upon the building or other structure but also "upon the material and machinery so furnished." And the lien was also granted "upon the interest, leasehold or otherwise, of the owner in the lot or land on which the same may stand, or to which it may be removed." This was the last amendment on this subject until the law of 1913.

Sec. 99. Contiguous Lots. 

"Where the construction, excavation or improvement consists of two or more buildings united together, situated on the same lot or contiguous or adjacent lots, or of separate buildings upon contiguous or adjacent lots, or where machinery, material, fuel, or labor has been furnished for improvements or structures which are located on separate tracts or parcels of land but operated as an entire plant or concern, and erected under one general contract, the lien for the labor, machinery, material or fuel so furnished, shall attach to all such constructions, excavations or improvements, together with the land upon, around or in front of which such labor, machinery, materials and fuel are furnished, the same as hereinlien in Ottawa County, while the plans and specifications were prepared in Lucas County, is not sustained by either reason or law. While it may be true that the labor on the plans and specifications was principally done in Lucas County, yet the mere result of that labor in Lucas County was to put upon paper figures and facts and drawings which were valueless until used and put into the form and proportions of a building. That could only be done in Ottawa County.

That was where the practical use was made of whatever labor was done in Lucas County. The benefit having resulted to the parties because of the application of the labor of the architects in Ottawa County, the lien should be filed there, where the building and the real estate were situated."

 more than passing mention. In this case it appears that the owner acquired several adjacent parcels of land on which it proceeded to erect three separate and independent buildings. There was no general contractor. Some contractors had general contracts with the owner applying to all the buildings. There were other contractors whose contracts were separate and distinct, and not general. It was urged that before G. C. 8316 could become effective so as to allow a lien claimant to perfect his lien by the filing of one affidavit, there must be one general contractor, having a contract covering the construction of all the buildings in detail. This contention the court denied. The words, "erected under one general contract" are not to be confined to a case where the owner may contract for the erection of the buildings in one general contract. They apply, equally as well, to a case where the owner erects his own buildings and enters into contracts for some portion of the work, as where he may let one contract for all the work and material. The question is not whether someone else had one general contract, but did the lien claimant have one general contract. 

The term "general contract" is defined as "a contract that is not confined to any single or definite building, but relates to all the buildings. A contract is not general where it relates to a single building and not to all." So, where one of the lien claimants had entered into three separate and distinct contracts, each complete in itself and each providing for a certain type of labor and material in each separate and distinct building, he could not, by filing one affidavit, acquire a valid lien against all the buildings and the lots on which they stood. Obviously, the work was not done "under one general contract," but

Sec. 99

 under three distinct contracts.23 It was urged by this claimant that the owner was constructing these buildings pursuant to one general plan and that it did not keep separate accounts of the material and labor that went into each building. Very properly the court held this was not the test. It is of no consequence what was in the mind of the owner. The test is whether the claimant did his work under one general contract. Another claimant in this case was a materialman. Having previously decided that the words "one general contract" are not restricted to the contractor for the erection of the buildings, the court rightly held that a material man, as well as a contractor, had the right to the benefit of G. C. 8316. The materialman, it appears, agreed to furnish lumber for the three buildings as would be ordered from time to time by the owner. Thereafter every order given, every delivery made, and price agreement entered into, was pursuant to this original agreement. It was contended that this was not "one general contract" but a series of contracts. But the court held that the term "one general contract" as used in G. C. 8316, does not mean necessarily one entire contract. So, in the language of the court, "where the owner informed the materialman that he wished to erect three buildings on a certain tract of land; that he wanted prices and a contract for material, 23.  Sec. 101. Lots Held in Severalty. 

Where two persons have made a joint contract with a builder for the erection of a single building to be placed on two adjoining lots owned in severalty by each of said persons, and a subcontractor furnishes materials which are used in the construction of the building under an entire contract with the builder, he is entitled to a joint lien, but not a separate lien against one lot and the part of the building standing thereon.30 So, too, a single building constructed on two lots owned by different persons, by the owner of one lot, with the knowledge and consent of the owner of the other, so connects the lots. that a single lien on the building will cover both lots.31 

In an early Ohio case,32 two married women, owners in severalty of adjoining lots, contracted with a builder for the erection of a house on the line of their lots, so as to provide a home for each on their respective lots. The builder filed a lien for a gross sum, being the balance claimed on the contract, against both lots. After conceding that the owners, being married women, were incompetent (under the law as it then existed) to bind them-

Sec. 102. Tenants in Common.

The interest of one tenant in common may be subjected to a mechanics lien for labor or material furnished for the construction of an improvement at his request, but the lien so acquired will not attach to the interest of the other tenant in common who has not consented to such improvement, or who is not, by his conduct, estopped from denying the authority of his cotenant to make such improvement upon their joint estate. No relation of agency is to be implied from the mere fact that they are tenants in common.34

Sec. 103.

Lien When Contracting Person Has No Title to the Land Improved. 

As a general rule, where buildings or other structures are annexed to the realty, in such a way as to become a part thereof, by a trespasser or by one having no authority, express or implied, they become the property of the owner of such real estate, and as such he may retain them.35 And since the person so erecting such buildings has no contract with the owner for their construction on his land, it would seem that no mechanics lien could be acquired against such buildings or the land on which they stand.36 In the absence of specific legislative authority for a lien under such circumstances, it is undoubtedly the rule that no lien could be acquired against either the buildings or the land.37 To a certain extent, this rule has been modified by the provisions of Section 8317 of the 

General Code: 

"Any person furnishing labor, machinery, material or fuel for the erection of a new building or structure upon land to which the person contracting for such erection has no legal title or to which the title shall be defective, shall have a lien therefor upon such building or structure, and the forfeiture or surrender of any title or claim of title, or equitable interest by such contracting person to such land shall not defeat the lien upon such building or structure of such per- 

35. Perley vs. City of Cambridge, 220 Mass. 507. 

36. See Section 39, ante. 

37. Where B, owning lot 5, gets material from C, and by mistake builds on lot 6, belonging to D. C has no lien either on lot 5 nor on the building as against D. 

Smith vs. Barnes, 38 Minn. 240. 

See also-Wagar vs. Briscoe, 38 Mich. 587. 

Jones on Liens-1258.

Sec. 198 

 son furnishing labor or material, as aforesaid. In case the property covered by a lien is held by the vendee in a land contract, or by a lessee, and he surrenders or forfeits his rights thereunder, the person or persons holding such liens may be subrogated to the rights of such vendee or lessee, as his rights existed immediately before such surrender or forfeiture, by performing the covenants contained in such contract or lease within thirty days after he shall have actual notice of such forfeiture. Any lien claimant may pay off any prior recorded lien, incumbrance or mortgage, and shall thereupon be subrogated to all the rights of the prior holder of such lien, incumbrance or mortgage."

Whether this statute may be invoked by a contractor, subcontractor, materialman or laborer, in a case where the person contracting for the erection of a new structure has no legal title to the land improved and no shadow or color of any contractual or equitable rights in the land improved, is a question upon which there may reasonably be some difference of opinion. In other words, can a bare trespasser improve the lands of another by the erection of a new building and thus create, by virtue of this statute, a right of lien on such building in favor of those who have furnished labor and material therefor? An examination of the whole context of this statute seems to disclose a definite purpose on the part of the legislature to confine its benefits to those cases only where the new structure has been erected by the contracting person in the belief that he has the legal title or the reasonable expectancy of acquiring the legal title or where he has some recognized contractual or equitable interest in the land improved. The following language of the statute—

Sec. 103

"and the forfeiture or surrender of any title or claim of title, or equitable interest by such contracting person to such land"-seems to imply necessarily that the contracting person must be more than some mere intermeddling trespasser. True it is that, "Possession itself is a species, though the lowest species, of legal title."38 It is prima facie evidence of the highest estate in land, namely a fee simple, and as such is alone sufficient to support ejectment against all the world except the true owner.39 

It involves such right and interest as makes the possessor an "owner" within the meaning of G. C. 8310.39 And such possessor will not be permitted, as against those whose labor and materials he has procured, to deny that he has any real or beneficial interest in the land improved.40 

Nor can he divest himself of such interest voluntarily, by abandonment or surrender, for the purpose of defeating the rights of lien claimants upon his interest therein, whatever it might be, unless his successor in interest can show a stronger equity than that of the lien claimant.41 

Upon these principles, it was held, even prior to the enactment of G. C. 8317, that a person in possession, under the mistaken belief that he had a right thereto, had, by the principles of equity analagous to the "occupying claimant" law42 a right to the value of lasting and valuable improvements erected by him upon the land; and 

38. Paine vs. Mason, 7 Oh. St. at 204. 

39. Dakin vs. Lecklider, 19 

C. C. 254. 

40. Williams vs. Webb, 2 Disn. 430. 

41. O'Brien vs. Meyer, 9 Bull. 337. 

42. G. C. 11908 et seq.

For discussion of this law see 

31 0. L. R. 263.

Sec. 200 

 that persons furnishing labor or materials for such improvements had the right to a lien upon such rights of the person in possession. The measure of value of such interest was not the cost of the buildings erected, but how much more valuable the land was in consequence of the improvements erected thereon. Inasmuch as both the owner and the lien claimants, in this case,39 desired a sale of the premises, there was no decision as to how the lien might be enforced if the owner did not choose to sell his land.

In all of these cases, however, the person in possession was in there under some color of right. He was no bold trespasser intruding upon another's property without the slightest justification or excuse. It still remains an open question whether the statute was intended to protect mechanics or materialmen who have trusted an unconscionable trespasser in the unwarranted invasion of another's rights and the commission of an unlawful act. 

But, be this as it may, the statute does provide a new right and a new remedy for those who have furnished labor or material for the erection of a structure for one claiming some equitable or legal estate in the land improved. It seems appropriate to discuss these cases separately. Before doing so, however, attention should be called to certain features of the statute that apply generally to these various types of cases. At the outset it will be noticed that the statute applies only where the labor and material are furnished "for the erection of a new building or structure." If the work performed is for the repair or alteration of a building or structure already

upon the land, the statute has no application.43 The lien is granted only upon the building or structure. It does not affect the land upon which the building is erected. 

Since the lien is upon the building only, it is obvious that the lien can be enforced against the building only. 

Though the statute does not specifically provide for its sale and removal, this right is necessarily implied. Having granted the lien, the legislature must be deemed to have granted also, by implication, the right to its enforcement; for, without this right of enforcement, it would certainly serve no useful purpose to grant the right to a lien. Since the land of the true owner cannot, without his consent, be sold, it would seem that the only way the lien on the building itself can be effectually enforced is to permit of its sale and removal from the premises. Such is the interpretation placed upon a similar statute by the 

Supreme Court of Michigan.44

The right to such a lien upon the new building or structure erected by one upon the land of another having once been acquired, "the forfeiture or surrender of any title or claim of title, or equitable interest by such contracting person to such land shall not defeat the lien upon such building or structure of such person furnishing labor or material, as aforesaid.”44a

As has already been seen from the general discussion in the previous section, the right to a lien upon the building or structure itself, where the building or structure is a new one, cannot be defeated by the forfeiture or surrender, voluntarily or involuntarily by the vendee, of his interest in the land improved. Accordingly, the familiar provisions in land contracts permitting the vendor to forfeit the interests of the vendee upon failure to pay the installments of the purchase price as they become due or for other specified causes, have no longer any effect, insofar as the rights of laborers and materialmen to a lien on the new building or structure are concerned.49a 

In addition to this, it is also provided that "In case the property covered by a lien is held by the vendee in a land contract, *** and he surrenders or forfeits his rights thereunder, the person or persons holding such liens may be subrogated to the rights of such vendee ***, as his rights existed immediately before such surrender or forfeiture, by performing the covenants contained in such contract*** within thirty days after he shall have actual notice of such forfeiture."49b

This right, it would appear, is not limited only to those cases where the labor or material is furnished for a new structure or building. It would also seem to apply

Sec. 104

 in those cases where the liens have been acquired for repairing, altering, or removing an old structure or building. Since the lien claimant is permitted to stand in the shoes of the vendee and thus to carry out his contract of purchase, it is of no consequence to the vendor whether the claimant acquired his lien in the erection of a new building or the repair of an old one. In the case of a contracting person who has no title to the land, and no contract or equity entitling him to acquire the title, it is obvious that no lien should be permitted for the repair, alteration or removal of another's building already standing upon his land. This would be forcing him to pay for something which he might not desire to have. By limiting the lien in such cases to the new building or structure erected upon his land, he is deprived of nothing to which he is in good morals entitled. He is simply being denied the right of keeping something he does not own and to which he is not entitled. He is not permitted to enrich himself at the expense of another's innocent mistake. In the case of the vendee, however, the vendor has agreed to sell him the land and all the improvements thereon. 

With its sale, his interest ceases. Whether the buildings thereon are new or old, whether the work is that of new construction or merely repairs and alterations upon old buildings cannot affect him. By his contract he has agreed to part with his title. New or old, the buildings, such as they are, pass with it. His anxiety is for the payment of the purchase price. Whether he gets it from the vendee, or from the lien claimants of any class, should make no difference, and certainly whether, in the latter case, he gets it from a lien claimant whose claim arises out of work done on a new structure, or for work done on an

Sec. 206 

 old building, is a distinction that deserves no serious discussion. It is unfortunate that the two distinct remedies provided in this section should have been incorporated in one section. Confusion, with the attendant uncertainty of interpretation, is the only result of such a combination. 

Even the last four lines of this section it seems, should form no part thereof. It is a provision that could well stand alone. It is one of general application and should not necessarily be limited to the restricted title of this section. 

Sec. 105. Licensee.

Where one not in possession of land is permitted to build a structure thereon under license from the owner, no lien for labor or material furnished the person contracting for the erection of such structure can be enforced against the interest of the true owner of the land. The rule that one encouraging an act to be done cannot afterwards exercise his legal right in opposition to such consent, if the other party was induced to change his position to his pecuniary prejudice, cannot be invoked so as to create a materialman's or laborer's lien upon the land, since there is no fraud, actual or constructive, by the true owner.50 But by virtue of G. C. 8317, the lien would undoubtedly attach to the structure itself, if it were a new one.

Ia. 291. 

In Westport Lumber Co. vs. 

Harris, 131 Mo. App. 94, it was said: "Where the owner does nothing more than consent to the improvement, we know of no rule of law or principle of justice that will extend such permission into a delegation of authority to bind his estate to answer mechanics liens created by the contracts of his licensee."

Leasehold.

By the express provisions of G. C. 8310, a mechanics lien may attach to the interest of a lessee of the land upon which the building may stand, to the extent of the right or interest of such lessee at the time work was commenced or materials were begun to be furnished by the contractor, under the original contract, and also to the extent of any subsequent acquired interest of such lessee. 

Even before specific authority for such a lien was granted by express provisions of the statute, the courts had held that the word "owner" is not limited to an owner in fee, but includes also an owner of a leasehold estate.51 

But since the lien attached to the interest of the lessee, it could affect his interest only. It could not reach beyond that interest so as to affect any rights of the lessor in his land or the buildings thereon. So where a lessee of land erected thereon a building and a mechanic filed a lien against the same and, having obtained a judgment therefor, sold the building to a purchaser at a sale upon execution, and the purchaser removed the building from the premises, it was held that, since by the terms of the lease all the improvements erected thereon by the lessee were to be delivered up, on the expiration of the lease, to the lessor, the purchaser acquired by his purchase no greater estate than what the lessee had, and as he had no right to remove the building, the purchaser acquired no such

Sec. 108. Appurtenance. 

By the provision of G. C. 8310, the lien extends not only to the principal structure but to any appurtenance thereof.62 

Sec. 109.

Machinery. 

It was very generally held by the courts of the various states during the early history of mechanics lien laws. that no lien could attach for machinery, which had been furnished for the construction, alteration or repair of a manufactory or other building, unless it had become affixed or so far attached to the realty that its existence as personal property had been lost by reason of its having been merged with the realty. The idea of a mechanics lien attaching for the furnishing of personal property, as such, was unthinkable. The whole theory of the mechan- 

62. See-Brush Electric Co. vs. Warwick Electric Co., 6 0. 

D. 475, where a reservoir was built for the purpose of storing water for the use of an electric light plant, and the court held that such reservoir was an appurtenance to the plant and a lien for work upon such reservoir extended not only to it, but to the whole electric plant.

Sec. 109

 ics lien laws was that the labor or material of the mechanic or materialman had become a part of the realty and had so enhanced its value as a permanent improvement that it was unjust to deny him a lien to secure the payment of his claim, since neither the law nor equity afforded him any real relief under the circumstances. 

Accordingly a lien was allowed for furnishing machinery only when it became a part of the realty. But such lien was upon the real estate, although in effect it covered the machinery too. It was not a lien upon the particular machinery furnished, but a lien upon the whole building and premises. It did not attach directly to the machinery, but only indirectly when that machinery became a part of the realty affected by the lien.63 

The question did not present much difficulty when only the rights of the owner of the realty and the person furnishing the machinery were involved, but it did offer many perplexing problems when the rights of the furnisher were at odds with the vendor and vendee, lessor and lessee, and mortgagor and mortgagee. In the latter cases, the question usually turned on whether the machinery was or was not a fixture. This had always been a troublesome question and the courts of the same jurisdictions were often contradicting themselves in the application of their own rules upon this subject of fixtures. 

The Ohio courts seem to have adopted the rule that all machinery used to supply power was a part of the realty and therefore subject to a mechanics lien, while everything to which power was supplied from the completed 

63. Hall vs. St. Louis Mfg. Co., 22 Mo. App. 33. 

Rose vs. Persee, 29 Conn. 256.

Sec. 

214 

 plant was personalty and as such was, of course, not subject to a mechanics lien.64 Of course, under this rule, the machinery had to be affixed to the realty in order to become a part thereof. If machinery was sold and delivered to the plant, for the purpose of being used therein, but was not actually set up and used, it retained its character as personalty regardless of whether it was of the kind that supplied power or to which power was supplied.64

So far then as the right of a mechanic or materialman to have a lien upon machinery furnished by others than the lien claimant himself is concerned, it is undoubtedly the rule that his lien will only affect such machinery as is a part of the realty, against which his lien is filed, under the law relating to fixtures.65 64.

There is undoubtedly an increasing tendency to relax the former strictness and technicalities of the old rules relating to fixtures in connection with the question as to what property a mechanics liens will attach. "The true rule is that in a controversy between the claimant of a mechanics lien and the owner of real estate upon which the property of the lienor has been placed, or between vendor and vendee, or between .mortgagor and mortgagee, engines, machinery, houses, buildings, and every other thing which is essential to the particular use to which the realty is applied, or between which and the balance of the realty there is a manifest and necessary dependence, or which is intended to be and is permanently and habitually used as a part of the property constituting the real estate of the owner upon which it is placed, becomes a part of that realty, whether it can be removed without physical injury

Sec. 109

Such was the rule, too, as far as the rights of a person furnishing the machinery were concerned. Unless the machinery became a fixture and therefore a part of the real estate, the seller of such machinery had no right to a lien, for the reason that he could not be said to have improved the real estate upon which the lien was sought. 

The machinery still retained its personal character, and as such did not afford the seller the right to a lien upon the real estate upon which it temporarily stood.66 

By the amendment of April 15, 1889,67 however, this rule was changed as the lien was, by this amendment, granted not only upon the real estate and structure, but also upon "the machinery so furnished." This provision is now a part of G. C. 8310 which, abridged, provides, "Every person who * * * furnishes machinery for erecting, altering, repairing or removing *** a *** manufactory *** shall have a lien to secure the payment thereof upon such *** factory *** and upon the machinery or material to the realty or not, however slight its physical connection with the real estate, and even when there is no actual fastening of the one to the other."

If such material or machinery becomes a part of the realty, he is entitled to a lien therefor, but it is only to be worked out through the realty, and there can be no lien upon the material, machinery, or other structure, as such alone."
