Sec. 110. Public Property. 

The authorities are practically unanimous in asserting that a mechanics lien does not attach to and cannot be enforced against the public property of a state, county, municipality, or other political subdivision, acquired and used by and for the benefit of the public.74 It is clearly against public policy to permit an individual to secure a lien upon public property and thus deprive the public of one of its useful instruments of government. "The possessor of a mechanics lien on real estate can gain title to it by foreclosure. If such a lien can be imposed upon public buildings, they can thus be turned into private buildings. If it can attach to a schoolhouse, it is difficult to see why it would not equally attach to a city hall, a county courthouse, or a county jail. It would be intolerable to put it in the power of a private citizen, in case the negligence of a county should result in his obtaining a foreclosure of a mechanics lien, to take possession of a courthouse, and turn out the courts, or of a jail, and turn chanics liens upon such real estate.

Sec. 111. Religious and Charitable Societies.

While it has been held in a few instances that a mechanics lien cannot be obtained on the property of religi ous or charitable institutions,87 there seems to be no good reason for such exemption; and the great weight of authority, therefore, sustains the right to a mechanics lien upon the property of institutions of this character.88

The lien may attach to an equitable interest in property,92 unless there is some condition in the title under which the property is held which prohibits the person who owns the interest to place the lien upon it. The duty of ascertaining the nature of the interest and the title of the person who contracts to have the work done or materials used upon property which might be the basis of a mechanics lien, and to ascertain whether such person was authorized to encumber it with such lien, is imposed upon the one furnishing the labor or materials. He who fails to investigate acts at his own risk.93 Property held in trust, therefore, is not subject to a mechanics lien where the deed creating the trust, which is duly recorded, expressly provides that no contract creating a lien shall be made.94 And of course, what the trustee cannot do directly, he cannot do indirectly, as by failing to object to the furnishing of labor or materials upon the trust property on the order of other persons.95 A trustee, having full power to manage, improve, and repair the property, may usually do so where the property is a trust estate, but the trustee of an express trust cannot create a mechanics lien upon the trust estate, unless a power is conferred upon him by statute or by a court of competent jurisdiction, or

As a general rule, administrators and executors have no inherent power or authority by reason of their appointment and qualification to enter into a contract out of which the right of another to acquire a mechanics lien upon the decedent's estate, might arise. The administrator or executor of an estate is not the owner or proprietor of the lands of the estate, nor the agent of the heirs within the meaning of the statute relating to mechanics liens.107 

Nor will the express authority of a court confer upon them the power to bind the estate by contracts made for improvements out of which the right to a mechanics lien may arise.108 By virtue of G. C. 8323-5, however, “executors and administrators of deceased owners shall have the rights and be subject to the liabilities under this chapter that such owners would enjoy and be subject to, if alive." This provision undoubtedly authorizes a lien for work already begun by the decedent, but, it is believed, does not permit the making of an entirely new contract for the construction of an improvement not commenced by the decedent.

 Sec. 114. Registered Land Titles. 

Real estate registered under the so called "Torrens" law109 may be subjected to mechanics liens. By virtue of the provisions of G. C. 8572-75 the right to file mechanics liens against such registered land is specifically granted. It must be born in mind, however, that the Torrens law provides the only method by which liens may be acquired upon registered land and altho its provisions may be in conflict with the general law relating to mechanics liens, the provisions of the Torrens law will control and only such mechanics liens which are recorded in accordance with the Torrens law will be valid as against registered land.110 The statutory requirements for obtaining such liens will be discussed in a subsequent chapter.111 

Sec. 115. Lien upon Proceeds of Sale.

Money derived from the sale of property upon which there is a valid mechanics lien will be treated by a court of equity as it would treat the property before sale, and such court will follow it into the hands of the party who has converted the property into money. Thus, where property subject to mechanics liens is sold by a receiver the liens are not thereby lost, but attach to the proceeds of the sale in the hands of the receiver.112 It not infre

Sec. 116. Proceeds of Insurance Policies. 

Policies of insurance against fire are mere personal contracts of indemnity, which do not attach to the property insured as an incident, nor take its place when the property is destroyed, so as to entitle any one having a mechanics or other lien upon the property to any interest therein, unless by contract the owner was obligated to insure for the benefit of such lien claimant.113 Thus, the holder of a mechanics lien has no claim on the proceeds of insurance policies taken out by the owner and payable been sold, but remained upon the premises, the prior lien of the mechanics upon it, to the extent of its value, would be undoubted.

It having been sold and converted into money in violation of this prior right, the relief should be to award the money realized from its sale. A court of equity cannot allow rights to be thus destroyed by the wrongful act of one who is substantially claiming to have converted the property of another into money which he may claim as his own."

Sec. 117. Dower.

A widow's dower is not affected by the lien of a mechanic. She is entitled to dower in all the real estate of which her husband was seized during coverture, unless she has released it in the form prescribed by law, except when a lien is created for the purchase money at the time the husband became seized. Mechanics are bound to know dower will attach, and, on the death of the husband, vest in the widow.116 In an action to foreclose a mechanics lien, in which mortgagees intervened, and their claims were found superior to the dower estate, and a sale pursuant thereto was required to be made free of such dower estate, so that the wife was divested of her dower by such sale, it was held to be the duty of the court to ascertain the value of such dower and pay the same out of the proceeds of the sale. In such case the wife was not estopped to claim that her dower rights were superior to the rights of the mechanics lien claimant for placing an improvement on the property under contract with the husband, because she stood by while the mechanic was improving the property, since she had no duty to speak.117

A mechanics lien is purely a creature of the statutes. 

It has no existence, either in law or in equity, independent of the statutes. Since they alone prescribe the only meth-

Sec. 119

Proceedings to Perfect the Lien od by which a mechanics lien may be acquired, a substantial compliance with the statutory requirements is necessary in order to perfect a valid and enforcible lien.1 

It is, therefore, the purpose of this chapter to discuss the steps required to be taken by the contractor, subcontractor, materialman and laborer, in order to acquire and perfect their respective rights to a lien.

Sec. 134 Proceedings to Perfect the Lien 

Sec. 133. Who Is An "Agent."

The term "agent" as used in the mechanics lien law refers to one who is the representative of the owner of the building, generally, or is his agent with reference to the erection, repair, or improvement of the structure upon which a mechanics lien is attempted to be asserted for labor or material furnished, or who represents him in the control and supervision of the premises. An attorney at law employed only in an action pending in court is engaged in a special employment, his agency is limited, and he does not by reason merely of such employment and service represent the owner with reference to a building contract, or the erection or repair of a structure pursuant to such contract, or in the control or supervision of the premises of such owner.26 Nor is the vendee under a land contract, in any sense, the agent of the vendor so as to bind the interest of the latter in the premises for improvements erected thereon by the former.27 

Sec. 134. 

Materialman or Laborer Not Required to Furnish Statement. 

The provisions of G. C. 8312, requiring a sworn statement to be served upon the owner of a structure being erected or repaired under a contract, do not apply to a material man or laborer. By the express language of the statute this prerequisite to a lien is required of the contractor and subcontractor only.28

Sec. 147.

Duty of County Recorder. 

"The county recorder shall endorse upon every such affidavit the date and hour of its filing, and record the same in a separate book to be kept therefor."42 With the filing of the affidavit in the office of the recorder the lien claimant has done all that he is required to do. He is under no obligation to see that the affidavit is recorded. 

The lien is created by the filing of the affidavit with the recorder and not by the recording of the same.42a Thus, a recorder's mistake in recording the affidavit for a lien in the wrong book will not defeat the lien.43 Nor will the

Sec. 148. Elements of the Affidavit-In General. 

The contents of the affidavit as now required by G. 

C. 8314 have been materially simplified as compared with the former requirements as found in R. S. 3185. 

Under the earlier law an affidavit containing an itemized statement of the account was required, together with a description of any promissory note or notes given, with all credits or offsets thereon. If the contract was in writing a copy thereof had to be attached, together with a statement of the amounts and times of payment to be made thereunder. A description of the property improved completed the affidavit. The obvious chances of errors and omissions in the preparation of such affidavits gave rise to frequent litigation on questions of technical departures from the requirements of the statute with the result that many otherwise valid liens were defeated by the innocent failure of the lien claimant to comply with these technical and rigid requirements. With the redrafting of the whole law in 1913, a more simple and, at the same time, a sufficiently informative affidavit was prescribed. 28.

Sec. 258 

 Sec. 149. Who May File the Affidavit. 

"Every person, or his agent or attorney, whether contractor, subcontractor, materialman, or laborer, who wishes to avail himself of the provisions of this statute, shall make and file for record *** an affidavit” ***. 

The statute does not require that any particular person or agent shall make the statutory affidavit. Undoubtedly any one acquainted with the facts may make it.45 Thus, a bookkeeper, though not a member of the lien claimant firm, but familiar with the transaction, may sign the affidavit.46 The oath is in no respect binding or conclusive upon anyone; it is only intended to prevent vexation and unfounded liens being entered upon the records; for this reason the oath of any one familiar with the transaction and acting for the claimant will be sufficient.47 Nor is it required that the person making it should have personal knowledge of all the facts contained in it, if he is satisfied of their truth and is willing to make oath thereto. 

It is immaterial, therefore, whether the affiant had personal or hearsay knowledge of their truth.48 Where a contract is let to a partnership but, before the work is completed, one of the partners abandons the job and the other carries it on to completion, he may file the affidavit for lien in his own name.49

Sec. 152. Where Affidavit Sets Forth an Exces sive Amount.

It must be born in mind that the affidavit sets forth the amount which the lien claimant alleges is due him. 

The purpose of the affidavit is to notify persons dealing with the property, as well as the owner, what amount the affiant claims is due him. Quite naturally the claimant is justified in asserting a claim for all that he in good faith believes is due him, altho upon the trial of his case it may be found that several of the items of his alleged claim are not lienable items. The correctness of his claim, therefore, is not infrequently a perplexing question of law. For these reasons the courts have uniformly held that the filing of an affidavit for an amount in excess of what is finally allowed will not of itself defeat the lien, unless it be shown that the claimant, knowingly and in bad faith, undertook by false charges to subject the owner's property to an improper burden. In other words, in order to defeat the lien, it must appear that the amount claimed is so grossly incorrect as to be fraudulent.52 

51a. See Section 88, ante.

St. 153.

In Robinson vs. Brooks, 31 

Wash. 60, it was held that where nonlienable items had been wilfully included in the lien notice to such an amount that, when taken in connection with the facts and circumstances of the case, clearly established bad faith, the whole lien should fail.

Proceedings to Perfect the Lien Sec. 153. Affidavit Must Contain a Description of the Property. 

The affidavit must contain a description of the premises on which the lien is sought to be obtained. Without such description the affidavit would frequently be of no use to the owner, and never of value to other lien claimants, mortgagees, purchasers, or creditors. Accordingly, the failure to describe the particular premises upon which a lien is sought to be obtained renders the affidavit fatally defective.53 But technical exactness is not required. It is a matter of common knowledge that the claimants themselves, without the aid of counsel, usually prepare their own affidavits, and hence courts have been reluctant to set aside such claims merely on account of loose or technically inexact descriptions. Only such descriptions which are calculated to mislead subsequent lienors, mortgagees, purchasers and creditors, or which wholly fail to locate the premises, will invalidate the lien. Some courts, very properly, require greater certainty in the description where the rights of third persons are to be affected by the lien than in cases where the contest in entirely between the lien claimant and the owner. 

Generally speaking, the rule seems to be that a description will be sufficient if it locates the premises with convenient or reasonable certainty. If there be enough in the description to enable a party familiar with the locality to identify the premises with reasonable certainty to the

Sec. 270 

 Sec. 157. When the Affidavit Must Be Filed. 

"Such affidavit shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which the last of the machinery, materials or fuel shall have been furnished at the building, or the last of the labor shall have been performed by the person claiming the lien.”75

It must be borne in mind, at the outset of this discussion, that the mechanics lien law as found in 103 Ohio Laws, 369-379, and amended and supplemented in 106 Ohio Laws, 522-534, is the exclusive method by which a mechanics lien may be acquired against the property of a private individual, firm or corporation, and the same must be filed within sixty days, as provided therein. The provisions of G. C. 8324 et seq., providing for the filing of a sworn and itemized statement of account within four months from the performance of the labor or the delivery of material, have reference only to construction work on public jobs as distinguished from private contracts.76 

As the lien has no existence except by force of the statute, it is essential to its validity that it be taken and perfected within the time allowed by statute: that is, that the affidavit be filed within sixty days from the date on which the last of the labor, machinery, material or fuel shall have been furnished. 

Smalley vs. Bodinus, 120 Mich. 363. 

If a notary, who has administered the oath signs the affidavit and states that the affiant signed and swore to it before him, the failure of the notary to affix his seal will not invalidate the affidavit. 

Ashley vs. Wright, 19 Oh. St. 291. 

75. G. C. 8314. 

See-Acorn Supply Co. vis. 

Fingerhut, 6 Abs. 588. 

76. Cott-Mohrman Co. VS. 

Massillon Foundry & Machine 

Co., 12 Oh. App. 51.

Sec. 157

Proceedings to Perfect the Lien 

It will be noted that the period for filing the affidavit expires 60 days after the machinery, materials or fuel "shall have been furnished at the building." Does this mean that actual delivery upon the building site is essential to the acquiring of a lien? G. C. 8310 and 8311, in creating the right to a lien, prescribe no such limitation. By these sections one who furnishes material-"for constructing, altering or repairing" a structure by virtue of a contract with the owner, or who furnishes material to a principal contractor or subcontractor "in carrying forward" such contract shall have a lien. No place for delivery of such material is prescribed. In many cases the materialman's contract calls for delivery at other places than the building site. Not infrequently the material is fabricated at the plant of the materialman and delivered to the yard or warehouse of the contractor or a subcontractor for delivery by him to the site whenever he shall be ready to install the same. In other cases, delivery upon the site would be impracticable, there being no room for the storage of large quantities of bulky material. As has been stated,76a the rule generally seems to be that the material is "furnished", within the meaning of G. C. 8310 and 8311, when it is delivered at the place designated in the contract, whether it be upon the building site or not.

These words of limitation, (“furnished at the building") as found in G. C. 8314, should, therefore, under the liberal construction permitted by G. C. 8323-8, be so construed as to allow a constructive delivery at the building. Thus, where a materialman fabricates or sells mate- 

76a. See Sec. 82, ante.

Sec. 

272 

 rial for use in a particular building and delivers it to the owner, a contractor or a subcontractor at the place designated in his contract for such delivery, his title to such material has passed and it may be said to henceforth be in the constructive possession of the owner at the building for such is its ultimate destination if the owner's contractor properly performs his contract. The materialman has done all that he has agreed to do. He has "furnished” his material within the meaning of the statute. Such is the decision of the Common Pleas Court of Cuyahoga County.76b

In this case the lien claimant had several contracts with the general contractor to provide cut stone for a building. The rough stone was shipped to the lien claimant and placed on a lot a short distance from the actual building site. Here the stone was cut and prepared. The owner failed to proceed with the completion of the building. Nevertheless the lien claimant was allowed to perfect his lien for the cut and prepared stone, the title of which had passed to the owner of the building, altho the material still remained in the yard of the lien claimant. 

Constructive delivery at the building may be said to have been made, but certainly there was no actual delivery. 

It would surely not be in keeping with the general spirit of the law to hold otherwise. To make it necessary for the materialman to make an actual delivery of his materials at the building in order to qualify himself to acquire a lien would often require him to do a futile thing, as in the case where an owner has been unable to 

76b. Harriman National Bank vs. Boulevard Co., 25 N. P. (N. 

S.) 263. 

See lien claim of John M. 

Woods on page 284.

Proceedings to Perfect the Lien Sec. 158 

go forward with his building and the materialman has in his possession, or in the possession of the contractor or subcontractor, a large amount of valuable and perishable material which might be ruined or greatly depreciated if left to the mercy of the elements on the site of an unfinished building.

Thus, it would seem, altho the question may still be an open one, that delivery of materials at the building may be constructively so delivered if actually delivered at the designated place or to the designated person named in the materialman's contract.77

In all cases, then, when delivery is actually made at the building, it being immaterial by whom such delivery was made, the affidavit for lien should be filed within sixty days from the date on which the last of such material shall have been furnished at the building. 

However, where no actual delivery is made at the building but constructive delivery only is made, the lien claimant should file his affidavit within sixty days from the date on which the last delivery of such material has been made to the person or at the place specified in the contract for such delivery.

Sec. 159. Eastern Standard Time Governs. 

The standard of time throughout the state is, by virtue of G. C. 5979, eastern standard time, "and when, by a law, rule, order or process of any authority, created by or pursuant to law, an act must be performed at or within a prescribed time, it shall be so performed to such standard of time."

Sec. 160. Filing Affidavit after Office Hours of 

Recorder on Last Day.

The mere fact that the office of a recorder may, by virtue of his own rule or custom, close at four o'clock, is not sufficient of itself to invalidate a lien filed with the recorder after such time on the last day of the statutory period allowed for filing the affidavit for a lien. In order to accommodate a lien claimant, a recorder may, in spite of his usual rule for closing his office, keep it open until midnight of the last day to receive and file the claimant's affidavit for a lien.79 And where a lien claimant gained access, on the last day of the period within which to file a lien, to a recorder's office on Saturday afternoon after the usual hour for closing such office, and tendered his affidavit to the recorder who was still there, but the latter refused to receive it on the grounds that it was after

Contract Entire or Severable. 

The question often arises in the filing of mechanics liens as to whether the contract under which it is to be filed is an entire or severable one. If it is an entire contract only one lien need be filed; if it be severable, a separate lien for each particular performance, whether it be for labor or the delivery of materials, must be filed.81

Sec. 162. What Is the Last Date of Performance of Labor or Delivery of Material. 

It is not always an easy task to determine the last date on which the last labor was performed or the last delivery was made "at the building." Not infrequently, after the work of construction appears to have been completed, it becomes necessary for laborers to perform additional work and materialmen to deliver additional material to remedy defects in their work or to complete certain items of work, which, by oversight, were omitted. But great care should be exercised by courts in scrutinizing such additional items of labor and material, to see wheth-

This may be true, but we are unable to find that it was something which was not required to be done by the original contract between the parties. If there was a defective installation originally, then a correction of that defect would be a thing done under the contract, and ought to be regarded as part of the duty of the plaintiff in the fulfillment of its contract; and, if done, ought to carry with it the right to file a lien for the whole amount, altho there had been a lapse of more than a year between the original installation of the furnace and the work performed on January 27, 1927."

Sec. 165

Proceedings to Perfect the Lien Sec. 165. New Work or Extras. 

If the labor performed or material delivered is furnished under a separate and distinct agreement, it will not serve to extend the time within which the lien for the original labor and material should be filed. Thus where the contract is only for furnishing machinery, and labor is performed in placing it in position, or otherwise in the construction of the building, under a separate agreement, or gratuitously, the lien for the machinery must be taken within the time limited by statute, after the contract under which it was furnished has been performed. Separate contracts cannot be tacked together so as to extend the time for taking the lien under either.93 The Ohio lien laws contemplate a definite time limit, namely, the termination of the original contract of construction, from which the time runs for the filing of a materialman's lien. 

Thus, the furnishing of drawers for breakfast tables and window frames for windows not specified in the original plans, after the work had been completed according to the plans, are not acts "of carrying forward, performing or completing the contract," within the meaning of the lien laws, and do not have the effect of extending the time in which liens may be filed.94 So, where a material-

Work done or materials furnished by one, who derives his authority from a contractor, after the latter has abandoned the job and has lost his right to continue the work and with knowledge that the contract had been abandoned and that the owner had taken possession for the purpose of completing it on his own account, is not done with the owner's consent and the time within which whereas it is denied if the rights of third persons are involved.

The contractor's abandonment is an abandonment of the entire contract, and not a part of it. The subcontractor, therefore, having borne no contractual relation whatever with the owner, is without lawful right to complete the installation of the heating plant against the will of the owner, after the abandonment of the principal contractor. To have preserved his right to a lien the subcontractor should have filed his affidavit within sixty days from the date on which the last of the materials were furnished or the last labor performed, while the contract for the construction of the house was still in force.101

Generally these questions are not promptly solved. Efforts to refinance are often made and are not always successful. Sec. 286 

Sec. 169.

Death of Original Contractor. 

Subcontractors, materialmen and laborers cannot, after the death of the principal contractor, either perform labor or furnish material so as to charge his estate. Their rights are fixed and determined at the death of the head contractor unless his personal representative should, with the consent of the owner, see fit to complete the same under the original contract.104 As the death of the contractor terminates the contract, the subcontractors, materialmen and laborers, having borne no contractual relation with the owner, are without authority to complete the contract against the will of the owner. In such case then the time within which to file their liens would seem to be sixty days from the date on which the last item of labor or material was furnished during the lifetime of the contractor.105 Of course, if, after the death of the contractor, his administrator with the consent of the owner, elects to complete the work and the subcontractor, materialmen and laborers continue to perform labor and furnish material to such administrator for completing the original contract, the statutory period for filing liens for such work will commence to run from the date of the last performance of labor or the furnishing of material, by the respective lien claimants, under such contract so completed by the administrator.106

Sec. 170.

Affidavit Must Show Date of the Last Item of Labor or Material Furnished. 

An affidavit for a lien, filed with the county recorder, which fails to state either the date when the last labor was performed or material furnished, or that the same was performed or furnished within sixty days, is ineffective to perfect a lien.107 G. C. 8314, it is true, does not in express terms require that the affidavit should show when the last labor was performed or material was delivered, but it does provide that the affidavit must be filed within sixty days of the time when the last labor was performed or material furnished. Moreover, the holding of the courts under G. C. 8314, as it existed before 1913, were to the effect that the affidavit must show affirmatively on its face that it was filed within the statutory period after the date of the last item of labor or material furnished.108 This requirement being thus interpreted as essential to the validity of the lien, the lien claimant will not be permitted to supply such deficiency in his affidavit by parol.109

Sec. 173. Who Is the "Owner."

The statute requires that the copy of the affidavit be served upon "the owner, part owner or lessee of such premises or his agent." Not infrequently it happens that the contracting owner will sell the premises, on which the building is being erected, to another before the lien period has expired. The question arises, therefore, as to whether the contracting owner is the party to be served or the owner of the premises at the time the lien is filed. 

Two early cases held that the owner designated in G. C. 

8315 is the owner to whom the materials were furnished or for whom the labor was performed, and not some subsequent purchaser who acquired title after the date of the furnishing of the first item of labor or material.118

C. 

8315.119 And where one, who is the owner, leases the premises under an oral lease to another, who enters into a contract with a contractor for the erection of a building on the leased premises, a materialman who furnished materials for such building may perfect a lien against

Mechanics Lien Law and the Torrens Act. But they are not incompatible; the privilege granted by the former of acquiring liens being merely restricted in its exercise by the latter law. The Torrens Act is therefore given effect as an exception to the Mechanics Lien Law.127 The right to acquire a mechanics lien upon land registered under the Torrens Act is not denied, but the method of acquiring it is governed in part by the Torrens Act and not exclusively by the Mechanics Lien Law. It is plain that the provisions of G. C. 8572-54 recognize the right of one to file a mechanics lien against registered land. But something a little different from the affidavit required by G. C. 8314 is necessary in order to perfect the lien. It becomes the duty of the lien claimant, therefore, who is about to file a lien, to ascertain whether the land which he seeks to charge with his lien is registered land or not, for his failure so to do may result in defeating his lien if he has not properly complied with the special requirements of the Torrens Act with regard to the steps necessary to be taken to acquire a lien upon registered land.

In the case of land not registered it has already been seen that a mechanic or materialman has an inchoate lien, dating from the commencement of the furnishing of labor or material, which may become a valid and subsisting lien upon the premises so improved by the filing of an affidavit for a lien within sixty days from the date of the last item of labor or material furnished. Purchasers or encumbrancers of such property after construction has commenced acquire their rights in such property subject to the right of mechanics and materialmen to perfect their liens within the statutory period. But such is not the case where registered land is involved. By virtue of 

G. C. 8572-54 and G. C. 8572-89 no mechanics lien can affect the title to registered land, until after the same is noted upon the registered certificate of title. A bona fide purchaser, therefore, who has purchased the land, upon which an improvement has been erected, during the stat utory period of sixty days within which the mechanic (in the case of unregistered land) might file his lien, has the right to rely solely upon the certificate of title or certifi-

There is, however, a method provided by the Torrens Act for the protection of mechanics and materialmen in such case. This is accomplished by the filing of an affi davit of adverse claim or what is known as a caveat. Any person desiring to assert any interest in or claim or lien against registered land adverse to the title of any registered owner may make affidavit thereto setting forth his claim or lien and how and under whom derived, and the character and nature thereof. He shall also state his full name, place of residence and post office address and shall designate a place within the state at which all notices relating thereto may be served upon him. "Upon the filing of such affidavit in the recorder's office the recorder shall enter forthwith a memorial thereof, upon the registered certificate of title, stating the exact time when said affidavit was filed and the purport and nature thereof "136 Within ten days thereafter the lien claimant must "notify the registered owner by registered letter with five days' return card thereon directed to his registered address, of the filing of such affidavit and claim and make proof thereof to the satisfaction of the recorder.

The filing of the caveat itself creates no lien; it merely preserves the right to one until the lien claimant shall have filed his affidavit for the lien. This affidavit must be filed in accordance with the provisions of G. C. 8314.

Sec. 178. Inchoate and Perfected Liens. 

At one time it was held in Ohio that the right to acquire a lien, being a personal right given to the mechanic for his own protection, was not assignable.¹ On the other hand, it was conceded that once a lien had been perfected it became the proper subject of an assignment.2 This distinction is no longer made, and an inchoate lien as well as a perfected lien is, by virtue of the statute, assignable.³ 

Sec. 179. In Whose Name Lien Perfected and 

Enforced.

Whether an inchoate lien, if assigned, should be perfected in the name of the assignee, or whether a perfected lien, if assigned, should be enforced in the name of the assignee, are questions which the courts of Ohio have apparently not yet passed upon. Unlike the Michigan act, 1. City of Hamilton vs. Stillwaugh, 11 C. C. 182. 

2. In re Engle, 1 N. P. 110. 

3. "All liens or claims for liens which may arise or accrue under the terms of this act shall be assignable." 

G. C. 8323-6.

Sec. 179

Assignment of Lien or Contract the Ohio act is silent upon these questions. The Michigan act, after using the language later adopted in the Ohio act, then says: "and proceedings to enforce such liens may be maintained by and in the name of the assignee, who shall have as full and ample power to enforce the same as if such proceedings were taken under the provisions of this act by and in the name of the lien claimants themselves."4 This section of the act has been construed to mean that the assignee has not only the right to enforce in his own name a lien perfected by his assignor, but also to perfect in his own name the right to a lien possessed by his assignor.5

There is, of course, some room for speculation as to why the legislature of Ohio, with the language of the Michigan act and the interpretation of the Michigan Courts before it, omitted the directory provisions of the Michigan law with reference to the manner in which an assigned inchoate lien may be perfected and an assigned perfected lien may be enforced. To the writer it does not seem to necessarily follow that by the omission of this clause the Ohio legislature intended to repudiate the principles enunciated therein. It may well have been regarded as mere surplusage, on the theory that the general power to assign inchoate and perfected liens carried with it, as a necessary complement thereof, the right to perfect and enforce the same in the name of the assignee. 

The obvious purpose of the act (in making inchoate as well as perfected liens assignable) was to enable the mechanic, if in need of funds, to readily dispose of his 

4. See-Wyke's Michigan Me chanics Liens-127. 

5. McAllister vs. Des Rochers, 132 Mich. 381.

Sec. 302 

 claim for cash. This purpose would seem to be more surely accomplished if the purchaser be entitled not only to the debt and to the security of the lien of his assignor, but also to the very valuable right of perfecting and enforcing the lien in his own name. 

Sec. 180. Form of Assignment.

No particular form of assignment is prescribed by the act. Any agreement, whether it be oral or written, will be sufficient, if the intent of the parties to effect an assignment is clearly established.6

Sec. 181. Assignment of Lien on Registered Land. 

As the Torrens Act prescribes the only method by which mechanics liens may be acquired on land registered within the provisions of the act, so also it prescribes the only method by which such liens may be assigned.7 

Sec. 182. Effect of Assignment by Principal Con tractor or Subcontractor.

As the lien of the subcontractor is superior to the lien or right to a lien in favor of the principal contractor, and as the lien of laborers and materialmen is superior to that of the principal contractor or subcontractor, it necessarily follows that "an assignment or transfer by the principal contractor or subcontractor, of his contract with the owner or principal contractor, *** shall save and be subject to the claims of every laborer, mechanic, subcon-

Sec. 199. Instances of Estoppel as Affecting Mechanics Liens

The distinction between a "waiver" and an "estoppel" is not always apparent, and the terms are sometimes (quite improperly) used interchangeably. The term "waiver" generally implies an intention on the part of a person possessing some right under a contract, or the law, to relinquish it for the benefit of another. "Waiver" is ordinarily personal, and, in the absence of some special agreement or consideration, its existence is to be determined solely from the conduct of the party making it, independent of the acts of any other party affected by it. 

In "estoppel", this distinctly personal element is not an essential, nor is the intention to relinquish the right necessarily present. An estoppel in pais arises, where, by the fault of one party, another has been induced, ignorantly or innocently, to change his position for the worse. Its

Waiver and Estoppel existence is determined by the acts, knowledge and conduct of both parties.1

Sec. 184. Waiver-By Agreement. 

The right of a person to acquire and enforce a mechanics lien, being but a statutory privilege which he, in his discretion, may exercise or not, it necessarily follows that he may voluntarily waive it and if he does, the courts, out of consideration for all parties affected by it, will not hesitate to give such waiver its full force and effect.2 Thus, if labor or material be furnished upon an agreement or understanding that no mechanics lien will be asserted, the right to assert it is waived and cannot later be enforced either as against the owner, a subsequent purchaser or another lienor.3 In the absence of express language or of convincing circumstances clearly indicating an intention not to assert a lien, it is not to be inferred from doubtful language or casual circumstances that the claimant intended to relinquish his right to a lien. 

So, where the terms of the contract are ambiguous on the question or the circumstances are not such as to leave no 

1. Johnson vs. Spencer, 49 Ind. 

App. 166. "A waiver is an intentional relinquishment of a known right." 

Whitmer vs. Arthur, 23 N.P. (N.S.) 481. 

2. "The principle that a person of full age and acting sui juris can waive a statutory or even a constitutional provision in his own favor, affecting simply his property or alienable rights and not involving considerations of public policy, applies to mechanics liens." "Mecanics Liens"-40 C. J. 313.

As has already been indicated the understanding or agreement of waiver may be either express or implied,5 and, since the right to a mechanics lien is not an interest in land, it may be waived without the usual formalities required in the transfer of real estate.6 

A consideration such as is necessary to support a contract is not necessary to support a waiver. A waiver is not a contract, but a mere relinquishment of a personal right and as such does not require a new consideration to support it.7

Sec. 185. No Waiver by Retention of Title. 

The retention of title to material or machinery furnished for the repair, alteration or improvement of a building or other structure, as security for the purchase price, will not operate as a waiver of the right to acquire a mechanics lien therefor.8

Sec. 186. Taking Promissory Notes or Other Se curity. "No lien provided for in this act shall be defeated or waived by the taking by the lien claimant, from any person of any promissory note or notes or of any security for such debt other than upon the real estate itself, in the absence of a written agreement that the taking of such note or notes or such security shall be a waiver of the lien."9

It has been held that one who has obtained a valid mechanics lien upon an owner's property waives such lien by operation of law if he accepts from the owner a mortgage upon the real estate covered by the lien, notwithstanding that the mortgage covers other real estate and is given to secure a note of the debtor which includes not only the original debt but other indebtedness due from the owner to the mortgagee.9a 

In arriving at this conclusion, the court said that the words "any security" in the statute quoted above "refer to any kind of security the lien claimant is willing to accept, different from that which he then has, which is the real estate which his lien then covers; so if the lien claimant accepts the lien-covered property as security for his debt, it being the property then covered, it is not 'security for such debt other than upon the real estate itself' but is security upon the real estate itself' and is by the language of said section a waiver of the lien."

Sec. 187. Taking Judgment on the Account. 

The right to a mechanics lien is not waived or merged upon the obtaining of a judgment at law upon the account

9a. Black River Lumber Co. vs. Kent, 8 Abs. 744.

The Mechanics Lien Law prescribes an additional remedy, not an exclusive one.10 And since the remedy by enforcement of a mechanics lien is merely cumulative under the statute, it is not affected by the submission of the claim to arbitrators, except as to the amount to be collected by its enforcement in case the arbitration is successfully conducted.11 

Sec. 188. Effect of Waiver by Principal Contractor. 

A waiver of a lien by the principal contractor under an agreement, express or implied with the owner, is not binding upon subcontractors, materialmen and laborers not assenting thereto. Their right to a lien is created by statute and cannot be taken away from them by reason of

Sec. 189. Effect of Waiver by Owner. 

If the contractor, subcontractor, materialman or laborer, through no fault of the owner, abandon the job before its completion or fail to substantially perform their work according to the provisions of their respective contracts, they forfeit, of course, any rights they may have to a lien. 

If, however, the owner himself has waived the right to insist upon their substantial performance of the contract, their right to a lien will remain unimpaired.13 Such waiver of performance, differing from the mere waiver of a right to a lien, must, in order to be effectual, be based upon a new consideration.14 It must be borne in mind, however, that "while the owner may perhaps, so far as he is personally concerned, waive compliance with statutory provisions for his protection, he cannot by contract or conduct waive compliance with the substantial requirements of the statute so as to affect, limit or cut off the rights of third persons or so as to give to lien claimants a preference as against third persons which they have not acquired by perfection of liens in the prescribed manner."15 Thus, the furnishing of the sworn statement required by G. C. 8312 cannot, as against other lienors, be waived by the owner or avoided by the con-

Sec. 190. Extension of Time for Payment. 

The extension of the time for payment of a claim, for which a lien may be filed, beyond the period for acquiring such a lien is a circumstance that may be considered on the subject of the waiver of the right to such a lien, but is not conclusive. To show such waiver, the intention to waive the lien must be clearly established. But an extension of the time of payment beyond the time within which the lien could be enforced would clearly show an intention to waive the lien.17

Sec. 194. Pleading and Burden of Proof. 

A waiver, being in the nature of new matter, must be specially pleaded and the burden of proof is upon him who asserts it.25 The proof of waiver must either be in writing or by such clear and convincing evidence as to leave no reasonable doubt about it.26 Claimants for labor and material who plead performance by complying with G. C. 2365-3, and who allege also that such compliance was waived by the conduct and representations of the surety, do not plead inconsistent causes of action, but plead rather two distinct grounds, either one of which, if proven, would sustain a recovery; and they cannot be required to elect upon which of the two grounds they will stand.26a

Sec. 195. Estoppel-In General. 

Equitable estoppel is defined as "the effect of the voluntary conduct of a party, whereby he is absolutely precluded, both at law and in equity, from asserting rights which might perhaps have otherwise existed, either of property, of contract, or of remedy, as against another

This estoppel arises when one, by his acts, representations, or admissions, or by his silence when he ought to speak out, intentionally or through culpable negligence induces another to believe certain facts to exist, and such other rightfully relies and acts on such belief, so that he will be prejudiced if the former is permitted to deny the existence of such facts. 

It consists in holding for truth a representation acted upon, when the person who made it, or his privies, seek to deny its truth, and to deprive the party who has acted upon it of the benefit obtained. When a party unjustly contrives to put another in a dilemma, and to subject him to necessity and distress, and he acts one way, it is not for the wrongdoer to insist that he should have acted another way."27

This is not the true rule.28 It is not necessary, to an equitable estoppel, that the party should design to mislead; it is enough if the act or declaration was calculated to and did in fact mislead another acting in good faith and with reasonable diligence.29 

Sec. 197. Who May Assert an Estoppel. 

A necessary element to the doctrine of estoppel is that the party claiming it must have proceeded upon the act, omission, silence or declaration, of the person sought to be estopped, to his prejudice; that is to say, the party relying upon the estoppel must have been in some way induced by the representation or concealment to do, or fail to do, something to his injury, which act or failure to act would not have occurred but for the conduct of the party against whom the estoppel is charged.30 But it is not every one who may rely upon an estoppel. What Constitutes "Commencement of Work." 

As it becomes necessary, in determining the priority of other titles, liens and incumbrances which may attach to the premises upon which the work of construction is being done, to fix the time when the "commencement of said construction, excavation, or improvement” takes place, it may be well to attempt to describe what constitutes the commencement of construction. 

There seems to be a universal agreement among the courts that the commencement of the work of construction contemplates such visible evidence of the beginning of actual building operations on the premises as will readily notify anyone interested therein that an improvevs. Richmond, N. Sec. 203. Interruption of Work or Change of Plans. 

Where the work of construction is for some reason temporarily stopped but is later resumed again and carried through to completion, the liens will nevertheless date back to the original commencement of the work. So where the plans are slightly altered during the course of construction the liens will take effect as of the commencement of the work under the original plans. However, if the plans are so changed as to call for the erection of an improvement wholly different from that originally contemplated the liens would seem to date as of the commencement of work under the new plans, although there is some authority to the effect that the rights of subcontractors and materialmen are not affected by such changes and their liens take effect as of the beginning of the work of construction.24 Where, however, a party who has commenced work as a subcontractor, but, the principal contractor abandoning the work, afterwards completes the work under a contract made directly with the owner, his mechanics lien for work as such contractor will not date back to the commencement of his work as a subcontractor but only from the beginning of his work under the new contract with the owner.25

(a) Persons Contracting Directly with Owner. 

As between the owner and a person contracting with him the lien may be enforced for the full amount of the contract price of the labor or materials furnished or for such balance of said contract price as may remain due and unpaid him at the time the lien is sought to be acquired, together with interest thereon from its due date, provided, of course, the necessary steps required by statute for perfecting the lien have been properly taken.26

Sec. 208

 Sec. 206. Laborer's Claims Preferred. 

As between several liens obtained by several persons on the same job and the liens of laborers thereon, it is expressly provided by the statute that "liens filed by persons performing manual labor shall have priority to the extent of the labor performed during the thirty days immediately preceding the date of the performance of the last labor."31

Sec. 207. Superiority of Liens as between Con tractor, Subcontractors and Others. "The lien of a subcontractor shall be superior to any already taken or to be taken by the principal contractor in respect of the same labor, machinery, material or fuel, and the liens of laborers, mechanics or persons furnishing machinery, material or fuel to a contractor or subcontractor, shall be superior to any lien already taken or to be taken by such contractor or subcontractor indebted to them in respect of such labor, machinery, material or fuel."32 

Sec. 208. As between Several Liens on Same Job.

Except as noted in the two preceding sections there is no priority among lienholders on the same job. And this is true whether the lien claimants are subcontractors, materialmen and laborers or whether they are principal contractors having separate contracts with the owner. In the case of Geer vs. Tuggle,33 it was urged that the word "job", as used in G. C. 8321, clearly indicates a subdivision of the entire structure, and that each person hav-

The principle underlying the

Sec. 209

Sec. 209.

Other Liens or Incumbrances— 

In General. 

By the express provisions of G. C. 8321, mechanics liens are preferred to all other titles, liens or incumbrances which may attach to or upon the improvement, or to, or upon the land upon which it is situated, "which shall either be given or recorded subsequent to the commencement of said construction, excavation or improvement." From this it readily appears that titles, liens, and incumbrances already attached to or existing upon the premises upon which the improvement is made, prior to the commencement of such improvement, are unaffected by subsequent mechanics liens. "The lien does not override or interfere with prior bona fide liens. The idea that denial of priority among lien claimants is ably stated in the early case of Choteau VS. 

Thompson and Campbell, 2 Oh. 

St. 114, wherein the court says: "The idea upon which the law proceeds is, that the building is the result of the labor and materials of various personsmaterial-men, stone masons, bricklayers, carpenters, painters, etc. The work of some of these must precede that of others, but each contributes his proper share to the value of the structure. Its value, when finished, is derived from these several contributions. It is not the product of one man's materials, or another man's labor, but is the result of the contributions of all. All, then, should share its proceeds, if it go to sale. There is no good reason why the man who, of necessity, or by accident, begins before another, should have priority. The painter and glazier may add far more to the value of the building than the mason who merely lays the foundation yet, if priorities exist, he may get nothing whatever, while the latter is fully paid. The bricklayer and carpenter usually commence at the same time and if priorities are allowed, the accident of one beginning a day before the other, may give him a ruinous advantage. In any view we can take of the subject, we can come to no other conclusion than that the legislature intended the money, whether arising from rents or sales, to be distributed pro rata."

Sec. 334

For obvious reasons they will be discussed separately.

(b) The Vendor's Lien Today 

By the express provisions of G. C. 8543-1, "as between the vendor and vendee of land the vendor shall have a lien for so much of the purchase money as remains unpaid." "But such lien shall not be effective as against a purchaser, mortgagee, judgment creditor, or other encumbrancer, unless there be a recital or a reservation of the lien in the deed, or in some instrument of record executed with the same formalities as are required for the execu tion of deeds and mortgages of land.”46

Sec. 210

The obvious purpose of this provision is to destroy the secret lien of the vendor. It is now no longer possible for the unpaid vendor, who has clothed his vendee with all the evidence of legal title by conveying the premises to the. vendee who thereupon records his deed, to assert his vendor's lien against subsequent purchasers or encumbrancers unless he duly notifies them of his lien by a recital or reservation thereof in his deed to the vendee.47 

It would seem, however, that this amendment affects only those cases where the vendor has actually conveyed the premises to the vendee. The earlier rules as to vendor's liens where the vendor still retains the legal title are therefor probably unaffected. 

Is a mechanic or materialman who perfects his lien upon the title in the vendee an "encumbrancer"? The same principle that protects a purchaser, a mortgagee, or a judgment creditor, would seem to apply with equal force to a mechanic or materialman who, relying upon the legal title of the owner and in ignorance of the vendor's lien (if it is not recited or reserved in the deed to the vendee) have by their labor and materials enhanced the value of the vendor's security. They, like the mortgagee, have a right to rely upon the apparent legal title, with which the vendor has clothed the vendee, as security for the payment of their claims. Certainly such must have been the intention of the Legislature in the use of the words "or other encumbrancer." 

47. Prior to this amendment it was held that while the lien of the vendor did not affect the rights of bona fide purchasers or mortgagees without notice, a judgment creditor was not considered as a purchaser and the vendor's lien was therefor superior to a judgment lien. 

Miller vs. Albright, 60 Oh. St. 48. 

Campbell vs. Sidwell, 61 Oh. 

St. 179.

Sec. 338 

 (c) How the Vendor's Lien May Be Waived 

"By taking back a mortgage, for any unpaid purchase money, on the land conveyed or any part thereof, the vendor shall be deemed to have waived his vendor's lien, and the filing for record of such a mortgage with the recorder of the county wherein said land is located shall be constructive notice of the waiver of the vendor's lien."48

Prior to this amendment, it was uniformly held that a vendor did not waive his lien by taking back a mortgage upon the premises conveyed to secure the purchase price, even though liens, other than those of purchasers or encumbrancers without notice, had intervened.49 The amendment, however, has distinctly abrogated this earlier rule.

The question remains, however, whether this amendment was intended to provide the only means of waiving a vendor's lien or to provide an additional one. It must be borne in mind that prior to this amendment the courts had held that a vendor might by his conduct or agreement waive his right to a vendor's lien. Thus, where a vendor accepted the notes of his vendee with a surety thereon he forfeited his right to a lien,50 or any other collateral

In the opinion of the writer, the sole purpose of this clause in the amendment was to abrogate the former rule which permitted the vendor to take back a mortgage upon the premises without affecting his lien. In other words, the amendment provides an additional means of waiving the lien-not an exclusive one.54

Sec. 214. Income Taxes, 

In a case which seems to be one of first impression, it has been held that mechanics liens properly filed have priority under the Bankruptcy Act over the claim of the United States for additional income taxes accrued for the same tax year as that in which the mechanics liens were filed, where the notice of assessment of additional income tax was filed with the collector more than three years after the mechanics liens were filed and the adjudication in bankruptcy.58

Sec. 215. No Lien upon Proceeds of Fire Insur ance.

Where the owner of real estate insures his interest therein against loss by fire, the holder of a mechanics lien on the property has no claim upon the proceeds of the insurance money, unless by contract the owner was obligated to insure for his benefit.59 Thus the owner may pledge the proceeds to secure a debt and since they constitute no part of the debtor's estate in bankruptcy, but belong to the pledgee, other creditors can claim no interest therein either by virtue of mechanics liens on the property or otherwise.60

Sec. 342 

 Sec. 216. Creditors of Corporation Whose Char ter Is Forfeited.

Mechanics liens, properly perfected, for work and materials furnished to a corporation for the erection of an improvement after the cancellation of its charter by the Secretary of State for non-payment of its franchise tax, are not void but are valid and subsisting liens against the property of the corporation and as such are entitled to priority of payment as against the claims of general creditors of the corporation existing before the forfeiture of its charter.61

Sec. 217. Mortgagee of After-Acquired Property. 

A materialman's lien for the value of materials sold to an owner and attached to his land is superior to that of a prior recorded mortgage covering after-acquired property. The mortgagee's interest attaches only to the interest of the mortgagor at the time the property is acquired, which in this case are subject to the lien rights of the seller.62

Sec. 218. Assignee for Benefit of Creditors. 

A valid and subsisting mechanics lien is not lost or its priority impaired by an assignment by the owner of the premises for the benefit of creditors. The interest of the assignee is no greater than that of his assignor.63

Sec. 219

 Sec. 219. The Construction Mortgage- 

In General.

For a proper understanding of the purpose and scope of the so called "construction mortgage" provision of the 

Mechanics Lien Law (G. C. 8321-1) a brief review of the development of the Mechanics Lien Law is necessary. 

Under the law as it existed prior to 1913, only those persons who contracted directly with the owner were entitled to a lien. Subcontractors, materialmen and others not contracting with the owner had no direct lien upon the premises improved, but only the right to file an attested account which might reach funds, still due under the contract, in the hands of the owner. Each claimant's lien (those contracting with the owner) operated as a lien from the date of the first item of labor performed or material furnished by him. Thus, one taking and recording a mortgage on property, on which a building was in the course of construction, could do so with the assurance that the mortgage would be prior to the lien of any person who might perform labor or furnish material after the recording of such mortgage. In such case the mortgagee could readily determine who had begun to furnish labor or material, or both, before his mortgage was recorded and govern his action accordingly, as was usually done, by paying those who had furnished labor or material prior to the recording of his mortgage, or by arranging to have them waive their rights to a lien. Persons not contracting with the owner, as has been pointed out, could be ignored.

With the enactment of the Mechanics Lien Law of 

1913, the whole theory of the lien was changed.

A direct

Sec. 344 

 lien upon the property of the owner was accorded to all persons furnishing labor and material upon the job, whether they had contracted directly with the owner or not. By virtue of G. C. 8321, it was provided that all mechanics liens on the same job shall be superior to any mortgage given or recorded after the commencement of the excavation, construction or improvement described in G. C. 8310, 8311, regardless of the time when the particular first item of labor or material was performed or furnished by any lien claimant. All lien claimants shared pro rata and their liens thus dated as of the date of the commencement of the work of construction. In other words, there was no priority among them. The effect of this amendment was that the mortgagee, whose mortgage was recorded after construction started, took his mortgage subject to the liens of all who furnished labor or material, or both, for the work of construction (within the meaning of G. C. 8310, 8311) regardless of whether the same was furnished before or after the mortgage was recorded. "If a mortgage was filed after any construction was begun, it was therefore subject to be superseded by mechanics liens filed thereafter for work done thereafter. 

The mechanics liens related back to the beginning of construction. There was no way in which a mortgagee could possibly protect himself against such subsequent mechanics liens, if construction had been begun prior to the filing of his mortgage."64 This naturally would have the effect of stopping building operations entirely unless a method might be secured whereby the improvement could be finished by means of a mortgage loan procured after the work had commenced."65 

64. In re Taylor 20 F. (2nd) 8. 

65. Rider vs. Crobaugh, 1000h. St. 88.

Sec. 220

Such was the situation that confronted the Legislature two years after the enactment of the Mechanics Lien Law of 1913. For the purpose, therefore, of making it possible, as well as safe, for a person to furnish money to an owner to complete his building after the rights of mechanics and materialmen have attached, and to secure himself by a mortgage on the premises which would be superior to the lien rights of such mechanics and mate rialmen, Section 8321-1 of the General Code was enacted. 

Unfortunately, there is a woeful lack of clarity in the act, and it is the view of many careful lawyers that some of its provisions are incapable of performance or enforcement. Suffice it to say, it is perhaps the most misunderstood section of the entire act. If it is to subserve the useful purpose for which it was designed, it should certainly receive the early consideration of the Legislature with the view to its revision so that mortgagees, owners, laborers, materialmen, contractors, subcontractors and other persons may know with reasonable exactness the nature and extent of the respective obligations and benefits incurred by or conferred upon them thereby. 

Sec. 220. To What Mortgages the Amendment 

Applies. "Except as hereinafter provided in this section, the lien of a mortgage given in whole or in part to improve real estate, or to pay off prior encumbrances thereon, or both, the proceeds of which are actually used in such improvement in the manner contemplated in sections 8310 and 8311 of the General Code, or to pay off prior encumbrances or both, and which mortgage contains therein the correct name and address of said mortgagee, together with a covenant between the

Sec. 346 

 mortgagor and mortgagee authorizing and empowering the mortgagee to do all things in this act provided by said mortgagee to be done, shall be prior to all mechanic's, materialmen's and similar liens and all liens provided for in this chapter that are filed for record after said improvement mortgage is filed for record, to the extent that the proceeds thereof are used and applied for the purposes aforesaid and pursuant to the provisions of this section, and such mortgage shall be a lien on the premises therein described from the time it is filed for record for the full amount that is ultimately and actually paid out under said mortgage, regardless of the time when the money secured thereby is advanced."66

It was obviously not the intention of the Legislature that every mortgage given for the purpose of improving real estate should come within the purview of this statute. 

It is clear that this section applies only to construction mortgages given and filed after the commencement of the work of construction.67 Thus, the lien of a mortgage, although given for the avowed purpose of improving real estate and not containing the covenants provided in G. C. 

8321-1 is prior to mechanics and materialmen's liens if such mortgage was filed for record before work was be-

 Fourth. (Payments to Materialmen and Laborers 

Who Have Filed Notices). "Such mortgagee shall pay on the order of the owner, the accounts of such materialmen and laborers, as have filed with such mortgagee a written notice as hereinbefore provided, the amounts due for material then furnished and labor then performed on said improvement; and shall retain out of said mortgage fund, such money to become due as is shown by said notice so served and shall hold such money, and shall pay on the order of the owner, the amounts due to such persons, firms or corporations who have served such notices as aforesaid, if said mortgagee has sufficient money in his hands so to do and also to complete said improvement as aforesaid; but if such mortgagee has funds in his hands insufficient to pay all such laborers and materialmen in full and to complete said improvement, he shall retain sufficient to complete said improvement and to distribute the balance pro rata among said materialmen and laborers who have filed such notices."90

This subsection obviously directs the mortgagee to pay on the order of the owner the accounts of materialmen and laborers who shall have given the mortgagee written notice of the amounts then due for material then furnished and labor then performed; and to retain out of the mortgage fund such money to become due, as shown by the notice served, until such time as the owner may direct that these sums, too, be paid, at which time the mortgagee must pay these also. But the mortgagee's obligation to comply with such orders of the owner is subordinate to the obligation to retain sufficient money to 

90. G. C. 8321-1.

Sec. 227

 complete the building according to the original plans and specifications. If the funds are insufficient to accomplish this result, he shall in any event retain enough to complete the improvement, and, if there is any surplus, distribute the same prorata among materialmen and laborers who have filed notices; otherwise they get nothing.91 

This subsection seems to have been designed particularly to favor the mortgagee, so that he might have a completed structure as his security, even though, under the circumstances, laborers and materialmen might not be paid in full. It does not appear to have any other purpose.92 In this connection, as Judge Westenhaver has pointed out, “it might be interesting to speculate as to how the mortgagee could perform these requirements if the mortgage fund were not sufficint to pay for completing the building and laborers were unwilling to work and materialmen were unwilling to sell on credit.93

It appears then, that the Legislature did not, by this act, create any new rights in favor of contractors and subcontractors, and did not have in mind to make the money loaned a trust fund in their favor."99 

As the act makes no provision for the payment of any money by the mortgagee to contractors and subcontractors, except in advancing payrolls as provided in subsection 3, it therefore follows that no claims of payment made during the course of construction to contractors or subcontractors can be justified. Their only chance to be paid out of the mortgage fund lies in subsection 7, which applies only after the improvement is completed and only when the owner directs such payments to them by the mortgagee out of the balance of the fund then remaining in his hands.

Legislature in using these words did so designedly. The words are not, therefore, to be used interchangeably.100

Sec. 236.

When Mortgage not Complying with 

G. C. 8321-1 May Be Subrogated to Prior Liens. 

While mortgages given to improve real estate or pay off prior incumbrances may not be, strictly speaking, construction mortgages and, therefore, not entitled to all the privileges provided by G. C. 8321-1, nevertheless money actually advanced under such mortgages and used in satisfying the claims of laborers and materialmen should in equity be considered as applied to the claims of such lienors, and the lender should be subrogated to the rights of such lien holders to the extent that they were benefited by the payments so made. Of course, as to any money that was paid to the owner which did not reach the lien holders, the mortgagee would have no right. Moreover, if upon final disposition of the fund, it appears that any lien holder received a larger proportion of the money due to him by reason of the fact that he received money from the mortgagee, to the extent of such excess so received by such lien holder by reason of such payment by the mortgagee, the mortgagee would have no right of subrogation. In other words, the mortgagee "would have the right of subrogation only to the extent the payments
