Sec. 301. Conflict of Laws 

It is a very common practice nowadays, in connection with a contract providing for the construction, alteration, repair or demolition of a building or other structure or

Sec. 

366 

 improvement, to require the contractor, as one of the conditions of the acceptance of his bid, to execute and deliver to the owner a bond with sureties conditioned that the contractor shall perform all of the provisions of his contract according to the terms thereof, pay all claims for labor and material employed or used in connection with the work, and indemnify and hold harmless the owner against liens, damages, or other claims arising out of the performance or non-performance of such contract by the contractor. In most jurisdictions, of which Ohio is one, such bonds are required by statute of contractors who engage in the construction, alteration, repair or demolition of a public improvement. Of course, in all jurisdictions, independently of statute, an owner may require a bond of his contractor as one of the conditions of his employment.

Not a little confusion, however, has resulted from the failure of courts to distinguish between the types of bond which may be furnished the owner by the contractor; a failure due, in part at least, to a misunderstanding of the owner's intention and purpose in requesting the contractor to furnish such bond. There can be no doubt but that an owner should be permitted, in the case of a private contract, to require the contractor to furnish a bond which will indemnify only him (the owner) against any claims, liens or damages which might be asserted against him or be filed upon his property as the result of some default of his contractor. The owner's interest in such case is a purely personal one—in fact—a very selfish one. He is seeking to protect himself alone. He is not concerned with the payment of the claims of laborers, subcontractors, or materialmen except insofar as their non-payment

Contracts of Indemnity and Suretyship Sec. 241 

may affect his own purse or property. It may be a matter of entire indifference to him whether his contractor pays or does not pay his laborers, subcontractors or materialmen. Not without reason he may be unwilling to consider their prospects of payment as an obligation or duty resting upon him to provide for in the making of his contract with the contractor. Aside from any altruistic impulses that might have moved him, there is no reason why the owner should insist that the contractor furnish a bond that will not only indemnify the owner against loss but will also insure the payment of the claims of laborers, subcontractors and materialmen. The Mechanics Lien Law was designed to accomplish the latter purpose. If the owner complies with this law the claims of those furnishing labor and material upon the job will be paid out of the contract price. If he does not comply with this law then they may acquire a direct lien upon the premises of the owner to secure the ultimate payment of their claims. More than this they should not ask. 

There is, therefore, no legal or moral obligation upon the private owner to procure a bond from the contractor which will guarantee to those furnishing labor and material the payment of their claims upon default of the contractor so to do.

In the case of a public improvement the situation is quite different. No mechanics lien can be obtained upon a public improvement. The courts having taken away or denied this right to a lien, the Legislature has seen fit to substitute in its place a right of action upon a bond which specifically provides for the payment of all claims of laborers, subcontractors and materialmen who furnish their labor or material for the construction of such improve-

Sec. 368 

 ment and permits such persons to maintain a suit thereon in their own names and for their own benefit. In addition to this liability to persons furnishing labor and material the bond also indemnifies the obligee against any loss it may sustain by reason of the contractor's default in the performance of any of the conditions of his contract. 

It is quite right that the bond securing the performance of a contract relating to a public improvement should indemnify the obligee and guarantee the payment of claims for labor and material. Surely the public has a right to a bond insuring the full performance of the contractor's obligations to it; and since, for reasons of public policy, a lien upon a public improvement has been denied, the State, or any of its political subdivisions, is justified in exacting from the contractor a bond which will assure the payment of the claims of those who furnish labor and material for such improvement. "Such conditions in the bond are for the public benefit, because they insure confidence in the contractor, and therefore encourage responsible and capable persons to furnish labor and materials, and to contract for certain portions of the work, and at the same time insure a better quality of performance. The surety cannot justly complain, because the character of the risk is fully known, and he may inquire as to the responsibility of the person or firm whose contract he agrees to insure. The principal contractor may likewise protect himself by requiring a bond of subcontractors. It is difficult to see therefore how there can be any impairment of the obligations of a contract, or how any hardship can be inflicted if the parties will take ordinary business precautions."

Contracts of Indemnity and Suretyship Sec. 242 

Thus, in the case of a private contract, it would seem that an owner should have the unqualified right to contract with reference to his own protection; or, if he so chooses, to contract with reference to the protection of those who contribute to the improvement of his property, even though he may have no legal or moral obligation so to do. In other words, no reason can be assigned why he should not be the sole judge of whether he should contract with reference to his own protection, or to that of others. Unfortunately, the courts have failed in some instances to recognize this right of the private owner and have construed a bond, intended and given him by the contractor for indemnity solely, as one which also assures to those furnishing labor and material the payment of their claims, even though the latter may have furnished their labor and material in entire ignorance of the existence of such a bond. In other words, the courts, by construction, have extended the intended narrow purpose of a private bond to the very broad purpose of a public one. 

They have generously created in the mind of the private owner a benevolent intention which he seldom, if ever, entertained and have held the surety for a liability which it doubtless never intended to assume. Neither justice, good morals nor grim necessity seem to have required such a strained construction.

Sec. 242. Construction of the Surety's Contract. 

The day of the voluntary or accommodation surety has about passed. The day of the corporate compensated surety has arrived. With the retirement of the former, the doctrine that "a surety is a favorite of the law" has

Sec. 242

370 disappeared.1 Courts do not have the same solicitude for corporations engaged in executing contracts of suretyship for profit that they formerly had for the individual surety who, for no consideration of benefit to himself, voluntarily undertook to answer for the obligation of another. 

The whole trend of our decisions, federal and state, is to distinguish between individual and corporate compensated suretyship. And there is some reason for this. The private surety usually had little to do with the preparation of his contract. He knew it was a bond of some sort, but scarcely ever read its entire contents before signing it, and thought little, if anything, about the possibility of loss in the event of the default of his friend, the principal obligor.2 The corporate compensated surety, however, 1. This earlier and well known doctrine is best exemplified in 

Ohio in the case of State vs. 

Medary, 17 Ohio 554: "The bond speaks for itself; and the law is that it shall so speak; and that the liability of sureties is limited to the exact letter of the bond. 

Sureties stand upon the words of the bond, and if the words will not make them liable, nothing can. There is no construction, no equity against sureties." 

See also: Birdsall vs. Heacock, 32 Oh. St. 177; Morgan vs.

Their liability is limited to the exact letter of the bond, and presumptions cannot be indulged in to aid plaintiff in enforcing a liability against them." 

2. "The law, by its carefully considered precedents, has developed the rules for the determination of the respective rights and liabilities of the parties who contract in this way, making provision for certain defenses in suretyship, such as those resulting from fraudulent concealment, material alteration of the contract, extension of time to the principal and other equitable defenses impressed upon the contract, without any specific reference in the contract to such possible defenses." engages in its contract only for the purpose of anticipated pecuniary gain. Its premium has been determined by a skillful analysis of other experiences similar to the risk involved. Its contract, except in those instances where the form is prescribed by statute, is usually prepared by its own attorneys with great skill and precision. It seldom undertakes a risk of any material size without a careful examination thereof by competent agents employed for that purpose. As a preliminary to the execution of its bond it usually requires, not only from its principal but often from the obligee, an application for such bond wherein the principal and the obligee unite in making answers to interrogatories propounded by the surety regarding the risk to be undertaken. In addition, the contract of the corporate compensated surety generally sets forth in exact terms the conditions upon which its liabil ity may commence or be terminated, the privileges or rights of subrogation and contribution, matters pertaining to notice of default, and the limitation of time within which suit must be brought upon the bond. For these reasons the courts do not construe the contract of the corporate compensated surety with that same solicitous regard that for so long characterized their decisions involving the liability of the accommodation surety."

At the outset of this discussion it must be borne in mind that the private owner is under no legal obligation whatsoever to pay the debts of his contractor for either labor or materials used in the construction of his improvement, and he is likewise under no legal obligation to procure a bond of a surety which will agree to pay such claims. As has been said before,5 the owner is entirely within his rights in procuring a bond which will protect himself alone. On the other hand he may with equal right, procure a bond which will protect those furnishing labor and material, in addition to protecting himself. At first glance it would seem then to be purely a question of intention on the part of the owner. Did he intend to procure a bond for himself alone, or did he intend to protect not only himself but also all those who furnished labor and material for the improvement he was

One of the earliest cases involved the bond of a contractor to a board of education. There was, no law at that time requiring a contractor to furnish such a bond. The case may therefore be considered as one involving a private contract—not a public one; to this extent at least, that the bond was voluntarily procured by the owner. 

The bond was conditioned that the contractor "shall well and truly perform all and singular, the stipulations of said agreement by him to be performed, and shall pay all just and legal claims for labor performed upon, and for materials furnished for the work specified in said agreement." The contractor defaulted, having failed to pay the account of one of his subcontractors. The latter brought suit upon the bond in his own name. Recovery was allowed. This case has since been regarded as one of the leading authorities for the general proposition that a bond, conditioned upon the payment by the contractor of claims for labor and material, is not only one which holds harmless the owner from such claims, but also one which confers a right of action thereon in favor of those furnishing labor and material whose claims have not been paid; the suit being one which may be brought

The surety having expressly contracted for a liability to laborers and materialmen was properly held to such liability. No other conclusion was possible in view of the plain language of the bond.9

The rule announced by the majority of the court in the Gaspard case, however, was destined to a short life. 

Five years later the court changed its point of view. The complexion of the court had changed also. Not one of the majority who joined in the judgment in the Gaspard case now sat upon the bench of the Supreme Court. The three judges who had joined in the dissent from the view of the majority in the Gaspard case were still on the bench. Of the four new judges, two did not participate in the decision. Thus two new judges, with the aid of the three former dissenting judges, were then able to overrule the decision of the court in the Gaspard case. 

The facts of the later case14 were these: A contractor entered into a contract with the City of Cleveland to repair a viaduct. One of the terms of his contract was that he would "at his own risk, cost and expense do all work and furnish all materials, labor, tools, appliances, ways and means" in repairing the viaduct. Contracts of Indemnity and Suretyship Sec. 246 Sec. 244. When the Action in Favor of Owner 

Accrues.

A bond with a condition for the performance of the covenants and conditions of a building contract, the payment by the contractor of all claims for labor and material, and the completion of the building free from mechanics liens, is a contract of indemnity against liability. 

The condition of such a bond is broken by the acquisition of a mechanics lien on the property by a materialman, and the obligee (the owner) has an immediate right of action on the bond for the recovery of the amount of the lien and the costs incident thereto. Payment of the claim of such materialman by the obligee is not a condition precedent to his right of action, but he may sue and recover the full amount of the claim, or as much thereof as will not exceed the penal sum named in the bond, without first having paid such claim.27 

Sec. 245. Surety May Be Sued Alone.

A bond of this character is one of joint and several liability. The contractor and surety may be sued together or either one may be sued alone.28 

Sec. 246. Illegality of Contract. 

Courts will not lend their aid to the enforcement of an illegal contract. A surety upon the bond of a contractor is not estopped by the recitals of its bond to set up the defense that the principal contract is illegal and therefore that the bond is void.29

 Sec. 247. Alteration of Principal Contract. 

It is a general principle in the law of suretyship that a material alteration of the principal contract without the consent of the surety will discharge the latter from all liability upon his bond. Such changes constitute a new contract and create one which the surety has not agreed to secure the performance of. It is not entirely a question of whether the risk of the surety has been increased or not. He is entitled to stand upon the letter of his bond and say "in hoc foedere non veni."30

This rule, however, has of necessity been somewhat relaxed with respect to building contracts. It is hardly conceivable that any building or other improvement is ever wholly constructed in exact compliance with all of the provisions of the principal contract or with the plans and specifications relating thereto. As the work of construction progresses minor alterations, here and there, seem not only wise but in some cases necessary. It is impossible to foresee all of the contingencies that may arise and therefore to contract with reference thereto. 

Parties must be held to have contemplated the possibility of such changes and to have impliedly assented thereto. 

Upon this theory, if the alterations are slight and trivial, involving no prejudice or loss to the surety, the surety will not be released from his obligation by reason thereof. This is particularly true where such changes are reported to the agent of the surety during the progress of the work and he makes no objection thereto.31 Even if

Contracts of Indemnity and Suretyship Sec. 248 

the rule may be otherwise, insofar as an accommodation surety is concerned, it is clear now that a corporate compensated surety will not be released from its obligation of suretyship by changes in the contract guaranteed by it unless such changes operate injuriously to affect materially its rights and liabilities.32

Sec. 248. Changes in Manner or Time of Pay ment.

Building contracts, as a rule, provide for payment to the contractor by the owner of certain stipulated percentages of the contract price as the work progresses, upon certificates or estimates of the architect. Under this arrangement the owner is permitted to retain a certain percentage of the amount earned until the entire job is completed to the satisfaction of the architect. While there is not a wholesome uniformity of opinion upon this question, the general rule seems to be that insofar as the liability of the surety to the owner is concerned, these stipulations are considered covenants for the benefit of the surety as well as of the owner, and a violation of such provisions of the principal contract by premature pay. ments by the owner to the contractor will release the surety from liability to such owner upon default of the contractor in the performance of his contract, to the extent of the damage sustained by the surety by reason of such premature payments.32a

The surety is bound by the estimates of the architect upon which the owner makes payments to the contractor, even though such estimates are erroneous and excessive in amount, no bad faith being shown.35 Loans made by the owner to the contractor to enable him to obtain material, and upon the agreement that such loans are to be repaid out of the estimates when made, are not to be considered as advance payments on the contract price and will not release the surety.36

Where, however, the bond is designed to serve two purposes, to wit, (1st) to indemnify the owner, (2nd) to pay the claims of mechanics and materialmen, the question may well arise as to whether such alteration of the principal contract by the owner which results in a discharge of the liability of the surety as to him, will also discharge the liability of the surety to mechanics and materialmen who in good faith have furnished their labor and material in the construction of the improvement. 

With reference to statutory bonds, whether they secure public or private contracts, the question has been fully answered. Many courts, both Federal and State, have held that such bonds contain two specific agreements; one, to protect the owner; the other to protect mechanics and materialmen. These agreements are as distinct as if they were contained in separate instruments. 

When the owner in such case has executed the contract and taken and approved the bond, it ceases to be the agent of third parties whom the contractor employs in the execution of the work or from whom he obtains materials and the rights of such persons are unaffected by subsequent transactions between the owner and the contractor. 

The owner may, by consenting to an alteration of the contract, discharge the surety from liability to him, but he cannot change the liability of the surety to mechanics and materialmen, where the general nature of the work and materials remains the same.37 Thus in a suit by a mate-

There would seem to be no reason for a different rule where the bond is furnished by a contractor to secure his contract with a private owner. If, at the request of a private owner or his contractor, a surety executes a bond by the terms of which it assumes not only to indemnify the owner but to pay all claims for labor and material furnished in the building or improvement, the same rule which applies to statutory bonds would seem to have the same force and effect. In either case the surety deliberately contracts for the benefit of two distinct classes of persons, the owner and the mechanic or materialman. 

Neither one of these two classes has any authority, express or implied, to alter the surety's obligation to the other and the surety must be held to know this. The mechanic or materialman is not conversant with the terms of the original contract, nor should he be. His is a special work and he should not be held to have knowledge of something clearly beyond his power to obtain, or, sometimes, to understand. The surety knows this too. To defeat the liability of a surety to mechanics and materialmen because of changes in the contract not knowingly participated in by them would be to invoke a somewhat obsolete principal of suretyship which has no application to the dual risk which the surety deliberately, and with full knowledge of the possibilities of loss, undertakes.42

Sec. 250. Extension of Time. 

It is a familiar rule of suretyship that an extension of time for a definite period upon a valuable consideration granted by the creditor to the principal debtor will discharge a surety not consenting thereto. This is not only upon the theory that there has been a material alteration of the principal contract but also for the reason that in some cases the risk of the surety is increased thereby. 

By postponing the date of maturity of the principal's obligation the surety is deprived of the right to pay the debt at its original maturity and to resort to his action of indemnity against the principal or of subrogation to the rights of the creditor.45 In the case of private sureties

Sec. 251. Notice of Default of Principal Con tractor. 

Usually, in bonds securing the performance of a private contract,50 it is provided that immediate notice shall be given to the surety of any default on the part of the contractor involving a loss for which the surety is liable. In the absence of an express provision in such bonds, requiring laborers, materialmen or subcontractors to furnish such notice to the surety, it will be held that such provision contemplates a notice only from the principal obligee in the bond and does not contemplate that laborers, materialmen or subcontractors must give such notice as a prerequisite to the enforcement of their claims. 

Nor will the fact that such principal obligee fails to furnish the surety such notice of the default of the contrac surety unless the arrangement is prejudicial to him."

Sec. 252. Bonds Given to Secure Public Contracts. 

As has already been stated52 it has been quite generally held that mechanics liens cannot be acquired upon public property. Persons furnishing labor or materials for the construction of a public improvement have not therefore enjoyed that same degree of protection which those who engaged in the construction of some private improvement have enjoyed. The former could file only an attested account-the latter had their rights to mechanics liens upon the structure or improvement. In order to afford persons furnishing labor or materials upon a public job a remedy of sufficient efficacy to put them on a par with those engaged in the construction of a private improvement, insofar as the payment of their claims was concerned, a number of states, prior to the year 1917, had enacted statutes which were deliberately drawn with the single purpose of achieving this result. 

Following the passage of these statutes, surety companies throughout the country executed their bonds to indemnify public bodies from loss in connection with the construction of public buildings, or other improvements, 51. American Fidelity Co. vs. 

Metropolitan Paving Brick Co., 35 Oh. Cir. 662, 667. While the contract involved in this case was a public one, yet there was no statute then in existence requiring such a bond for the benefit of laborers, materialmen or subcontractors. The case may therefore be regarded as if it were a private contract. 

52. See Section 110, ante. "In this state mechanics liens cannot attach to public ownership." Royal Indemnity Co. vs.

State, ex rel., Standard Sanitary 

Mfg. Co., 120 Oh. St. 378, 385.

Contracts of Indemnity and Suretyship Sec. 253 

which bonds, however, did not in some cases completely comply with the provisions of these statutes. Where, for instance, the statutes were quite clear that the bond should inure to the benefit not only of the public body but also to the materialmen and laborers engaged in the work of construction, the form of the bond sometimes executed by a surety and often accepted by the public body did not contain specific language creating a liability in favor of such materialmen and laborers, but merely to the public body-the only obligee named in the bond. 

In the resulting litigation, various state courts rendered conflicting decisions as to the liability of the surety upon such bonds. Some of the courts held that in such cases the bond is available for materialmen and laborers because the statute in force at the time of making the contract enters into the bond and becomes a part thereof as though specifically set forth in the bond. Other courts denied the liability of the surety under such circumstances, basing their opinion upon the proposition that the bond cannot be extended beyond its express terms. Many other questions arising out of these statutes became the subject of litigation owing to the looseness of the language employed in the statutes. With these conflicting decisions before it the Ohio Legislature convened in 1917.

Whether the Attorney General gave these numbers to the several sections of the act because he believed that the act applied only to buildings, or whether he gave the act these numbers as a mere matter of routine, is not significant, since the power conferred upon him by the Legislature to number does not attempt to confer upon him any power to legislate, and could not if it did so attempt.55

Sec.

The Legislature in its title to the act said the act was "to protect persons performing labor and furnishing materials for the construction and repair of public works." "Public works" is defined as "all fixed works contracted for public use."56 To construe the words "public works or improvements," in G. C. 2365-1, as meaning only public buildings, would be to adopt a strained, unnatural, and unusual construction rather than to follow the longrecognized canon of construction that, unless a contrary intention of the Legislature clearly appears, the words and phrases used by the Legislature in all legislation will be construed in their usual, ordinary meaning. Had the 

Legislature intended to confine the provisions of G. C. 

2365-1 to public buildings, there was no occasion for the use of the words, "or other public works or improvements," at all. With these rules of construction, the Supreme Court has therefore held that “the plain, ordinary meaning of the words, "public buildings or other public works or improvements," in connection with the words. immediately following them in G. C. 2365-1, comprehends all public works and improvements, constructed, altered, or repaired under contract, at the expense of the state, or any county, city, village, township, or school district of the state."57 Accordingly the act has been held, in the following cases, to apply to state highway contracts,58 county highway contracts,59 the contracts of

The penal sum named in the bond must be an amount equal to at least fifty per cent (50%) of the contract price.72 Unfortunately, however, no little confusion has been caused by the language employed in other statutes relating to special types of public contracts, in which a different way of stating the amount of the bond given to secure such contracts is used. For instance, in the same chapter in which G. C. 2365-1 to 2365-4, inclusive, are found, is this language: "The bonds provided for in this chapter required to be taken by a board or officer of the county, township, city, village, or school district of the state shall not exceed fifty per cent of the estimated cost of such public building * * *."73 In fixing the amount of the bond required for the securing of state highway contracts, the language employed is: "The bond required to be taken under the provisions of this section shall be in an amount equal to one-half of the estimated cost of the work ***"74 Similar language is used in fixing the amount of the bond required for securing the performance of county road construction and improvement contracts.75 The Supreme Court, however, has held that these statutes are not, in this respect at least, wholly irreconcilable, although it is admitted they are somewhat inconsistent. "In Section 2365-2 it is provided that the bond shall be ‘in an amount equal to at least fifty per cent (50%) of the contract price,' and in Section 6947 it is provided that the bond shall be ‘in a sum equal to

Section 2365-2, General Code, provides that the bond shall be in a sum at least equal to 50 per cent of the contract price, and contains no inhibition against the contractor giving a bond equal to one-half of the estimated cost of the work. 

It is not unusual in legislation for the Legislature to provide minimums and maximums. Compliance with these separate provisions of these two sections is in no way impossible of performance by the contrac tor. Sec. 410 

Legislature of Ohio, had been caused by a lack of uniformity in the bonds written by various surety companies in their efforts to comply with the provisions of laws requiring contractors engaged in the construction of public works to furnish bonds for the protection of laborers and materialmen engaged in such work. Many of such bonds did not contain provisions which the law plainly required. 

Others contained provisions which, in a measure, curtailed some of the rights which the statutes specifically granted. The Legislature of Ohio undoubtedly had this situation in mind when it determined to incorporate in the law itself a form of bond to be used.79 It is not necessary that the bond be in precisely the same form as that prescribed by the statute; it is sufficient that it be in substantially the statutory form.80 

Sec. 262. Recovery upon Bond not Complying with Statutory Form. 

Not only does the statute prescribe the form of bond to be used but it also contains a most unusual provision relating to the liability upon bonds given pursuant to the provisions of G. C. 2365-1, but which do not substantially comply with the form prescribed by G. C. 2365-4. This provision is: "The bond hereinbefore provided for shall be in substantially the following form, and recovery of any claimant thereunder shall be subject to the conditions and provisions of this act to the same extent as if such conditions and provisions were fully incorporated in said bond form."81 This clause was an innovation in

No statute in any other state, up to this time, had attempted to go so far.82 The first case involving the construction of this clause by the Supreme Court of Ohio was one in which the bond furnished by a contractor engaged in public work did not contain the required clause relating to the payment of the claims of laborers and materialmen. It was argued by the latter that the provisions of G. C. 2365-1 to 2365-4, inclusive, were written into the bond regardless of its express terms, and that hence the bond was available for recovery to materialmen and subcontractors. The surety company, on the other hand, contended that it was entitled to rely upon the face of the bond, and that the materialmen and subcontractors therefore had no right of recovery in spite of the provisions of the statute. The court made short shrift of the surety's contention. "It is the general rule," the court said, "that when parties enter into a contract and execute a bond required by statute with regard to this contract, they are chargeable with notice of the statutory provisions. We are asked to depart from this general rule in face of an express provision making this statute a part of all bonds entered into pursuant to its terms. It is seldom that we are called upon to construe an enactment in which the legislative intent is so plain. Hence we are compelled to the conclusion that the statute is written into the bond; that recovery was available thereunder for labor performed and materials furnished in the construction of the school building irrespective of the fact that materialmen were not men-

If they comply with the Code, he is protected, and hence he is not bound at his peril to ascertain the terms of the bond."85

Contracts of Indemnity and Suretyship Sec. 264 Sec. 263. The Statute Construed Liberally. 

The act of March 21, 1917, relating to the protection of laborers and materialman on public jobs, is a remedial statute, and hence that construction of its provisions consistent with and most favorable to the fulfillment of the purpose of the statute should be adopted.86 

Sec. 264. "Materials" and "Labor" within the Bond. 

G. C. 2365-1 and 2365-2 provide that the bond shall be conditioned upon "the payment by the contractor, and by all subcontractors, for all (on account of any) labor performed or materials furnished in the construction *** of such building." The form of bond prescribed by G. C. 2365-4, however, provides, as a part of the condition, that the principal "shall pay all lawful claims of subcontractors, materialmen and laborers, for labor performed and materials furnished in the carrying forward, performing or completing of said contract;" and further contains the provision: "We agreeing and assenting that this undertaking shall be for the benefit of any materialman or laborer having a just claim, as well as for the obligee herein." It is quite apparent that the wording of the form of bond provided in G. C. 2365-4, is different from the wording in G. C. 2365-1 and 2365-2, and, standing alone, somewhat broader in its significance. 

Nevertheless, "the scope of the bond is to be determined by the provisions of G. C. 2365-1 and 2365-2, since the

Contracts of Indemnity and Suretyship Sec. 265 

With these general principles of construction before us we may now examine some of the cases wherein these rules have been applied.

Sec. 265. Tools, Appliances and Equipment. 

"The general rule is that the bond is only liable for labor or materials furnished or supplied which have gone into and become a part of the work. Accordingly it is generally ruled under bonds given on state and city work that no recovery can be had for machinery used or repaired in the prosecution of the work. A contractor is presumed to be prepared with machinery, tools and appliances necessary to carry out his contract. These are furnished upon his own credit presumably and not upon the implied credit of the public. They survive the performance of the work, do not become a part of it and may be used upon other work."90 Upon this theory a bond furnished in accordance with the requirements of 

G. Sec. 270. Clothing, Food and Lodging for La borers.

It is difficult to lay down any rule as to whether clothing, food and lodging may be deemed to be “material" within the meaning of a bond given by a public contractor covering the payment of all claims for labor and material. A great diversity of opinion exists on account of the various clauses used in such bonds. The language of some bonds limits the liability only to such items as directly enter into the construction of the improvement; other bonds include all labor and material which contribute, directly or indirectly, to the performance of the contract. By analogy to the Ohio cases hereinbefore referred to it seems certain that such items as clothing, food and lodging for laborers are clearly outside the scope and purpose of bonds given to secure the performance of contracts for public improvements and for the payment of claims for labor and material furnished therein.97 

Sec. 271. The Federal Statute. 

The rule in the courts of the United States is much broader than that of almost any other jurisdiction. This

Sec. 273. The Right of the Public Is Superior to 

Other Claimants.

Where a bond is executed and delivered to the proper public officials pursuant to G. C. 2365-1, to insure the performance by the contractor of a contract according to its terms for the construction of a public improvement, the public has a right to enforce the bond in its favor so far as it may be necessary to reimburse the public for any loss sustained by reason of a default of the contractor in carrying out his contract, and such right is superior to the right of any subcontractor, materialman or laborer to participate to any extent in the amount due on such bond.

Thus, where a contractor, engaged in the performance of his contract with a village, abandons the job and the village and the surety on the bond of the contractor agree that the village shall complete the job and charge the

Sec. 274. Laborers and Materialmen.

Is the latter language a limitation of that which immediately precedes it? Was it the intention of the Legislature to limit the right of action on the bond to the "laborer" and the "materialman" in the strict sense in which those terms are defined by the Mechanics Lien Law?107

Such a construction would seem to eliminate a subcontractor from a right of action on the bond. A materialman is not a subcontractor,108 and surely a laborer is not a subcontractor.109 Therefore, if the language of the bond-"we agreeing and assenting that this undertaking shall be for the benefit of any materialman or laborer"-is to be construed strictly as meaning only those persons defined as such by G. C. 8323-9, then surely a subcontractor is not one for whose benefit the bond is given. This strict construction seems to be supported by the provisions of G. C. 2365-1 and 2365-2. What then becomes of the language of G. C. 2365-4, where it is expressly conditioned that the contractor "shall pay all lawful claims of subcontractors, materialmen and laborers?"

It would appear from the reading of the entire form of bond prescribed by G. C. 2365-4, taken in connection with the whole spirit and purpose of the act, that it was not the intention of the Legislature to exclude a subcontractor from the benefits of the bond. No good reason would seem to justify such a strained construction. Under

Sec. 277. 

Extent of Liability of the Surety. 

One of the provisions in the form of bond prescribed by G. C. 2365-4 is as follows: "it being expressly understood and agreed that the liability of the surety for any and all claims hereunder shall in no event exceed the penal amount of this obligation as herein stated." 

This provision in no wise limits the liability of the contractor, the principal in the bond. His liability is measured by the extent of his contractual obligations with his subcontractors, materialmen, laborers and others whose services he may have employed. Only the surety's liability is thus limited. 

As against the contractor, the principal in the bond, the claimants are entitled also to interest on their respective accounts from the time when their several accounts became due.

 Sec. 279. Form of Statement Furnished by Claim ant to Surety. "Any person, firm or corporation to whom any money shall be due on account of having performed any labor, or furnished any material in the construction, erection, alteration or repair of any such building, work or improvement * * * shall furnish the sureties on said bond, a statement of the amount due to any such person, firm or corporation."116

The statute does not prescribe the amount or character of information which the claimant must furnish the surety in complying with the section quoted above. It is significant, however, that the word "statement" is used. "It must be conceded that inasmuch as the Legislature employed the word 'statement' and did not employ the word 'notice' something more than a mere notice is necessary."117 On the other hand it would seem to be entirely unnecessary to prepare a formal document of forbidding length or one made up of a mass of intricate details. The surety is entitled to that information which will enable it to intelligently identify the risk it has assumed and to investigate, if it chooses, the nature and extent of its loss. 

Such statement, whether in the form of an account, letter, affidavit or otherwise, would seem to accomplish its full purpose if it notifies the surety of the name and address of the claimant, the nature of the claim, the amount thereof, the name of the contractor, the particular contract which its bond secured, and that such claim is within the of action against the surety on the bond when the claim has been perfected pursuant to the statutes."

Sec. 282. What Constitutes "Acceptance.” 

The statute does not define "acceptance" or in any way indicate what amounts to an acceptance, except that it is provided that the acceptance must be made "by the duly authorized board or officer." It does not refer to partial acceptance, nor acceptance of a part of the work. 

There is nothing in the statute to indicate that use and occupancy of the improvement constitute an acceptance. 

There is nothing to indicate that substantial acceptance, or something tantamount to acceptance, would be suffi cient. So, where the improvement is the construction of a public highway under contract with the director of highways, the use thereof by the public for purposes of travel, without the official approval thereof by the state highway commissioner or some duly authorized agent of such commissioner, before the completion thereof, does not amount to an acceptance within the purview of the statute.122 Nor does the passing of a resolution by a board of county commissioners, authorizing the payment of the final estimate of a road contractor by the auditor, amount to an "acceptance". In such case, a statement furnished by a claimant to the surety within ninety days after the

Sec. 291. Illegality of Principal Contract. 

The principle is of general application that contracts contrary to sound morals, public policy, or forbidden by law, will not be enforced by courts of justice. If an improper use be made of goods innocently sold, or if the results of honest labor be devoted to improper purposes the materialman or the laborer ought not to be deprived of their compensation; yet if they intend to assist in the illegal act, with full knowledge of its purpose, they are parties to its unlawfulness, and deserve no aid from the law. And if the ordinary use of the thing produced be illegal, he must be taken as intending the use, and as privy to the illegality, and therefore entitled to no benefit for his labor or material. Thus, where the keeping of a bowling alley, by the proprietor of a public house, was unlawful, the builder of such alley cannot recover his services in constructing it.141 

Where the provisions of G. C. 5660, relative to the

It has been frequently held, therefore, that the surety must contemplate such changes, where they are trivial and not so material as to be prejudicial to the surety, and he will not be discharged from liability under such circumstances.147 

Because of the uncertainty of judicial construction upon such questions, as for instance whether an alteration is prejudicial to the surety or not, the Legislature of Ohio has seen fit to incorporate in the form of bond prescribed by G. C. 2365-4, a clause which practically eliminates the entire defense of alteration of the principal contract. By virtue of this clause the surety expressly agrees that such alterations may be made. The bond provides: "The said surety hereby stipulates and agrees that no modifications, omissions, or additions, in or to the terms of the said contract or in or to the plans or specifications therefor shall in any wise affect the obligations of said surety on its bond."148 

147. De Witt's Stearns on Suretyship, Sections 76a, 76b. 

148. G. C. 2365-4.

Even without this clause, it is not likely that changes in the contract subsequent to the execution of the bond given to secure its performance, which do not alter the general character of the work contemplated by the contract would discharge the surety insofar as its liability to mechanics and materialmen is concerned. The bond serves two purposes (1st) to indemnify the principal obligee, (2nd) to pay mechanics' and materialmen's claims. An alteration of the contract by the principal obligee, of which mechanics and materialmen have no knowledge and can not prevent, will discharge the surety as to such obligee but will not release it

Sec. 440 

It is not to be inferred, however, that this clause would permit of such material changes as would amount to an entire abrogation of the original principal contract, the performance of which the surety agreed to secure, and the substitution of a new one in its place. Such changes would not be "modifications, omissions, or additions." A reasonable and fair construction of the language and purpose of this clause would seem to be that the assent of the surety applied only to moderate changes which do not greatly enlarge the burdens and financial responsibility of the contractor. Any other construction would defeat the very purpose of the act by making the surety's risk so uncertain and hazardous that few, if any, sureties would care to engage in it.149

It not infrequently happens that the contracts between the principal contractor and his subcontractors or materialmen are changed after the execution of the bond. For instance, a contract between the contractor and a materialman may provide for payment of the materials within sixty days after delivery. If the contractor and materialman agree that such payments may be extended for sixty days more, or that notes, maturing later, may be temporarily given to cover such account, will the surety on the bond of the contractor be discharged by such extension of time where he does not consent thereto? The modern trend of opinion seems to be that the mere execution and delivery of promissory notes by a contractor to a materialman or subcontractor, in the absence of an agreement that the said notes are in settlement of the indebtedness they represent, does not operate as payment or settlement of the claim or release the surety, nor does a reasonable extension of time for payment operate as a release of the liability of a surety on the bond of a contractor to such materialman or subcontractor, particularly where the surety can show no prejudice to himself by reason of such arrangements.150 

The same rule would seem to apply to other changes in the contracts between the principal contractor and his subcontractors and materialmen.

Sec. 294. Failure of Laborer or Materialman to Perfect Lien Does Not Release Surety. 

The mere failure of a laborer, materialman, or subcontractor to perfect his lien, if the job is a private one, 150. See Sections 248 and 249, ante.

Sec. 442 

 or to file his attested account, if the job is a public one, will not discharge the surety on a contractor's bond conditioned, among other things, upon the payment of claims for labor and material. Delay in pursuing remedies against the principal debtor, or the failure to acquire liens will not discharge the surety. While it may be the duty of the creditor to preserve any securities or liens which he may have already acquired, there is no duty upon him to acquire them. If the surety desires the benefit of such securities or liens, he may, by paying the claim of the creditor, be subrogated to his rights and thus obtain the securities or liens himself.151

Sec. 295. Effect of Effect of Notice to Surety of Suit 

Against Owner.

A surety having been notified of the pendency and nature of an action against an owner, to which owner it is liable on the bond of a contractor signed by it as surety, and having been given an opportunity to make a defense in the case, and having failed to do so, is concluded and bound by the judgment rendered in such action, and cannot thereafter question the correctness thereof in another action. Thus, where subcontractors and materialmen brought suit against a school board for the amount of their accounts left unpaid by a defaulting contractor and the board notifies the surety of such suit, but such surety ignores the notice and the case proceeds to judg ment in favor of such subcontractors and materialmen against such school board, which later paid the judgment, 151. Sec. 296. Surety's Right to Subrogation. 

One of the most valuable rights of a surety is that of subrogation. By this principle of equity, the surety, upon payment of the debt, becomes the owner of and is entitled to enforce all of the rights and remedies of the creditor against the principal debtor whose obligation he has discharged. This right of the surety to demand of the creditor whose debt he has paid, the securities he holds against the principal debtor and to stand in his shoes, does not depend at all upon any request or contract on the part of the debtor with the surety, but grows rather out of the relations existing between the surety and the creditor, and is founded not upon any contract, express or implied, but springs from the most obvious principles of natural justice.153

It is not the tendency of the law to restrict and narrow the instances in which a surety may pay and be subrogated against the principal debtor. On the contrary, the decisions all show that there is a continuing disposition on the part of the courts to extend the class of cases in which the right of subrogation obtains, with much liber-

Sec. 297. Rights of Surety to Funds in Hands of Owner. 

(a) Where There Is No Liability to Laborers, Materialmen or Subcontractors 

Before the enactment of G. C. 2365-1 to 2365-4, inclusive, the bond required of contractors engaged in public work was one which ran to the benefit of the public only. No provision was made therein for the payment by the surety of the claims of laborers, materialmen or subcontractors who performed labor or furnished material in the construction of the building or other improvement. 

Where, therefore, work on a state building was abandoned by the contractor and the contract was completed by the surety, the amount remaining due under the contract became the property of the surety, and could not be reached by creditors of the defaulting contractor who held claims incurred by him for labor and material which went into the building.156 (b) Where the Surety Is Also Liable to Laborers,

Materialmen and Subcontractors

If, upon the default of a contractor, the surety completes the work at its own expense, the question then arises as to whether the balance of the unpaid contract price remaining in the hands of the state belongs to the surety, through its right of subrogation to the position of the state against the contractor, or whether it belongs to creditors of the contractor who have furnished labor and material to such contractor before he abandoned the job. 

It seems to be the rule that where such claimants for labor and material have perfected their liens against the funds in the hands of the state prior to the forfeiture by the contractor, the surety, upon taking over the unfinished portion of said contract, receives it subject to all valid liens then attaching or that might thereafter be perfected against it. The surety being liable upon its bond to such claimants cannot invoke the equitable doctrine of subrogation against its plain legal obligation; and for the further reason that the doctrine of subrogation will not be applied to prefer one creditor over another where an inequitable result will be accomplished thereby.157 

But this rule does not apply as to those persons who are merely creditors of the contractor and who are not entitled to perfect liens against such funds for the payment of their claims, even though the sums so advanced by such creditors have been used to pay the claims of persons furnishing labor and materials, thus discharging a portion of the liability for which the surety would other-

Sec. 448 

(c) As Against Contractor's Trustee in Bankruptcy A surety cannot as a matter of right insist upon completing the contract of its principal who has been adjudicated a bankrupt. Whether or not a bankruptcy court will authorize its trustee to complete an unperformed contract, or will permit a surety of the bankrupt to make use of the property of the estate, is a matter within the discretion of the bankruptcy court. It is only when the situation warrants a belief that the bankrupt's estate will be benefited by such a course being pursued that the bankruptcy court will permit the surety to consume the supplies and materials or to use the equipment of the bankrupt for the purpose of completing the contract. This determination is entirely within the discretion of the referee, and is not subject to review.161 

A contractor's application for a performance bond, assigning to the surety, in the event of nonperformance, all of the contractor's interest in tools, plant, materials, and other equipment or supplies, has no greater force than a chattel mortgage, and, as between such surety and the contractor's trustee in bankruptcy, it is to be regarded as if it were on its face a chattel mortgage. Being unrecorded as such, the trustee takes the better title thereto. 

Nor can the surety upon any principle of subrogation to the rights of the state (the obligee of said contract) defeat this right of the trustee where the construction contract does not confer upon it any title or lien to such property of the contractor, or purport to give any right to use the same in completing performance thereof.162

966 (Ohio).

Sec. 299. Bond Given to Secure Performance of Contract to Erect or Alter State Buildings.

On the following day the Legislature passed an act “to protect persons performing labor and furnishing materials for the construction and repair of public works."165 

The former act applies only to public buildings or improvements erected by the state; the latter applies to public buildings or improvements erected by the state or any political subdivision of the state.166 The latter obviously is broader in its scope than the former and in fact includes all of the buildings and improvements to which the former applies.  Sec. 301. Conflict of Laws-What Law Governs Construction of Surety's Contract. 

Where an Ohio contractor was awarded a contract for erecting a building in the State of New York, and a surety bond was given for its performance, and both the contract and the bond were executed in Ohio and were treated as one instrument, and some of the work was done here, the contract became governable by the laws of Ohio, the state where it was made.174 except that which is now contained in G. C. 2365-1 to G. C. 

2365-4, inclusive. The latter embraces all types of public contracts; no other legislation upon this subject is necessary. It only affords a productive source of vexatious litigation. 

174. Indemnity Insurance Co. vs. Stamberger Co., 37 Oh. App. 

236, 33 O.L.R. 121. The Court said: "Why should the laws of a foreign state govern when the only reason assigned is that the work is performed there. It seems to us that the determining element is that the laws of the state wherein the parties meet, discuss terms and execute the agreement, should be decisive, because it is fair to assume that the parties themselves would be acquainted with and amenable to those laws, and it is not a violent assumption to say that acting under the environment of those laws, the laws themselves would become a determinable factor in the transaction".

Sec. 302. Historical Review. 

The first general Mechanics Lien Law in Ohio,¹ which gave to persons improving real estate under a contract with the owner the right to a mechanics lien thereon, also provided a method by which persons performing labor for or furnishing materials to the contractor for use in the performance of his contract might intercept the payments due such contractor from the owner. This method included the delivery of what the statute designated as an "attested account" by the claimant to the owner. The 

Act of May 4, 1877,2 substituted "sworn and itemized account" for "attested account", but the older name is probably more often used even now by courts and lawyers although the name itself has not appeared in the statute for over fifty years. 

1. The Act of March 11, 1843 

(41 Oh. Laws 66). 

2. 74 Oh. Laws 168.

Sec. 302 

Attested Accounts

The law relating to attested accounts developed with many changes until 1913, at which time almost the entire law was repealed by the Act of April 16, 1913,3 which created our present Mechanics Lien Law. There have been so many amendments, supplementary acts and repeals of the statutes relating to attested accounts that the present authority of the earlier decisions cannot be determined without careful consideration of the changes since made in the statutes.

The gradual growth of the law relating to attested accounts as now embraced in the existing sections of the General Code may be traced through examination of the following acts of the Legislature: Act of March 11, 1843, 

41 Oh. Laws 66; Act of May 1, 1871, 68 Oh. Laws 107; 

Act of March 30, 1875, 72 Oh. Laws 166; Act of May 

4, 1877, 74 Oh. Laws 169 (in which the act took substantially its final form); Act of May 11, 1878, 75 Oh. 

Laws 514; Revised Statutes of Ohio, January 1, 1880; 

Act of May 5, 1887, 84 Oh. Laws 46; Act of April 13, 1894, 91 Oh. Laws 135 (held unconstitutional); Act of 

April 18, 1902, 95 Oh. Laws 209; Act of April 20, 1904, 97 Oh. Laws 500; Act of May 10, 1910, 101 Oh. Laws 

229; Act of April 16, 1913, 103 Oh. Laws 369 (the present Mechanics Lien Law passed pursuant to the Constitutional Amendment of 1912); Act of July 23, 1929, 113 

Oh. Laws 474. For a complete list of Mechanic Lien

Acts see Section 4. 

All that remains now of the earlier statutes relating to attested accounts is embraced in G. C. 8324, 8324-1, 8325, 8326, 8327, 8328, 8329 and 8331. It is quite probable that G. C. 8314 so far as it relates to exemp- 

3. 103 Oh. Laws 369.

Sec. 456 

 tions, G. C. 8323-3, relating to the manner in which notices may be served, and G. C. 8322, relating to assignments, are also parts of the existing law pertaining to attested accounts.

As it stands today, the law provides only an incomplete and imperfect method by which unpaid subcontractors, materialmen and mechanics can enforce the payment of their claims by intercepting the funds due the principal contractor from the owner.

Sec. 303. Applies Only to Public Improvements. 

(a) Prior to January 1, 1880, the attested account law applied only to private improvements and not only gave the subcontractors, mechanics and materialmen a claim against the payments due the principal contractor but also permitted them to obtain a lien upon the real estate of the owner. From January 1, 1880, to May 2, 1913, this law included both public and private improvements but, of course, did not permit liens to be acquired upon public property. Since the general revision of the 

Mechanics Lien Law in 1913, the statutes relating to attested accounts no longer apply to private improvements. 

G. C. 8324, which expressly includes public improvements, also includes private improvements by a reference to G. C. 8308 and 8316, which embraced in their scope all improvements of real property under private contracts. The latter sections having been repealed, it has been held that G. C. 8324 was repealed by implication insofar as it relates to private contracts. The same case held that G. C. 8332 had been repealed by implication. 

The latter section, never expressly repealed, would in conjunction with G. C. 8324, continue to give subcontractors, mechanics and materialmen a lien upon private

Sec. 303

Attested Accounts property were it not for the repeal of these sections by implication.

This implied repeal was established in an action where it was contended that, since the revision of the law in 1913, there were two separate and independent methods by which a mechanics lien might be secured upon private property. In denying the efficacy of this contention the Court of Appeals said, with reference to the 

Act of April 16, 1913: “An examination of the entire

Act shows that it furnishes a complete remedy and it is evident that the General Assembly intended this act as a substitute for all existing laws relative to mechanics liens as between private individuals, firms or corporations. *** It is contended that Section 8324 is not specifically repealed and that it refers to Sections 8308 and 8316 *** and that this reference still leaves them unrepealed to all intents and purposes. However, we are of the opinion that that part of this section which refers to Sections 8308 and 8316 is repealed by implication and is inconsistent with the later enactments."4

While it is true that the Court of Appeals was dealing with the contention that a mechanics lien had been secured on the owner's real estate, the principles underlying its decision apply with equal force against the claim that a lien can be secured under G. C. 8324 upon payments due from a private owner to a principal contrac-

The Act of April 16, 1913, was complete and self-contained and the natural assumption throughout is that the provisions thereof are in relation to Mechanics Liens on private property only. 

An examination of the act shows that the Legislature clearly intended G. C. 8310, 8311, 8312, 8313, 8315, 8316, 8317, 8318, 8319, 8320, 8323, 8323-1, 8323-2 and 8323-4, to relate to liens on private property only.6

The Legislature was aware that the General Code contained a chapter entitled "Liens" and that the act would become a part of that chapter. Further, when it passed the amendment of June 5, 1915, it knew that the sections amended and supplemented were included in the above mentioned chapter. 

We shall examine various sections of the act to see how the Legislature employed the above terms. The italics in the quotations from those sections are ours. 

G. C. 8314 provides that any person "who wishes to avail himself of the provisions of this statute" shall file an affidavit with the County Recorder describing the property to be charged with the lien. Obviously this refers to a lien upon private property and has no relation to attested accounts. However, the same section concludes "There shall be no homestead or other exemptions against any lien under the provisions of this chapter.”7 

This provision was contained in the Act of April 16, 1913, and in the act as amended June 5, 1915, and by "chapter" the Legislature must have intended the chapter on Liens.

The Legislature seems to have used "chapter" here as meaning something more than the sections re lating to Mechanics Liens. 

G. C. 8322 is entitled "Superiority of liens; assignment". There are two sentences in this section, one stating that the liens of subcontractors, laborers and materialmen are superior to the liens of their contractors, and the other saving the rights of sub-contractors, laborers and materialmen when their contractor assigns his contract. The first sentence is not of great importance since in the absence of such a provision a court would make the same rule as to priorities between persons who contract to do certain work or furnish certain materials and the persons who actually do the work or furnish the materials. Standing by itself it would relate only to liens upon private property.7a The second sentence relating to assignments saves the claims of every person furnishing labor or materials "towards the construction *** or improvement as designated in this chapter." G. C. 8323-5, relating to executors and administrators, gives them the rights and subjects them to the liabil ity "under this chapter" that owners would have if alive. 

This is broad enough to include attested accounts but is, of course, inapplicable to the public as an owner.

G. C. 8323-6 makes assignable all liens inchoate or perfected "under the terms of this act." It also provides that the taking of security shall not be a waiver of the lien "provided for in this act" unless the security is "upon the real estate itself." This reference to the "real estate itself" makes it evident that the Legislature intended the lien upon private real property. This section does not apply to attested accounts. 

G. G. C. 8323-8 declares "this act is hereby declared to be a remedial statute" and continues with a reference to "the lien or liens hereinbefore provided for." Plainly, this cannot refer to the liens of attested accounts provided for in subsequent sections.

Sec. 304. No Lien on Public Property. 

Comparison of G. C. 8324, which expressly includes public improvements and expressly refers to public authorities, with G. C. 8332, which makes no reference to public improvements or public authorities, shows clearly that the latter gave a lien on private property only and was never intended to give a lien on public property. 

General statutes do not include the state unless it is

Sec. 305

Attested Accounts expressly named; and it is against public policy to grant a lien upon public buildings or property.10 

As stated by Judge Westenhaver in reference to a contract for highway construction: "It is sufficient to say that his (a mechanic's) remedy is exclusively against money due or to become due the contractor and that no lien is given or authorized upon either the public highway or the equipment, materials and supplies of the contractor assembled on the highway."11

Sec. 305. The Statute Does Not Apply to the 

State of Ohio.

G. C. 8324 does not apply to contracts for the construction of public improvements by the State of Ohio. 

Only those public improvements which are constructed under contracts with the counties, cities and other political subdivisions of the State are included within its scope. Thus, in an action arising out of a construction contract entered into by the trustees of the Ohio Soldiers' and Sailors' Orphans' Home, the court said: "That the words of the statute ‘or other public improvement or public building' are broad enough to embrace the claim of the relator could not be disputed; but it is contended that the State is not embraced within the general words of the statute and could be held to be within the purview of the same only when so declared expressly, or by necessary implication. *** Since the sovereign state in prescribing general laws intends thereby to regulate the conduct of its subjects only, and not its own conduct, the law for perfecting liens does not apply against the State when the

Sec. 307.

Brief Summary of the Statute. 

The subject of attested accounts is thus limited to claims against money due the contractor under contracts for public improvements with some public authority or political subdivision other than the state itself. Subject to the foregoing, it may be said in a general way, that a person supplying labor or materials to a contractor on 

16. Sections 8308 and 8316 repealed. See Section 303, (b), ante.

Sec. 

466 

 a public construction job may, within four months thereafter, file a sworn and itemized account with the Board or public authority for whom the work is being done. 

The Board must then detain subsequent payments due to the contractor as security for payment of the claim and of other similar claims filed before the next subsequent payment falls due or within ten days thereafter. The first claimant obtains no preference over others, unless he files a copy of the account with the County Recorder and even then shares with them pro rata if their accounts are filed with the Board or public authority before the ten-day period expires. The Board or public authority is required to furnish the contractor a copy of the account within five days and if the contractor does not object to its correctness within five days after receiving it, he will be considered as having assented thereto, and it then becomes the Board's or other public authority's duty to apply the money due the contractor upon the claims assented to or otherwise adjusted. The various questions which may arise in connection with such claims can best be considered in connection with the several sections of the act.16a 

Sec. 308. The Statute Liberally Construed. 

As a general rule of construction, statutes which are remedial in their character and purpose should receive such liberal construction as will carry out the intention of the Legislature in their enactment. G. C. 8323-8 defining the Act of April 16, 1913 as a remedial statute does not include the law of attested accounts, G. C. 8324

Sec. 309. The Contract for the Improvement and the Contractual Relation. 

The improvement must be "provided for in a contract between * any board, officer or public authority and a principal contractor." The statute contemplates an actual express contract existing between the public and the principal contractor. The procedure by which a Board can enter into a construction contract is prescribed by law. Generally speaking, the rights of anyone claiming through the principal contractor are no greater than the rights of the latter and if the principal contractor cannot himself enforce payment from the public, those claiming through or under him are likewise unable to do so. 

Not only must the improvement be provided for in a contract, but the labor and materials must be furnished "under a contract between such subcontractor, materialman, laborer or mechanic and a principal contractor or subcontractor." And generally speaking, the rights of anyone claiming through a subcontractor are no greater than the rights of the latter, and if the subcontractor for any reason cannot recover against the principal contractor, then neither can those persons claiming through the subcontractor succeed in obtaining any money due from the Board to the principal contractor. 

Accordingly, anyone contracting to perform labor or furnish materials to a subcontractor will find his right to recover under an attested account depending upon the provisions of the principal contract and of the subcontract and upon the performance of those provisions by the principal contractor and the subcontractor. "There is no reason for protecting an owner who has paid the con-

Sec. 468 

 tractor in full pursuant to the contract, which is not equally applicable to a contractor who in like manner has paid his subcontractor."19

How many such contracts may there be intervening between the Board and the claimant? As stated above, the labor and materials must be furnished "under a contract between such subcontractor, materialman, laborer or mechanic and a principal contractor or subcontractor. 

This at least gives the right of lien to a subcontractor, laborer or materialman having a contract with a subcontractor who has a contract with the owner. 

It has been doubted whether the right extends any further from the principal contractor or at least whether subcontractors of the third and more distant degrees are included.20 It has been said that to include such persons is not looked upon with favor by the courts, that it is rather considered to be against public policy, that it would be impracticable and that it would impose hardships. There are, however, no Ohio cases on this point. 

The case of Stephen vs. United Railroad Stock-Yards 

Company, 29 O. S. 227 (decided in 1876) merely held that under the early form of the statute persons claiming through subcontractors were not included at all because the statute taken as a whole was not applicable to such persons. That is, the procedure provided in that act did not seem adapted to enforcing the claims of such persons. 

Thereupon the legislature changed the law to its present form21 and the present form may be applied with almost 

19. Jones on Liens, 3rd Ed., $1295. 

20. Rockel & White, Ohio Me chanic & Sub-Contractor Lien 

Law, Pages 96-97. 

Treadway & Marlatt, Ohio

Mechanics Lien Law, Pages 166167. 

21. 74 Oh. Laws 169 (1877).

Sec. 309 

Attested Accounts equal ease to persons claiming through subcontractors of any degree. There is nothing unreasonable or impracticable in extending its benefits to such persons; at least such persons claiming mechanics liens are included under the Act of April 16, 1913.22

The words of G. C. 8324 in its present form seem expressly to include all such persons. Suppose a subcontractor, A, who subcontracts part of the construction to B, who in turn subcontracts a portion of the work to C. 

B admittedly has the right to a lien since in the words of the statute he is a subcontractor having a contract with a subcontractor. Why are not B's subcontractors, laborers and materialmen equally persons having a contract with a subcontractor? Why should it be supposed that the legislature uses the same word "subcontractor" in the same sentence with different meanings? If "subcontractor" in the first line of Section 8324 includes both primary and secondary subcontractors, at least, as it undoubtedly does, why should the word "subcontractor" later on in the same sentence be supposed to include only primary subcontractors? Going back to our subcontractors, A, B and C, it would seem that B's materialmen and laborers should have the right to the lien since they have a contract with a "subcontractor". And if they are included, then C must also be taken in since he equally has a contract with a subcontractor. There is no logical end to this process and there is no decision of our Supreme Court indicating that any person should be excluded from the lien however remote his contractual relation might be. The test in Ohio does not seem to be the nearness or remoteness of the 

22. See G. C. 8323-9.

Sec. 470 

 contractual relation; the right to a lien depends rather upon whether the labor and materials were furnished "for the construction" of the improvement. That phrase is elsewhere defined.23 The persons furnishing such labor and materials are regarded as having an equitable interest in the fund out of which the owner pays the principal contractor24 and it is difficult to see that their equity becomes less as their contracts become more remote provided the labor is performed on the improvement and the materials are delivered to be used in the improvement. We believe, therefore, that there is no good reason and no Ohio authority for excluding anyone from the benefit of this section on account merely of the remoteness of his contractual relation.

Sec. 310. Terminology and Definitions. 

(a) In General

In discussing G. C. 8324 and other sections of the act, we shall often use "board" as including "board, officer or public authority;" "improvement" as including all the public work or construction described in the statute; "construction contract" as including contracts to construct, improve or repair; "materials" as including also machinery and fuel; "account" or "attested account" for the sworn and itemized statement required by the statute; and "claimant" for any person claiming a right under the statute. 

(b) The Public Improvement 

The labor or material must be furnished for the "construction, improvement or repair of any turnpike, road

The Legislature probably intended by this section to include all improvements of real property undertaken by the public in the same manner that the now obsolete reference to private improvements was intended to cover all improvements of private real property.

Wrecking or removing an improvement or building would not seem to be included in "construction, improvement or repair," however, unless it should be a preliminary step towards some other improvement or construction. 

(c) The Subcontractor 

The definitions contained in G. C. 8323-9 apply only to the Act of April 16, 1913, but it would appear that its definition of a subcontractor as one who undertakes to construct a part of the improvement is in accord with the popular and legal concept of the term as previously used in Ohio. A subcontractor thus undertakes to furnish part of the labor that goes into the construction. He will frequently furnish materials also. This would seem to exclude persons who prepare materials specially for the construction, but who do not actually fit or adapt the materials to the improvement and such persons are classed as materialmen.25 Persons who sell materials to a materialman, and laborers employed by a materialman, have no claim under this statute since they have no contract with a sub-contractor. 

Materialmen, laborers and mechanics are persons furnishing materials, or performing labor under the circumstances described in the next subsection hereof.

Sec. 311. The Itemized Statement. 

The claimant is permitted to file "a sworn and \itemized statement of the amount and value of such labor performed, and to be performed, material, fuel or machinery furnished, containing a description of any promissory note or notes that have been given by the principal contractor or subcontractor on account of the labor, ma chinery or material, or any part thereof, with all credits and set-offs thereon."29

Sec. 313. Filing the Attested Account. 

G. C. 8324 provides that the claimant "may file" the attested account "with the owner, board or officer or the authorized clerk or agent thereof", and that proof that the attested account "was mailed by registered letter to the address of the owner, board or officer, shall be taken as prima facie evidence of the filing thereof." G. C. 

8323-3, a part of the Act of April 16, 1913, provides that "any notice, affidavit or copy required to be served under the provisions of this chapter" (the chapter on liens) may be served by registered letter. It also provides that proof that such notice was mailed by registered letter to the last known place of residence of such "person, firm or corporation" shall be conclusive proof of such service. Whether the "board, officer or public authority" of G. C. 8324 would be included in the terms "person, firm or corporation" under G. C. 8323-3 is questionable; especially so since G. C. 8324 has its own provision as to filing by registered mail. 

When the statute required the claimant to "deliver" the notice, the Supreme Court held, in a case in which a notice was left in the office of the clerk of a Board of Education and subsequently was actually received by the clerk: "Undoubtedly the claim of a subcontractor can be charged upon the owner only in the way prescribed by the statute by delivering his attested account against the contractor to the owner. But when the

The subsequent change in the statute permitting the claimant to "file" the notice, and the still later change making the mailing of a registered letter presumptive evidence of filing, indicate that it may no longer be necessary to deliver the statement to an agent authorized to act in respect to the contract, but that delivery to an em ployee, at the office of the Board, whose duty it is to receive incoming papers may be a sufficient filing.43
