Now, the statute as amended requires "filing", which seems a little less onerous than delivery and provides that sending the account by registered mail is prima facie evidence of filing.

Sec. 314. When the Account May Be Filed. 

The claimant who has performed labor or furnished materials, or is doing so or is about to do so, "may file" with the Board an attested account "at the time of beginning to perform such labor or the delivery of the material * * * or at any time not to exceed four months from the performance of the labor or the delivery of the material."45

The time of delivery has already been defined as the time at which title to the materials passes from the materialman.46 However, if a new contract is made covering the sale of the materials after the same have already been shipped under a former contract, the four-month period runs from the date of the new contract and not from the date of shipment.47

The present four-month period was, under an earlier statute a sixty-day period, and under another earlier statute ninety days. It commences to run not at the completion of the improvement by the principal contractor, but responsibility upon the board if the claimant should leave his attested account at its office with a person authorized by it to receive mail or other written communications.

Sec. 322.

Effect of Making Payments Before the 

Same Are Due.

Section 6 of the Act of March 11, 1843,67 provided that if "by collusion or otherwise" the owner paid money in advance of the sum due under the contract, he should be liable in the same manner as if no such payment had been made. The Act of May 4, 1877,68 substituted the phrase "by collusion or fraud” for the phrase "by collusion or otherwise" and added that payments made in good faith for completion of the construction should not be considered as made collusively or fraudulently. This addition was later omitted from the section by the Act of March 5, 1887,69 and the section remained in that form until as Section 8335 of the General Code it was repealed by the Act of April 16, 1913.70

The Supreme Court in considering this section said: "The section appears to be exclusive in defining the circumstances which will give to the sub-lienor a right to resort to an obligation which as between the owner and would have; and it is clear that a contract in a case like the present" (an express agreement by the commissioners to retain funds for the materialmen was claimed to have been made) "would be an act extra viam." 

Clements vs. Commissioners, 5 Dec. Rep. 126. 

67. 41 Oh. Laws 66. 

68. 74 Oh. Laws 168. 

69. 84 Oh. Laws 51. 

70. 103 Oh. Laws 369.

Sec. 490 

 contractor had been discharged when the sub-lienor's right accrued.”71

It would appear that the public is no longer liable to the lien claimant for amounts that have been actually paid to the principal contractor, whether or not the payments were made before they were due. Plainly, subcontractors, laborers and materialmen have no legal right, in the absence of express statutory provision, to funds due from the owner to the principal contractor. It is significant that when the Mechanics Lien Law was originally enacted, the Legislature included the section making payments made in advance ineffective as against lien claimants. The Legislature, having now repealed that section, must have intended that lien claimants could no longer question the validity of payments actually made by the board before the notice of the claimant's lien was filed, even though such payments were made in advance of the sum then due under the contract.

G. C. 8331 states explicitly that the amount to be recovered by the claimant shall not exceed "in any case the balance due to the principal contractor." In connection with the other existing statutory provisions, this seems to allow the board the benefit of all payments made before the first claim is filed.

If payment in advance is a breach of some public officer's oath to faithfully perform his duties, it is possible that a lien claimant injured thereby may have a right of action against such public officer, but certainly there can be no recovery from the public treasury. 

71. Stark vs. Simmons, 54 Oh. St. 435.

Sec. 323. Set-offs Against Subsequent Payments. 

It was said in an early case, that the act conferred upon claimants "only the right to be subrogated to the claims of the contractor under his contract with the owner at the time the requisite notice is given."72 The provision in G. C. 8331 that the amount to be recovered by the claimant shall not exceed "in any case the balance due to the principal contractor," necessarily implies that the owner is entitled against lien claimants to the benefit of any set-off against the principal contractor arising under the construction contract, at least.

The Supreme Court later held that as against lien claimants, the owner could not set off a claim against the principal contractor which did not arise under the construction contract and which was acquired by the owner after the claimant's labor was performed, although the owner then had no notice that the claimant was unpaid. The court construed the phrase "not exceeding in any case the balance due to the principal contractor" as "applying only to the monies due by the owner to the contractor under the contract" and refused to construe it as "implying balance due on general account."73 

Subsequently however, the Supreme Court held that an owner might set off against lien claimants, a claim against the principal contractor which the owner had acquired without the knowledge of the principal contractor and before the principal contract was made.74 It was in

After commenting upon these two decisions of the Supreme Court, a Common Pleas Court held that the owner of a building might set off an antecedent debt due him from the principal contractor to the exclusion of claims of sub-contractors and materialmen, although the contract did not provide for payment in advance or mention this debt due the owner.75 At a time therefore when the act forbade payments in advance of the time provided by the contract, our courts stated first that only set-offs arising under the construction contract were available to the owner as against sub-lienors. Later they held that all set-offs acquired before the construction contract was made were available to the owner against sub-lienors and stated that it was only when the owner had paid the contractor in advance of the time specified in the contract diminishing the fund available to the sub-lienor, he shall be liable as if such collusive or fraudulent payment had not been made. This section appears to be exclusive in defining the circumstances which will give to the sub-lienor, a right to resort to an obligation which as between the owner and contractor had been discharged when the sub-lienor's right accrued. The statute preserves the amount of the indebtedness for the satisfaction of the claims of those who take liens in accordance with its provisions, but it does not for the purpose of creating a fund to which they may resort, enlarge the owner's liability to the contractor as it may be fixed by the terms of the contract and by the rules of law relating to the subject." 

Stark vs. Simmons, 54 Oh. St. 435.

We believe the court considered the right as accruing when the claimant commenced furnishing the labor or materials and not at the time of filing the attested account with the owner, since if it meant the latter, the second Supreme Court case would squarely overrule the earlier case.

The situation as to set-offs, therefore, not arising under the construction contract, is that they are available to the owner if acquired by him prior to the making of the construction contract; that they are probably available, if acquired before the sub-lienor commenced furnishing labor or materials; and that they are not available as setoffs when later acquired. However, if the owner with the consent of the contractor applies the set-off as a payment upon the account, this would seem as effective as any other payment in reducing the amount due to the contractor and such a payment even though made before a payment was due under the contract, would diminish the amount available to lien claimants if they had not yet filed attested accounts. It may even be supposed that the repeal of the section forbidding payments in advance, and the limitation of the application of the act to public contracts only, has made the claims of sub-lienors subject to all set-offs acquired by the board before an attested account is filed with it.

Assuming that the contract was for a completed improvement, with payments to be made in installments as the work progressed, it would seem that if the contractor should abandon the work after a payment became due, but before payment was actually made to him, the amount of that payment would be available to claimants, subject, however, to the board's right to complete the improvement at the contractor's expense.

Sec. 326. For Whose Benefit Funds Are De tained.

By the express provision of the statute,84 the funds are to be detained "to secure such claims" (i. e., the claims set forth in the first attested account filed) "and the claims and estimates of other subcontractors, materialmen, laborers, mechanics, or persons furnishing materials to or performing labor for any contractor or subcontractor who intervenes before the next subsequent payment under the contract, or within ten days thereafter." 

The phraseology and punctuation of the foregoing quotation are such as to render its exact meaning doubtful, but presumably it means nothing more than that the funds are detained for the benefit of the first claimant and of other persons entitled to file attested accounts provided they intervene within a certain time. The time stated is "before the next subsequent payment under the contract or within ten days thereafter."

The expression "who intervenes," as originally enacted, read "who may intervene." The change was made by the Codification of 1910. In the present form of the phrase, the antecedent of "who" is the immediately preceding "contractor or subcontractor," but this can hardly be the correct construction of the sentence in which they appear.

 Sec. 328. Payment of Subcontractors Out of Subsequent Payments. 

G. C. 8328. All other subcontractors, materialmen, laborers, mechanics or persons furnishing material, fuel or machinery who, before the first subsequent payment falls due after the deposit of a copy of such statement with the county recorder by any subcontractor, material or machinery man, laborer, or person furnishing material, or within ten days thereafter, file with such owner, board, officer or authorized clerk, agent or attorney thereof, a sworn and itemized statement or estimate of the labor, machinery, fuel or material furnished or to be furnished by them under a contract with a principal or subcontractor, containing a description of any promissory note or notes given therefor, or any part thereof, shall be paid pro rata with the person first so filing such statement and with each other, out of such first and other subsequent payments so falling due. Upon failure so to do, they shall have no recourse against the owner, board, officer, or the clerk or agent thereof for any prior payments made under his contract with his head contractor or subcontractor.

Sec. 329. Priority Between Claimants. 

Prior to the amendment of May 1, 1871,96 the first claimant to file an attested account secured priority over the others, and the others were paid in the order of the filing of their accounts.97 By virtue of this amendment fees allowed. For filing the account the ordinary fee is twentyfour cents, plus six cents for each additional party if there are more than two parties to the account. The fee for recording such instrument is ten cents per hundred words. 

96. 68 Oh. Laws 107. 

97. "It has been settled that as the statute stood at the time this transaction arose, those first in time in delivering their attested accounts to the owner were prior in right.” 

Dunn & Witt vs. Rankin, 27 

Oh. St. 132, citing Copeland vs. 

Manton, 22 Oh. St. 398.

Sec. 330 

Attested Accounts all claimants took pro rata regardless of when the accounts were filed. 

The Act of May 4, 187798 was substantially like the present statute in contemplating that the first claimant would file a copy of his attested account with the county recorder, but penalized failure so to file by postponing the claimant to his fellow-claimants. 

The Act of May 11, 187599 amended this by providing that such claimant should have no preference over other claimants, unless he had filed a copy of his account with the county recorder. This provision has been incorporated into G. C. 8326, and, standing alone, would imply that the first claimant to file the copy with the recorder would obtain a preference over other claimants. 

However, G. C. 8328 is plain to the effect that certain other claimants are to be paid pro rata with the claimant who first files with the board and also with the recorder. 

Accordingly, we shall discuss who those persons are, what they must file, the time in which they must file, whether the fund in which the group has priority consists of all the subsequent payments under the contract, or include only the first subsequent payment, and just what is meant by pro rata payment. 

Sec. 330. Who Are Entitled to Pro Rata Pay ments.

It is clear that fellow-claimants under the same contractor and the same contract are the ones entitled to share with the first claimant. The persons claiming through a sub-contractor share only in that portion of the fund due their sub-contractor. If all the sub-contractors, 98. 74 Oh. Laws 168. 

99. 75 Oh. Laws 514.

Sec. 

504 

 mechanics and materialmen should file claims, the amount due the principal contractor will first be divided into as many parts as he has sub-contractors, mechanics, laborers and materialmen and the amount of each part would be in proportion to the amounts due such persons from the principal contractor. His mechanics, laborers and materialmen will be paid their share and the division of the amounts due the sub-contractors will then be made. 

These will be divided in the same manner with respect to persons dealing directly with each sub-contractor and so on down the line of claimants. We might borrow a phrase from another branch of law and say that the funds due the principal contractor descend among the claimants per stirpes. No contractor will receive anything for himself until the claimants dealing directly with him have been paid in full. 

It will be seen that the first part of G. C. 8322 relating to the relative superiority of liens of principal contractors, sub-contractors, mechanics, laborers and materialmen, if applicable to attested accounts, adds nothing to the rights of claimants under attested accounts. 

Sec. 331. Pro Rata Payment As Affected by Diversion of Materials. 

It has been questioned in an early case and discussed by text writers,100 whether the equity of a claimant who furnished materials for the construction but whose materials were diverted by the owner or contractor to some other improvement is equal to that of fellow-claimants 

100. Bender vs. Stettinius, 10 

Dec. Rep. 186. 

Rockel & White, Ohio Mechan ic & Sub-Contractors' Lien Laws, 

Pages 99-102. Treadway & Marlatt, Ohio, Mechanics Lien Law, Sections 212-214.

Sec. 331 Attested Accounts whose materials were used for the purpose for which they were furnished. The statute makes no distinction between such claimants; this should be sufficient reason for allowing the claimant whose materials were diverted to share pro rata with the rest. And after all, it is not plain that his equity is less than the equities of other materialmen. He does all that they do, i. e. furnishes material for the construction and the diversion of his materials to some other purpose is not his fault and is a mishap that might equally have occurred to the materials of any other claimant. His claim is superior to that of an assignee for value.101

However if a claimant has furnished materials which are unsuitable for the improvement as described in the principal contract and which are not used in the improvement, he is not entitled to share with the other claimants.102 When furnishing materials for the construction of the improvement, he is assumed to know the kind of materials required by the principal contract. This is not a defense that could be raised by the board or the contractor. The contractor cannot use his own fraud as a defense against the claim of the defrauded party and the board is not interested in what becomes of the money due the principal contractor provided no objections are raised by other claimants.103

Toledo Lumber Manufactur ing Company vs. Gross, 3 N. P. 322.

 Sec. 332. Time of Filing Claims. 

The statute leaves no doubt as to the time within which this sworn statement must be filed. It must be filed within ten days after a payment becomes due under the contract subsequent to the first filing of a copy of an attested account by some claimant with the recorder. 8324, this validates the claims of others who file before the expiration of the ten-day period, even though such claimants performed the last labor or supplied the last materials under their contracts more than four months previous thereto,104 and this is true even though the claim to be revived was filed with the board before the claim which was properly filed within the four-month period.105

Sec. 333. Priority in Subsequent Payments. 

Do the original claimant and the others filing their accounts within the ten day period obtain priority only in the first subsequent payment or in all subsequent payments?

It has been said by one court, that if a claimant filed after the expiration of the ten day period, he would share in the succeeding payments. 107 Another court has stated that a sub-contractor who files an attested account, obtains a lien on all payments then due or becoming due within ten days thereafter108 which might imply that the lien extended no further.

Nevertheless, G. C. 8325 states that the board must detain "all subsequent payments" to secure the claims and estimates of persons who intervene before the next subsequent payment or within ten days thereafter and G. C. 8328 states that the claimants intervening within the ten day period are to share pro rata "with the person first so filing such statement and with each other out of such first and other subsequent payments so falling due." 

106. "It is claimed * * that in order to share with them (the first claimant) the other subcontractors were required not only to file sworn and itemized accounts but also to file a copy thereof with the County Recorder. As to the latter requirement, a careful inspection of the law seems to indicate that it applies only to the first sub-contractor's account filed with the owner, and is intended to give notice to other sub-contractors that they may come in and share with him." 

Kennett vs. Rebholz & Carr, 6 Dec. Rep. 824. 

107. Bender vs. Stettinius, 10 

Dec. Rep. 186. 

108. Saginaw Bay Co. vs. En gle, 19 C. C. 632.

Sec. 508 

The Legislature could hardly have expressed more clearly its intention to give the group filing claims within ten days a priority in all subsequent payments. The fact that persons who expect to furnish labor and materials, but who have not yet done so, may file attested accounts enables all possible claimants to file their liens, and also enables them to determine whether they wish to continue on the job, since they know with whom they must share. 

Therefore, claimants who do not file within the ten day period, will have claims inferior to those filed within the ten day period and also subject themselves to the chance that the board after satisfying the other claims, may make payments to the contractor.109 The next question is as to the priority among themselves of claimants who file after the expiration of the ten day period. Do they share pro rata in what is left of the subsequent payments after the more diligent claimants have been paid in full, or do their claims take priority in the order of the times at which they were filed? It would seem that the rights of these subsequent claimants among themselves in what is left of the subsequent payments after satisfying the first group of claims is governed by the statute in exactly the same manner as the rights of the first group. 

Some one claimant of the second group in order to obtain 109. An attested account was filed with the owner April 10, 1913, when a payment was due under the principal contract. No other notices were filed until 

April 30th. In the meantime, the owner paid certain sub-contractors and materialmen. It was held that these payments "must be treated as proper payments" and should have been deducted from the owner's liability and that "the balance would be available for the claims of all sub-contractors and materialmen out of which the Enterprise 

Lumber Company," (the first claimant) "must first be paid and the balance pro rated among other claims."

Moesser vs. Enterprise Lum ber Co., 26 C. C. (N.S.) 28.

Sec. 334

Attested Accounts priority in what is left, must file a copy of his account with the recorder, and other claimants desiring to share in what is left must file their claims with the board within the period ending ten days after the first subsequent payment falls due under the contract. In a case in which the first claimant did file with the recorder and none of the other claimants filed until after the expiration of the ten day period, the first claimant was paid in full and the balance due the contractor was ordered distributed pro rata among the other claimants.110

An opposite opinion has been expressed that claimants filing attested accounts after the expiration of the ten day period would not share pro rata but would take in the order of time in which they filed their claims.111 

Sec. 334. What Is Payment Pro Rata? 

Usually each claimant entitled to share in the payments detained by the board is paid that fraction of his claim then due equal to the proportion between the total amount due all such claimants and the amount of the detained fund. Sec. 342. Construction of the Statute.

G. C. 8322 expressly provides that assignments are subject to the claims of persons furnishing labor and materials for improvements. Sec. 344. Triangular Cases. 

If all claimants under attested accounts must file copies of their accounts with the Recorder in order to make their liens good against previous assignments, such filing should also be necessary as against subsequent assignments and the same rule should apply as to attachments and other legal proceedings in which it is sought to subject the amount due the contractor to the claims of creditors.

So called "triangular" lien cases will result in which there will be holders of attested accounts who filed copies of their accounts with the Recorder, assignees, attaching creditors and the like, and other claimants under attested accounts who filed their accounts with the board within the ten day period, but who failed to file copies with the Recorder. The liens of the claimants who filed both with the board and the Recorder will be superior to the claims of the assignees and attaching creditors, whose claims in 

146. G. C. 8328; Kennett vs. 

Rebholz & Carr, 6 Dec. Rep. 824, and see Section 332, Subsection d, ante.

Sec. 522 

 turn will be superior to the attested accounts filed only with the board, which have, under the statute the right to share pro rata with their fellow claimants who filed both with the Board and the Recorder. 

The Ohio law under such circumstances appears to be that if the claims are in all other respects equal, priority of time gives the better equity and that otherwise the claim having the weakest equity must stand the loss. 

Further, that every such case "rests upon its own facts and conditions."147

Courts would, therefore, in cases arising under the law of attested accounts, satisfy first the lien claims filed both with the board and the Recorder, next the claims of assignees, attachment creditors, etc. and last of all, the attested accounts that were filed only with the board, since their equity would be impaired by their failure to comply with the statute. This was the order of distribution adopted in the two cases holding that the rights of previous assignees were superior to those of lien claimants who failed to file copies of their account with the Recorder.148

Sec. 349. When Cause of Action Accrues. 

After complying with the provisions of the statute as to filing of attested accounts, the earliest time at which the claimant can bring an action is five days subsequent to the adjustment of the account between the claimant and the contractor. Nor can the action be commenced at that time unless the ten-day period within which other claimants have the right to file attested accounts has expired. 

While we find no case actually holding that the attested account must be assented to by the contractor or adjusted between him and the lien claimant before the lien claimant can commence an action, such is the effect of G. C. 8331. If there is no duty upon the board to pay before such assent or adjustment, there can be no right in the claimant to commence an action prior thereto.156

Sec. 350. Forms of Action. 

The nature of the action which may be brought is suggested by G. C. 8329 and 8331. After the account has been assented to by the contractor or adjusted between him and the claimant, there is, under G. C. 8329, a duty upon the board to pay the claimant, which may be enforced by a mandamus action. It is clear that the mandamus action cannot be brought before the assent or the adjustment. 

The right of the claimant and the absolute duty of the board to make payment must be clearly shown. It must appear that no other person is entitled to the fund as against the claim of the relator.157

It seems plain that a mandamus action is unsuitable for the settlement of disputes over claims and priorities and that such an action will lie only in a case where all claims have been assented to or adjusted with the contractor and the claimants are agreed among themselves. 

This being true and the board being now only liable for money actually due from it to the principal contractor, it is not likely that a board will ever hold up payment under circumstances justifying a mandamus action. of the claim given him by the owner has assented to the correctness of the claim, or an arbitrament has determined it, is the basis of such right." Sec. 352. Pleadings.

Sec. 536 

 (b) The Board's Answer 

If there are no other claimants to the fund and the amount due the claimant from the contractor has been assented to or adjusted between him and the contractor, the only issue to be raised by the answer is the amount due from the board to the contractor. This would depend upon the terms of the principal contract and upon the performance or the default of the contractor. It has been held that the board has no right to make the contractor a party defendant in the action and to establish as against him also the amount due him under this contract, but that he may be made a new party defendant if he disputes the amount due to the claimant.181 While the point has never been raised, it would seem that if the plaintiff failed to prove that the amount due him had been adjusted before the commencement of the action, his action would be prematurely brought and would be dismissed upon that ground.182 However, if the board waived that point (as it should), the court could proceed to determine the actual amount due to the claimant,183

(c) Pleadings of Other Claimants 

Other claimants under attested accounts must show their right in the fund in the same manner as the plaintiff. Besides pleading facts, establishing their claim to the fund, and their right to share pro rata with other lien claimants, they should allege that they filed copies of their accounts with the Recorder. If they cannot or do not plead this, they may find their claims inferior to those of assignees or attaching creditors of the contractor.185 

Sec. 353. Exemptions. 

There are no exemptions against the lien of an attested account. G. C. 8314 provides at its close "there shall be no homestead or other exemptions against any lien under the provisions of this chapter." The chapter referred to is the General Code: Part second, Civil: Title VII, Commercial Regulations: Division IV, Liens: Chap ter I, Liens, which includes G. C. 8309 to 8380. The right of the claimant who may file an attested account even before he has furnished any labor or material, or who may file his notice subsequent to furnishing labor or material and make his claim relate back to the date upon which the first labor or material was furnished by him, to the exclusion of assignees, attaching creditors and the like, is a lien. It is a lien as against the contractor who sees money due him paid directly to the claimant by the board, and after the notice has been filed, at least, it 

184. Section 351 ante. 

185. Section 350 ante.

Sec. 353a 

538 

 has the nature of a lien as against the board which can no longer pay its creditor, the contractor. 

G. C. 11721 to 11740, relating to exemption from execution, do not in any event seem from their terms applicable to cases in which the liens of attested accounts are enforced. Those sections allow certain persons to hold property "exempt from execution, attachment or sale to satisfy a judgment or order." The procedure under which the lien of an attested account is enforced seems entirely distinct "from execution, attachment or sale." 

A public authority is, of course, not entitled to exemptions. It is conceivable, however, that a contractor might claim some exemptions against the lien of an attested account. We believe such a claim would be denied. 

Sec. 353a. Limitation of Actions: Interest. 

No time is fixed in the statute within which suit must be commenced against the board. G. C. 8321, providing a limitation of six years for actions upon mechanic liens against the real estate of private persons, relates only to the liens authorized by the Act of April 16, 1913. G. C. 

11222 seems applicable. It provides "an action upon a contract not in writing, express or implied, or upon a liability created by statute other than a forfeiture or penalty shall be brought within six years after the cause thereof accrued." Considered either as an open account or as a liability created by statute, the claim is barred in six years. No reported case on this point has arisen nor is any case likely to arise since a board will usually hold up payment after the filing of an attested account and the various parties concerned will not allow this to continue for six years. It is, therefore, unimportant whether the six-year period begins to run from the time the first

Sec. 354 

Attested Accounts labor or material was furnished, or from the date the attested account is filed with the board, or from five days after the date upon which the amount of the account is assented to or adjusted, or from the earliest date at which the action could have been filed against the board. Presumably the cause of action does not arise and the sixyear period does not commence to run until the time at which the claimant is authorized by G. C. 8331 to file suit against the board.

Interest will accrue against the contractor from the date of the adjustment of the account between himself and the claimant. The board is liable for this interest up to any amount in its hands due to the contractor. If the claims exceed the amount in its hands, it is liable for interest from the date upon which the action against it is rightfully filed, unless it pays the money into court under an order of interpleader. It would seem the board should also be liable for interest from the date upon which it becomes its duty under G. C. 8329 to pay the claimant, provided it has notice of the adjustment of the account between the claimant and the contractor. 

Sec. 354. Appeal and Error Proceedings. 

This subject is discussed elsewhere in this book.186 

Only chancery cases are appealable. A mandamus action. is not a chancery case and is not appealable. An original interpleader action brought by the board is a chancery case and is appealable.

It was held prior to the constitutional amendment creating our present Court of Appeals and giving it jurisdiction to hear chancery cases de novo that an action of the claimant against the board and the contractor was not 

186. Section 372 et seq. post.

Sec. 

540 

 appealable. The Court emphasized the fact that the action authorized by the statute was one for money had and received in which a judgment for money only would be rendered and in which the parties had the right of trial by jury, 187

There remains for consideration cases in which a lien claimant sues the board and other lien claimants become parties to the same action through an affidavit of interpleader or otherwise and the various claimants are compelled to adjust their accounts among themselves. It has usually been considered that the Court would exercise equitable powers in adjusting the claims and that there would be no right to trial by jury and that the action would be appealable.188 The right to appeal such proceedings has not, however, been definitely established and it would appear safer to perfect proceedings both in appeal and in error. 

187. "To enforce the right thus secured by the plaintiffs against the board of trustees the statute itself prescribes the remedy; and where a statute gives a new right, and also prescribes the remedy for its violation, the remedy so prescribed must be taken as exclusive, unless it appears from the statute that the legislature intended otherwise. The remedy prescribed by the statute is as follows: 'And which amount (retained) due may be recovered from the said owner by the creditor of said contractor in an action of money had and received to the use of said creditor.' In such action of common law the parties would have been entitled to demand a jury trial. The same under our constitution. Hence as an action between the plaintiffs and the board of trustees, neither party was entitled to an appeal from the final judgment therein."

Sec. 355. Suggestions to Claimants. 

The lien claimant who files an attested account, hopes to obtain payment without suit. He may be sure that suit will be necessary if by some mischance the board pays the contractor after the sworn statement is filed, for the board will not without suit pay the same account twice. 

Therefore, aside from any provisions of law, it is important that the sworn statement identify the contractor and the work being performed by him for the board so unmistakably, that the board will know immediately what funds are to be detained. It is equally important that the notice, upon being filed with the board, gets at once into the hands of the person in charge of making payments to the contractor, so that this person will not pay out the fund after the board has received the notice. 

The lien claimant should, in preparing and filing his sworn statement, assume that there will be a lawsuit in 

189. Brenneman vs. Brown, 30 

Oh. App. 84. In this action the plaintiff's appeal was dismissed because his petition did not state a cause of action.  which his claim will be contested. Although the court will be liberal in determining the sufficiency of the sworn and itemized statement required by the statute, that statement should be carefully drawn. The affidavit should be made by someone knowing the facts, and that person should swear that the contents of the itemized statement are true, not that they are "true as he verily believes." 

While the law probably permits this affidavit to be sworn to before the claimant's attorney, some other Notary Public might better be used in view of the conflicting decisions of the courts of appeal.

Since filing by registered mail, correctly addressed, is probably only prima facie evidence that the notice was received, it appears that the better plan is to deliver the sworn statement to the public officer, or to some member of the board or to the clerk of the board. When the original is delivered, the person to whom it is delivered should be asked to sign a receipt written upon a carbon copy of the original and the time and place of the receipt should be noted upon this carbon copy. Under no circumstances trust to ordinary mail for delivery of notice. 

Ordinarily there will be no trouble in obtaining such a receipt and this will avoid the necessity of relying upon the testimony of a messenger who may not even remember or be able to identify the person to whom the statement was delivered, or upon the admission of the person who received the statement and who perhaps mislaid it and may not desire to remember the incident.

A copy of the sworn statement should be immediately filed with the recorder. Very likely the Supreme Court may decide that only the first claimant need file a copy of the sworn statement with the recorder and that his fellow claimants need not file with the recorder in order to

Attested Accounts have priority over assignments, but a claimant should not expose himself to extended litigation. 

If the claim gets into the courts, one may be sure that any time saved by skimping in the preparation or filing of the account will result in expending a much greater amount of time in preparing for trial, even if it does not result in the total loss of the claim.

Sec. 358

Release of Lien 

Destruction of Building. 

A mechanics lien attaches to the building, and to the real estate upon which the material or labor is bestowed, at the time it is furnished, and is not devested or lost by the subsequent destruction of the building. The lien may still be enforced against the land alone.¹ The lien will be valid even though the improvement be destroyed by fire before the claimant has had the opportunity to perfect his lien.2 The lien may also be enforced against the land notwithstanding the fact that the building, into which the labor or materials of the claimant have gone, has been sold under execution to satisfy a former lien.3 

Sec. 358. Transfer of Title. 

The lien given by the statute to a mechanic or materialman for work done or material furnished in the erection or repair of an improvement will attach from the date the first labor was performed or materials furnished under the original contract.4 Whoever purchases or otherwise acquires the property after such date acquires it subject to the right of any mechanic or materialman to perfect his lien, and is bound by it. The sale of the premises will therefore not divest such lien claimants of their inchoate liens upon the property.5 A purchaser of

Sec. 359. Bankruptcy of Owner or Contractor. 

As a general rule, it seems to be well settled that a valid mechanics lien, once acquired, is not defeated by the subsequent bankruptcy of the owner. The trustee in bankruptcy takes his titles subject to any valid liens that may have been acquired by contractors, materialmen, subcontractors or laborers.10

Sec. 361. 

Failure to Furnish Statements on Re quest of Owner, Mortgagee or Contractor. "Each person claiming a lien as aforesaid, shall from time to time, whenever required by such owner, part owner, lessee, mortgagee, or contractor or his agent, and within ten days from demand thereof furnish such person demanding the same a written statement of the amount of work and materials furnished to date of statement and then unpaid, as nearly as can then be ascertained under penalty of a forfeiture of his lien ***"12 The written statements referred to in this section quoted above apparently need not be prepared with the same particularity or formality as those required under the provisions of G. C. 8312. The latter are required in connection with the claimant's request for payment upon his contract, while the former are sought primarily for the purpose of obtaining information to enable the inquirer to estimate, "as nearly as can be ascertained," the status and approximate amounts of outstanding and unpaid accounts for labor and material furnished up to the date of the furnishing of such written statements. 

Failure to furnish such statements upon request will result in the loss of the lien. Thus where an owner requested all subcontractors to furnish it with written statements of their respective accounts with the principal con-

 tractor, and one of such subcontractors failed so to do with the result that the owner paid the principal contractor all that was due him without holding back any sums to protect the possible claim of such subcontractor who failed to respond to the owner's request, the subcontractor was held to be estopped from asserting a mechanics lien upon the property of said owner. 13 

Sec. 362. Failure of Lien Claimant to Sue. 

(a) Notice from Owner. "The owner of any real estate or any interest therein upon which a lien has been taken may notify the person then owning said lien or his agent or attorney to commence suit thereon."14

The purpose of this remedy is plain. The acquiring of a mechanics lien upon the property of an owner, by a laborer or materialman, is clearly an ex parte proceeding. The owner is not consulted, seldom has knowledge of the claimant's intention to file the affidavit for the lien, and cannot prevent it, even if the claim is an unconscionable one. Thus, without the opportunity of protecting himself, his land is encumbered, his credit impaired, the chances for the sale of his property somewhat curtailed, and the value thereof sometimes depreciated. 

By the means of this notice to the claimant to commence suit upon his lien, the owner is afforded the pri vilege of compelling such claimant to present his claim to the courts where the same may be properly established if it is a valid one, or justly and permanently extinguished if it is an invalid one. 

13. Hachmeister-Lind Chem ical Co. vs. Gund Realty Co., 27

O. L. R. 378 (Court of Appeals for Cuyahoga County). 

14. G. C. 8319.

Sec. 362

Release of Lien (b) Service of Notice by Sheriff.

The sheriff shall thereupon serve said notice upon the person then owning said lien, or his agent or attorney mentioned in said notice, in the same manner provided by law for the service of summons in civil actions, and shall thereupon certify upon such notice his return of such service in the same manner provided by law for returns of service of summons, and deliver the notice. with said return endorsed thereon to the owner of said property upon the payment of the same fees and mileage provided by law for the service of summons.  persons, upon the public records of the county in which his property is situated, the fact that there has been served upon the lien claimant the statutory notice to commence suit on his alleged lien. Without this public record of the fact that such notice had actually been served upon the lien claimant by a public officer duly authorized to make such service, the owner had no adequate means of proving to any person who might be desirous of acquiring some estate or interest in his land that the lien of the claimant had been lost by his failure to bring suit thereon within the period of sixty days from the receipt of notice from the owner so to do. By virtue of this new method of service of the notice from the owner, any person may now consult the records of the county recorder and of the clerk of courts and determine for himself whether the lien claimant has forfeited his lien by his failure to commence his suit within the time required by law. 

Of course, this method of service by the sheriff is not exclusive. The owner may still make the service himself, or by mail, or otherwise. But the difficulty of such latter methods is that there exists no public record of the facts of such service. They exist only in the knowledge of the owner himself upon whose veracity or accuracy of statement a third person may not wish to rely. The owner is therefore helpless, unless he himself file a suit to quiet title to his property, making the lien claimant a party thereto, and proving to the satisfaction of the court, by such oral testimony or other evidence as he may be able to produce, that the notice to commence suit was served by him upon the claimant and that the latter has failed to commence such suit within sixty days thereafter. This is often a long and expensive procedure and results generally in the payment of some money to the lien claimant in order

"No lien provided for in this act shall be defeated or waived by the taking by the claimant, from any person of any promissory note or notes or of any security for such debt other than upon the real estate itself, in the absence of a written agreement that the taking of such note or notes or such security shall be a waiver of the lien."21

Sec. 365. Release of Lien. 

(a) In General.

A person who has procured a mechanics lien upon the property of another may, if he chooses, release his lien. There must of course exist in the mind of the claimant an intention so to do, and like any other agreement such release must not be tainted by the fraud, duress or overreaching of him who benefits thereby. "The lien is a privilege for the exclusive benefit of the mechanic or materialman, and as such is at every stage of its existence under his complete control, and may at any time be discharged by such acts on his part as evidence such intention. An order to the proper officer to enter a discharge of the lien will have such an effect. This intention should be clear, and the act of discharge complete."23

The fact that such release may be voluntary and unsupported by any new or valuable consideration is immaterial. Being merely the relinquishment of a right personal to the lien claimant, it requires no consideration to support it.24

A dismissal of proceedings to enforce a lien is not to be confused with its discharge or abandonment, in the absence of any intention to actually release such lien. If

But a lien which has been intentionally released may not, in the absence of express agreement to that effect with the owner, be afterwards revived.25

The effect of the release is to destroy all recourse of the lienor against the particular property of the owner upon which the lien has attached. It does not necessarily discharge the debt, nor the right of action for its recovery. 

But payment of the debt would, of course, discharge the lien.26

The lien claimant, in releasing his lien, may do so for the benefit of the owner, or for the benefit of subsequent lienors, or both. It is purely a matter of intention. Thus, where a lien claimant gave to a building and loan association a formal release of a lien, which he had already acquired upon the property of the of the owner, and of any which he might later acquire upon such property, without limiting the benefits of such release to the loan association, which intended to furnish funds to such owner in order to enable him to complete the building, the court held that such unqualified release of the lien inured to the benefit of the owner as well as to the loan association although addressed to the latter only.27 Where, however, 25. Sec. 366. Tender of Payment.

As a general rule a tender of money in payment of a debt does not operate to discharge the debt, nor will it later bar an action to collect such debt. It may discharge the debtor from liability for interest accruing upon such debt after the tender or for costs afterwards incurred.31 

But such tender, while it does not prevent the creditor from later collecting his debt, may deprive him of any rights in the property of the debtor which he holds as security for the payment of such debt.32 So a refusal to accept a tender of payment made by the principal debtor to the creditor will release the surety on such obligation.33

And upon the same principle, a tender of payment to a mechanics lien claimant by an owner upon whose property such claimant has filed his lien, will extinguish such lien if the tender be not accepted.34 The obvious purpose of such rule is to deprive the lien claimant of his lien after he has been given the opportunity of accepting payment of the debt to which his lien is but an incident. If he does not care to accept his money that may be his own folly, but he should no longer be permitted to encumber the property of his debtor who has offered to do all that he is obliged to do to relieve his property of the lien. 

The penalty for the lien claimant's obstinacy is, as it should be, the forfeiture of his lien. 

The tender, however, must be an unconditional one, free from any conditions which the creditor may rightfully reject.35 Thus, where a creditor believes in good faith that he is entitled to a larger sum than that which is offered by the debtor, he should not be required, at the price of losing his mechanics lien if the amount tendered be later found to be correct, to accept the lesser sum tendered.36 In such case he should be permitted to accept such payment on account and litigate his rights as to the balance37 34.

Release of Lien Sec. 367. Payments by Owner to Contractor as 

Affecting Rights of Subcontractors, Materialmen and Laborers. 

It is elementary that a payment of the debt for which a lien is claimed will discharge such lien. And where the question is one which concerns only two persons, the person paying and the person paid, as, for instance, the owner and a laborer, or the owner and a materialman, the solution is simple. But where the rights of third persons are involved, as they most certainly are under the Mechanics Lien Law, the problem is often a perplexing one. In the case of payment by an owner to a contractor, or in the case of payment by such contractor to his subcontractors and materialmen, the application thereof affects not alone the immediate parties to such transaction. 

As has been before stated,38 payments made to the principal contractor, in accordance with the provisions of G. C. 8312, will protect the owner as to such payments and as to all materials and labor furnished or performed prior thereto, except where the owner has received actual notice, in accordance with the provisions of G. C. 8313, of the furnishing of material or the performance of labor prior to the payments made under the sworn statement be induced to purchase their peace at an unjust sacrifice of their rights. "Kortright vs. Cady, 21 N. Y. 243. Subsequent decisions have mollified the harshness of the majority's opinion, however. Sec. 368. Application of Payments Where G. C. 

8312 and 8313 Do Not Apply. 

(a) Where Debtor Designates the Application. 

Where one person is indebted to another on various accounts, he has an undoubted right to choose which debt he will pay first; and where he tenders a sum sufficient to fully discharge any particular debt, he has a right, at the time, to direct its appropriation accordingly. But this right must be exercised at the time of payment. A debtor cannot, without the consent of the creditor, thus dictate the application of partial payments, nor can he require the creditor to accept choses in action, from the collection of which money may be obtained, and to apply the proceeds in payment of a debt. It is at the option of the creditor to accept such partial payment, or to receive anything else than money in discharge of his debt. But if a partial payment be accepted by the creditor, or if, without objection, he receive promissory notes or other choses

Sec. 395. Appeal and Error Nature and Form of Remedy. 

It is necessary to determine the nature and form of the action to enforce a mechanics lien for two reasons: first, to determine the right of trial by jury; second, to determine the method of appellate review. In order to properly understand some of the peculiarities of the practice in Ohio, some examination of the earlier statutes is advisable. The Act of 1823,1 this being the first me- 

1. 21 Ohio Laws 8. This was merely a local Act, affecting persons within the corporate limits of Cincinnati only.

Sec. 570 

 chanics lien law passed by the Legislature of Ohio, provided "that every person or persons holding such lien, may proceed to obtain a judgment for the amount of his or their account thereon, according to the course of legal proceedings in like cases, ***"2 The sole purpose of this provision was to provide a method of procedure by which a mechanics lien might be enforced by an action at law, and also that such lien should continue until the suit was finally "determined and satisfied.”

To provide a more satisfactory procedure, an act was passed in 1851,³ the essential part of which is as follows: "That any person or persons, who now hold or shall hereafter hold a lien, under the above recited act, may, in addition to the remedy therein provided for, proceed by petition in chancery, as in other cases of liens, against the owner *** of (an improvement) and the lot or lots of land on which the same shall stand, and obtain such final decree therein for the rent or sale thereof, as justice and equity may require ***"4 Thus was the right to foreclose the lien by a "petition in chancery" granted. It will be noted that the earlier remedy, an action at law, still remained. The action in equity was an additional remedy.

Prior to the passage of this amendatory act of 1851, the holder of a mechanics lien could not have proceeded in equity to enforce it until he had first ascertained and liquidated the amount of his account by a judgment at law. By virtue of this amendment the lienholder could

Sec. 372 Proceedings to Enforce the Lien now proceed in equity in the first instance; but he was not obliged to, since he still had the right to sue at law upon his account and obtain a personal judgment if he so chose.5

The action contemplated by this act of 1851, was one purely in chancery. It was plainly an action for the foreclosure of a lien. In 1853 the code of civil procedure attempted to abolish the distinction between law and equity, but also provided that wherever the Legislature had prescribed a remedy the code should not affect it.6 The remedy prescribed in the act of 1851 thus clearly came within this exception and hence the chancery practice continued to exist in the enforcement of mechanics liens. In 

1881, the act of 1851 was amended by omitting the words "in chancery" therefrom. This, however did not alter the purpose or effect of the earlier act and the practice continued as before. 

In the meantime an amendment to the code of civil procedure (1864) provided that an action to recover a personal judgment upon an account or debt and to foreclose a lien securing the payment of the same might be joined; the act further providing, "such proceedings shall be had and judgment rendered thereon, as in other civil actions for the recovery of money only."8 Prior to this amendment there had been some practice, without statutory authority, using such joinder.9

 ods of procedure to enforce a mechanics lien; first, action at law to reduce the amount to a personal judgment against the debtor; second, action in equity to foreclose the lien; third, joinder of these two actions. If the first method was pursued and the judgment could not be satisfied by execution then a levy upon the judgment debtor's land was resorted to. If an action in chancery was brought to foreclose the lien the remedy sought affected the land only as no personal judgment could be obtained in such action against the debtor.10 In the third method, wherein there are two causes of action, one for personal judgment and the other for foreclosure, the advantages of both of the former methods are retained. This form of action is essentially an action at law for money only and the equitable remedy of foreclosure is only ancillary to it.11

At the time of codification, when all actions on joinder were drawn together, the expression "as in other civil actions for the recovery of money only" was omitted,12 but this omission has not changed the effect of the statute.13

Proceedings to Enforce the Lien Sec. 373. The Statute. 

G. C. 8323—“Any person holding a mechanics lien, in addition to the remedies herein provided for, may proceed by petition, as in other cases of liens, against the owner and all other persons interested, either as lien holders or otherwise, in any such boat, vessel or other water craft, or house, mill, manufactury, or other building, or appurtenance, mentioned in (G. C. 8310) hereof, or in any street, turnpike, road, sidewalk, way, drain, ditch or sewer, as mentioned in (G. C. 8311) hereof, and the lot or land on which it stands or to which it may be removed, and obtain such judgment therein for the rent or sale thereof as justice and equity require. When judgment shall be rendered in such proceeding, in favor of the parties succeeding therein, the court may at its discretion allow a reasonable attorney's fee, to be paid out of the fund realized for lien claimants." 

In this statute no new method of enforcement is created but the provision of the act of 1851, "may proceed by petition as in other cases of liens," is continued in force and effect.

Brought. 

Where the foreclosure of a mechanics lien is sought, suit must be brought in the county where the land is situated.14 If the property covered by the lien is situated

If a personal judgment is sought in addition to the remedy of foreclosure, it has been held, in a case of mortgage foreclosure, "such (personal) judgment may be rendered against a defendant served with process in a county other than that in which the lands lie and the action is brought."16

But where an action to foreclose a mechanics lien and for personal judgment is brought in the county where the land is situated and the defendant owner is served in another county and the court finds the lien invalid, then the court has no jurisdiction to render a personal judgment.17

If a personal judgment only is sought for the amount of the lien, then action may be brought wherever service of summons may be lawfully had upon the defendant.

Where, under the attested account statute, the head contractor has assigned to a subcontractor all his rights against the owner, he is not a necessary party to an action against the owner by the subcontractor.37

In theory, at least, mortgagees claiming under mortgages precedent to the lien being foreclosed are not necessary parties. In practice, however, particularly under the rules cited supra,38 they should be joined as parties to the action since they claim an interest in the property. 

Grantees subsequent to the lien being foreclosed are likewise necessary parties to the action altho, unless they have expressly agreed to pay the lien, no personal judgment can be secured against them. 

Where the principal contractor has given bond to the owner conditioned upon the completion of the contract, and the lien claimant is entitled to the benefit thereof, the surety on such bond may be joined as a party defendant in a suit against the owner and the contractor.39 

Under the provisions of G. C. 8323-5, executors and administrators of deceased owners have the same rights and are subject to the same liabilities that such owners would have enjoyed or been subject to, if alive. When a party to the action dies the action may be revived in accordance with provisions of G. C. 11397 et seq.

And under the provisions of G. C. 8323-7 parties entitled to liens whose claims are not yet due may become parties to any suit to enforce a lien, or institute suit themselves, altho a judgment in such case shall not be enforcible until the claim matures.

Sec. 378. Misjoinder of Parties. 

In cases involving the enforcement of a mechanics lien the question of misjoinder of parties plaintiff rarely arises. By misjoinder is meant an excess of parties. If a misjoinder of parties defendant is evident from the face of the petition the question may be raised by demurrer.41 

Prior to the inclusion of misjoinder in the statute as a ground for demurrer, it was held that one party could not demur to a petition on the ground that another party has been improperly joined with him.42 In other states, with identical code provisions as to grounds for demurrer, it has been held that where a petition states a cause of action against one defendant it is no concern of his that another is improperly joined with him.43 Under the broad equitable principle of joinder applicable to mechanics lien cases it is difficult to conceive of a case where misjoinder of defendants would be ground for demurrer since a general allegation of interest is made as to all defendants.44

Sec. 380 Proceedings to Enforce the Lien Sec. 379. Defect in Parties Defendant. 

In theory, if a party having an interest in the subject matter is not made a defendant a demurrer will lie, but here again it is difficult to conceive of a case within this field where this defect is apparent from the face of the petition. If the defect is raised by answer, then in practice the plaintiff will correct the defect by amendment. 

Sec. 380. Pleadings-The Petition. 

The petition to enforce a mechanics lien must allege facts showing that the statutory prerequisites to obtaining a lien have been complied with. But for the statute no lien would exist and it is essential not only that the conditions precedent required by the statutes should be complied with, but that the fact of such compliance be averred in the petition. It should be noticed that by "conditions precedent required by the statutes" we mean, not only the filing of the lien but also compliance with the statutes in regard to notice, itemized statements, preliminary affidavits and other statutory steps necessary to the perfection of the lien and the right to sue thereon.45 If an essential allegation is omitted the petition is demurrable. 

So also, if it fails to state facts showing that the suit is filed within the statute of limitations pertaining to such lien.46 If the defect is not remedied by proof it may be

Proceedings to Enforce the Lien Sec. 382 Sec. 382. Amendment of Pleadings. 

Mistakes and omissions in parties or in material allegations are permitted to be corrected by amendment.67 

Thus where a materialman sued a contractor on account alone, he was later permitted to amend his petition by setting up a mechanics lien theretofor perfected upon the premises for which the material was furnished and asking the foreclosure of such lien.68 

If the lien is perfected after suit upon the account is instituted it would seem that a supplemental pleading should be filed under authority of G. C. 11368. 

But a court has no jurisdiction to amend by its decree the plaintiff's original affidavit for a lien by antedating the first item of the account "thus erroneously transcribed" so as to make it conform to the actual date of furnishing the material.69 Inferentially a lien claimant may be permitted to correct his description of property covered by the lien unless the rights of intervening claimants are involved.70

There is only one claim or obligation and that consists of the account for building material furnished. The amendment only asserts the perfection of a mechanics lien covering the account, and, in addition to a personal judgment, asks for the foreclosure of such lien. Statutes providing for mechanics liens do not create any new substantive right, but are remedial in character, providing an additional means of enforcing payment of the debt."

Sec. 588 

 Sec. 383. Defenses. 

(a) In General. 

The defense of an action to enforce a mechanics lien has no distinguishing characteristics. The general rules as to the contents of an answer are applicable.71 A general denial will put in issue any or all of the essential allegations of the petition. In the ordinary and usual case the defense conducted by the owner is generally directed to the amount due and the issue is raised on the cause of action seeking a money judgment. Matters affecting the validity or priority of the lien are generally brought in by other defendants, the priority of whose liens may be affected by the decree. This is not so much a matter of pleading as it is in requiring strict proof by the plaintiff at the trial. Questions of this sort are so frequently solved by negotiation between the various lien claimants that there is a dearth of judicial decisions upon the subject. In an action for personal judgment against an owner filed in this state it is no defense that an action is pending in another state for foreclosure of a mechanics lien and for a deficiency judgment against such owner even though both cases are based upon the same cause of action.72 (b) Matters to be Specially Pleaded. 

As in other cases, matters of affirmative defense should be specially pleaded. Thus, if a defendant relies upon facts constituting a waiver of a lien or an estoppel against asserting a lien, these should be specially set up 

71. G. C. 11314. For form of answer see-Dawson & Andrews -Supp. 

72. Fox vs. King Investment 

Co., 22 Oh. App. 469.

Proceedings to Enforce the Lien Sec. 385 

in the answer.73 An allegation of performance may be coupled with an allegation of waiver and the party asserting the same cannot be required to elect upon which of the two grounds he will stand.74 If an owner has given notice to the lien claimant to commence suit upon his lien within sixty days, as provided by G. C. 8319, failure of the lien claimant so to do should be specially averred in an answer to a suit subsequently brought.75 

Sec. 384. Counterclaim and Set-off. 

Under the Ohio code of procedure the defendant may file a counterclaim against the lien claimant.76 In the case of the foreclosure of a mortgage it has been held that the defendant mortgagor may set up a counterclaim for damages by reason of the fraud of the plaintiff mortgagee.77

Since the pleading of a set-off is limited to an action founded upon contract, it is doubtful whether a set-off may be pleaded in an action for the foreclosure of a lien, where no personal judgment is sought. Both counterclaim and set-off are limited to those defendants who are personally liable on the claim sued upon. There must be a possibility of a several judgment between the plaintiff and the defendant asserting a counterclaim or set-off.78 

Sec. 385. Cross Petition. 

In practice, a cross-petition is used by those defendants who claim some interest in or a lien upon the prem-

C. 8323-7, parties entitled to mechanics liens, whose claims are not yet due and payable, may nevertheless become parties to such action and their rights will be fixed by the decree. Wherever practicable, a defendant, whether his claim be due or not, should in his answer pray for some affirmative relief so that he may not lose his right to proceed in the event of dismissal by the plaintiff.79

The cross-petition of a defendant lien claimant is generally combined with an answer denying the plaintiff's allegation for want of information80 and usually denying the validity or priority of the asserted liens of other claimants.

The cross-petition should contain the allegations essential to an original petition, so that, in the event of a dismissal by the plaintiff, the cross-petitioner may proceed with his case as though he were the only plaintiff therein. In other words, good practice would recommend that each cross-petitioner should so draft his own petition that the court will have such complete jurisdiction of the case as to permit it to award judgment and grant the relief prayed for therein without reference to the pleadings or proceedings of other claimants.

Sec. 387.

Evidence. 

The burden of proof is upon the plaintiff in a suit to enforce his lien. Accordingly, he must prove all the essential allegations of his petition. In general, the rules as to the burden of proof and admissability of evidence are not essentially different from those of other cases. And it is vital to the establishment of a lien that the proof disclose that the material or labor was furnished under contract with the owner directly, or through a contractor who traced his contract to the owner.86

In the ordinary case of an action upon an account and the foreclosure of a mechanics lien securing the same, there are two issues: first, the establishment of the account and the amount due thereon; second, the validity of the lien. Both of these issues involve questions of fact.

Sec. 389. Receivers.

While the statute95 does not specifically provide that a receiver may be appointed in a case involving the foreclosure of a mechanics lien, yet the court undoubtedly has the right to do so where the usages of equity would seem to permit.96 Wherever the property subject to a lien is being wasted and the security of the lien claimants is impaired, a court, in the exercise of its general equity powers, is justified in appointing a receiver. 

And where an unfinished structure, the subject-matter of a lien or liens, is liable to deterioration as a result of its exposure to the elements, or its earning power lost by reason of its unfitness for use, it has been held that it is for the best interests of all parties concerned to empower the receiver to complete the building involved, and in such cases the receiver's certificates for funds required for such purpose are claims superior to the liens of mechanics and materialmen.97

Sec. 392.

Priorities. 

While it is true that there is, as between themselves, no priority among mechanics lien claimants,100 there may be, and usually are, conflicting claims as to priority between mechanics lien claimants, mortgagees, unpaid vendors, manual laborers, judgment creditors, a dower claimant, tax officials and others having an interest in the premises involved. The decree should therefore specifically establish the liens found to be valid, the amounts due thereon, and the exact order in which they are to be paid out of the proceeds derived from the sale. 

Taxes and court costs are, of course, superior to all other claims and should be paid first before any distribution is made to other claimants. 101 The decree should so provide.

Insofar as mechanics liens are concerned, the statute expressly provides that claims for homestead or other exemptions shall not be superior to such liens. 102

Sec. 395. Appeal and Error. 

The Constitution of Ohio permits two distinct methods of review by the courts of appeal of the proceedings and judgment of the lower courts: first, by appeal:107 second, by proceedings in error.108 The jurisdiction of the courts of appeals on appeal is limited by Section 6, Article IV 

of the constitution to chancery cases and the legislature can neither enlarge or diminish it.109 

The same section of the constitution gives the courts of appeals general power to review the judgments of the inferior courts "as may be provided by law." The legis lature has provided that this power of review shall be exercised by proceedings in error.110 Neither the constitution nor the statutes limit the jurisdiction of the courts of appeals in error proceedings to any type of case. It follows, therefore, that if a proceeding in the trial court

In chancery cases, where a party has a choice of methods of review, the circumstances of the particular case will govern his choice. If errors of law, such as rulings on demurrers or admissibility of evidence are apparent in the record of the trial court, then the matter can probably be presented to the appellate court more clearly by proceedings in error. If, however, the aggrieved party feels that the decision of the trial court is against the weight of the evidence, then the case should be appealed. 

The question of the weight of the evidence may be raised by proceedings in error but reversal thereon requires the concurrence of all the judges of the court of appeals. 

Even then a reviewing court is reluctant to disturb a judgment of the trial court on the facts unless as a matter of law it is manifestly against the weight of the evidence.126

Sec. 399

Liens upon Mines for Labor The lien provided by this statute is for labor only; and, furthermore, only such labor as is performed for the purpose of mining coal, removing coal from the mines, or other labor connected with such mining operations. It does not, by express language at least, authorize the taking of a lien for labor performed in the construction or repair of a mine, or of any of the buildings or other structures which make up the general plant; and clearly it makes no provision for the taking of a lien for furnishing material for constructing or repairing a mine or to facilitate the operation thereof. 

Sec. 398. "Labor" Defined. 

The terms "labor" and "manual labor" as used in this section undoubtedly limit the benefits of this section. only to those who toil with their hands-the common miners in the pit. It is doubtful therefore that such lien could be availed of by other employees, such as superintendents, engineers or clerks.

 Sec. 400. How to Perfect the Lien. 

While there are no decisions upon the subject, it would seem that the provisions of G. C. 8314 would govern as to the procedure to be followed in order to acquire the lien provided for by G. C. 8309. It must be borne in mind, however, that G. C. 8314 makes no special mention of the manner in which personal property may be described. While it is true that this section states that the affidavit for lien must contain "a description of the property to be charged with the lien," it is nevertheless plain that the Legislature had reference only to real estate, since, at the time the original law represented by G. C. 8314 was passed, a mechanics lien attached only to real estate or watercraft. In preparing the affidavit for the lien granted by G. C. 8309, therefore, it would seem wise to describe such personal property as may be sought to be subjected to the lien with sufficient certainty as to notify all persons interested therein of the claim of the lien claimant thereto.

G. C. 8339. Laborers shall have lien upon real property of employer.-Laborers and employees of any persons, association of persons or corporations, whether such employment be at agriculture, mining, manufacture or other manual labor, shall have a lien upon the real property of their employers for their wages, which is hereby declared to be superior to the following liens taken or attaching during the existence of such unpaid labor claim; liens of attachment, liens of mortgage given or taken at a time of actual insolvency of the debtor, or with a view of preferring creditors or to secure a pre-existing debt, and superior to all claims for homestead or other exemptions, except articles of personal property to the heads of families and widows. In all cases when property of an employer is placed in the hands of an assignee, receiver or trustee, claims due for labor performed within the period of three months prior to the time such assignee, receiver or trustee is appointed, shall first be paid out of the trust fund, in preference to all other claims against such employer except claims for taxes and the costs of administering the trust." 

G. C. 8340. When lien deemed waived. The lien above provided shall be deemed to be waived by the laborer or employee, as to any portion of such labor,

Sec. 401  unless within thirty days from the expiration of three months from the performance thereof, he files with the recorder of the county where the labor was performed, an itemized statement verified by affidavit, of the amount, kind and value of the labor performed within such period, with all credits and offsets, and the amount then due him therefor. Such statement, when so filed, must be recorded in a book kept for the purpose, and shall become and operate as a lien upon the real property of the employer without any specific description thereof, for the period of one year from the filing thereof."

G. C. 8341. What liens shall have priority.—If an action is brought to enforce the lien within such time, it shall continue in force until finally adjudicated. The proceedings to enforce it shall be the same as in other cases of lien, against the owner of the property and all other persons interested. But if several persons have to obtain liens under the provisions of the next two preceding sections, against the property of the same employer, they shall have no priority among themselves, but all must be paid pro rata. Nor shall they have priority over those obtaining liens under other sections of this chapter, providing therefor, but the persons obtaining liens thereunder shall have priority as provided therein.”

G. C. 8342. To whom foregoing section applies.- 

The provisions of the next three preceding sections shall apply to and include any laborer who indirectly performs labor for a general employer, or the results of whose labor is immediately enjoyed by a general employer, when such general employer assumes payment of his wages by passing a credit therefor upon his books of account or otherwise. When the provisions of this section apply, all proceedings hereunder shall be the same as provided in such preceding sections."

Sec. 

612 

 Sec. 402. Purpose of the Statute. 

On April 18, 1883, the Legislature passed an act "supplementary to section 3206 of the revised statutes of Ohio,¹ providing a lien for laborers, miners, mechanics and others, for their labor."2 The obvious purpose of this act was to provide a means by which manual laborers, as distinguished from other types of employees, could obtain a lien for their wages upon the real property of their employer which would be superior to certain other types of liens that might be asserted against such real estate; and, in the event the property of an employer was placed in the hands of an assignee, receiver or trustee, to create a lien, in effect at least,3 upon the funds derived from the sale thereof in preference to all other claims against such employer, except claims for taxes and the costs of the administration of such estate. 

In other words, the statute affords two remedies to the laborer each distinct and complete in itself; one to give a lien on real property, which will be waived unless an itemized statement be filed, and the other to provide that the claims due for labor shall be first paid out of funds of the employer in the hands of an assignee, receiver, or trustee. 4

 Sec. 403. Constitutionality of the Law. 

While there appears to have been only one case adjudicated wherein the constitutionality of the statute was questioned,5 the statute has been before the courts so many times and enforced by them so often that there seems to be no doubt but that the law is a valid one. 

Sec. 404. The Statute Not Repealed by the Mechanics Lien Law. 

The Mechanics Lien Law of 1913 did not repeal, either specifically or by implication, the provisions of G. C. 8339 et seq. Each law is distinct and independent of the other.6
