Sec. 406. To What Real Estate the Lien Attaches. 

The lien provided for by G. C. 8339 is a general lien, attaching to all of the real property of the employer,7 wheresoever situated in the county wherein the affidavit for the lien is recorded.8 In this respect it differs from the mechanics lien granted by G. C. 8310, since a mechanics lien attaches only to that particular parcel of real estate upon the improvement of which the laborer performed his labor, or for which the materialman delivered his material.9

Sec. 412. The Preference a Vested Right. 

In the fund realized from the administration of the trust, labor claimants who have performed service within three months before the property was taken to the uses of the trust have an interest. The statute charges the fund in their favor with the amount of their claims. 

This is a charge or lien which cannot be interfered with to the prejudice of those entitled to it under the statute. An attempt to raise the assignment or discharge the receiver, ignoring the statutory charge in favor of labor claimants, will be nugatory as to them.25 “The statute has vested this right in cases of this character by a distinct charge upon the fund, which, if it could be said not technically to constitute a lien, has, nevertheless, all the characteristics and effect of one."26

Sec. 413. How Preference Is Obtained. 

In order to obtain the preference granted by the second clause of G. C. 8339, it is not necessary that the laborer record a verified itemized statement of his claim in the county where such labor was performed. This requirement applies only where the laborer seeks to obtain a lien upon the real property of his employer. The statute alone creates a charge upon the funds in the hands of the assignee, receiver or trustee in favor of the labor claimant, and nothing further need be done by such claimant except to make proof thereof at the appropriate time for the presentation and proof of claims to such assignee, receiver or trustee.28

Sec. 416

Priorities under G. C. 8339. (a) As to Claims to Which the Laborer's Lien Is Superior. 

Insofar as the lien upon the employer's real property is concerned, the first clause of G. C. 8339 expressly provides that such lien shall have priority over certain specified liens or claims on such property taken or attaching during the existence of the unpaid labor claims.33 

The liens and claims thus designated by the statute as inferior to the lien of an unpaid labor claimant, properly perfected by the recording of his verified itemized statement, are: (1st) Liens of Attachment.

The lien of an attachment, acquired during the existence of an unpaid labor claim, is subject to such claim. 

But an attachment levied prior to the performance of the labor will take precedence over a subsequent laborer's lien. 

(2nd) Liens of Mortgage. 

The lien of a mortgage, acquired during the existence of an unpaid labor claim, and at a time of actual insolvency of the debtor, or with a view of preferring creditors, or to secure a preexisting debt is inferior to the lien of an unpaid labor claimant. (c) No Priority as Between Several Labor Claimants. 

As between several labor claimants, whether their claims are based upon liens filed upon the real property of their employer, or upon the preference granted them in the funds of their employer in the hands of an assignee, receiver or trustee, there is no priority among themselves. All must share pro rata in the distribution of the assets.45 

Sec. 417. Who Are "Laborers" and "Employees". (a) In General. 99 It is quite plain from a reading of the statute that its benefits accrue to manual laborers only. While it is true that the statute uses the terms "laborers and employees,' it also uses the expression "or other manual labor," thereby limiting the former general terms to only such laborers and employees as perform manual labor. While the statute enumerates certain types of employment in which such manual labor may be performed, i. e., agriculture, mining and manufacture, it by no means limits the labor, 44.  for which a lien may be had, to these types of employment only, since it goes on to state "or other manual labor." Thus, the act seems to be broad enough in its scope to include any and all kinds of manual labor, no matter for whom it may be performed or upon what kind of work, construction or business it is expended. 

It is also provided that the statute “shall apply to and include any laborer who indirectly performs labor for a general employer, or the results of whose labor is immediately enjoyed by a general employer, when such general employer assumes payment of his wages by passing a credit therefor upon his books of account or otherwise."46 It was probably not the purpose of this section of the act, by the use of the words "any laborer," to enlarge the scope of the entire act so as to include all persons engaged in the employment of another. Such a construction would open the doors so wide that the act would apply to any person on the payroll of another no matter what type of work or service he might render.47 Certainly, such was not the intention of the Legislature. The two sections of the act must therefore be read and construed together. Indulging in this construction, we arrive then at the conclusion that the act may be availed of by any manual laborer when the relation of master and servant exists between him and his employer.48

Sec. 417

 (b) Sections 8339 and 11138 Are in PARI MATERIA 

and Must Be Construed Together.

By the provisions of G. C. 11138, "each person who has performed labor as an operative in the service of the assignor ***” is entitled to a certain preference in the distribution of the assets of his employer. It is not to be supposed that it was the intention of the Legislature by its use in G. C. 8339 and G. C. 11138 of different definitions of the employees of an insolvent debtor, who are entitled to a preference in the payment of their claims, to enlarge the class of persons to whom the provision is applicable or to provide a preference for different classes. 

These statutes are in pari materia.49

However, there has been such a hopeless conflict among the decisions construing these sections with respect to the persons entitled to the benefits thereof, that it seems advisable to discuss separately the cases which apply to these sections respectively. 

(c) The Decisions Under G. C. 8339. 

One of the earliest, and possibly the most criticized case, under this section, was that in which a circuit court held that a manufacturer's agent, or travelling salesman, employed by a company on the basis of a monthly salary and a commission of 5% on all sales made by him, was entitled to the benefits of G. C. 8339.50 In reaching this direction of the farmer. He works for whomever comes along.

The relation of master and servant, or employer and employee, does not exist. He is therefore neither a "laborer" under G. C. 8339 or an "operative" under

 conclusion the court held that to constitute such employee, it was not necessary that he should give his whole time at the factory or warehouse of the company. The court said: "There are evidently two classes of persons designated in the statute, "laborers", which may perhaps only be intended to mean such as "work with their hands"; and "employees" to include any person employed to perform any services, whether manual or otherwise, necessary to be performed in and about the business in order to make it a success, and both are entitled to the preference of the statute.' 

It is plain in this opinion that the court lost sight of the fact that the statute, G. C. 8339, uses the words "laborers and employees, whether such employment be at agriculture, mining, manufacture or other manual labor, and that it uses the expression, "claims due for labor performed." Obviously, if the court was correct in interpreting the word "employees" to mean any person employed to perform any service, whether manual or otherwise, the door would be opened for all persons who do anything for compensation, or who are employed in any manner or capacity by the debtor, to secure preference for their claims.51 Such a construction as that employed by the circuit court seems out of harmony with the general purpose of the statute and to wholly ignore or disregard the plain and obvious limitation created by the use of the words "or other manual labor." signee of the Cincinnati Chair

This decision, however erroneous it seems, has been followed by other courts, not without some reluctance nevertheless. Thus, a bookkeeper and a travelling salesman were granted a preference for their unpaid wages.52 

It is not the basis of compensation, however, that determines the question as to whether or not the laborer is entitled to the benefit of statutes creating preferences for claims for manual labor. It is the character of his work, not the method of paying him that fixes the right to such preference. Thus, wages due for piece work are within the meaning of statutes such as these.53

Employees of a rubber company, who on its falling into difficulties, abandoned their work of superintendence and engineering and discharged manual labor in manufacturing rubber tires, are, despite their superior titles and higher rate of pay, entitled to priority as laborers under the provisions of G. Sec. 421

Sec. 420.

Purpose of the Statute. 

These sections appear in the chapter entitled "Insolvent Debtors." They provide for the distribution of the assets of the estate of an insolvent debtor in cases of assignments for the benefit of creditors, and for the payment of labor claims of operatives in the service of the assignor, not exceeding three hundred dollars; but such labor claims cannot prevail over securities given or liens obtained in good faith for value. Under these sections an operative is given no lien upon the real estate of his employer, as is the case of a manual labor under the provisions of G. C. 8339. 

Sec. 421. "Trust Funds".

It is clear that the fund out of which such labor claims can be paid in cases of assignees or trustees in insolvency, is the general fund remaining after the payment of all securities and liens obtained in good faith for value. This general fund corresponds to, and is the same as, the "trust fund" mentioned in G. C. 8339, and each of said funds is what remains after the payment of the valid securities and liens against the property in the hands of the assignee or trustee; and to the extent of such securities and liens, construing both sections together, the property in the hands of the assignee or trustee is not regarded as the property of the employer, but as the property of the owner of the security or lien, and as being so connected with the property of the employer or assignor as to require the whole to be administered by the assignee or trustee, rendering to the owner of the securities and liens, the proceeds of their property, and distributing by order of the court the remainder among

Sec. 

632 

 the general creditors, subject to the rights of labor claims.59 

Sec. 422. G. C. 8339 and 11138 Compared.

These two laws giving to "laborers" and "operatives" certain rights of preference in the assets of their employers, while they are said to be in pari materia and must be construed together,60 nevertheless exhibit marked differences between them. G. C. 11138 belongs to the chapter regulating the administration and distribution of estates of insolvent debtors, while G. C. 8339 is part of the chapter which in distinct terms provides for liens, and among others, for liens of "laborers and employees of any person." G. C. 11138 relates to "each person who has performed labor as an operative," while G. C. 8339 relates to "laborers and employes" engaged in certain types of employment "or other manual labor" whose claims are "for labor performed." G. C. 11138 limits the amount of the wages to be paid to three hundred dollars, while G. C. 8339 fixes no limit as to the amount which may be recovered. G. C. 11138 limits the time within which the "operatives" work may be performed to twelve months preceding the assignment, while G. C. 

8339 limits it to three months. 

Sec. 423. G. C. 11138 Applies Only to Assignments by Insolvent Debtors.

Sec. 426. Who Are "Operatives”. 

Under the provisions of G. C. 11138, "each person who has performed labor as an operative in the service of an assignor" is entitled to a preference. The term "operative", in the sense it is employed here, has been variously defined and the decisions are sometimes difficult to reconcile. Some courts have held that the terms "laborer" and "operative" are not synonymous.73 "Generally speaking, an operative is a person employed as a workman in mill or factory; a skilled workman; an artisan; especially one who operates a machine in a factory."74 “A laborer is defined by Webster to be ‘one who labors in a toilsome occupation, a man who does work

However, it is doubtful that the Legislature, by its use in G. C. 8339 and G. C. 11138 of different definitions ("laborers", "employees", "operatives") of the employees of an insolvent debtor who are entitled to preference in the payment of claims, intended to enlarge or diminish the class of persons to whom the provisions are applicable, or to provide preference for different classes. In this sense, at least, the two statutes are in pari materia.76 

From this it would appear that it was not the intent of the Legislature in the enactment of these statutes,77 to prefer one class of skilled laborers or more intelligent laborers over the equally if not more needy common laborers; to establish under a show of equitable protections of laborers, a class within a class. By a parity of reasoning it was evidently the intention to include all classes of labor, except that which might properly be distinguished as professional or scientific.78

In order to be included within the provisions of these statutes, however, the relation of master and servant must exist between the employer and the labor claimant. It is not alone the kind of labor that includes his claim; it is also the nature of his service. The language of G. C.

Therefore, if the person who performs the labor, such as a blacksmith shoeing the horses of a farmer, does so in pursuit of an independent calling, and does not while performing such labor, remain entirely under the control and direction of the person for whom the labor is performed, such person is not a servant and the relation of master and servant does not exist between him and his employer; as such he is not entitled to the benefits of 

G. C. 11138 nor of G. C. 8339.80

Sec. 428 

 Sec. 428. Subrogation to or the Assignment of th Preference of a Labor Claim. 

In an early nisi prius case,96 it was held that a laborer's claim, prior to the assignment of his employer, was not assignable and a person paying the same could not later assert the right to a preference in the funds in the hands of the assignee. However, after the assignment of the employer, the preference in favor of the laborer having become fixed and determined thereby, such claim, with the preference annexed thereto, became assignable.97 

This decision was probably based, too, although not so stated, upon the mistaken theory that no preference exists until the assignment by the employer, and therefore no lien or preference exists when the claim is assigned. The fact is true, however, that the inchoate right to such a lien or preference exists at the time the services are performed and continues until it may ripen into a lien or preference by the assignment of the insolvent employer. 

This is a part and parcel of the laborer's claim and adds to the pecuniary value thereof. To destroy its assignability, before the same may have been finally perfected as a lien or preference, is to take away some of its real value and in the end may utterly defeat a laborer's pressing 

96. In re Engle, 1 N. P. 110. 

97. "Their claims were purchased and assigned before steps were taken to perfect their liens. They had at all times, after the rendition of the services, a right to a lien, and this is not assignable. Had they perfected their liens, the negotiability of the same would be clearly within the scope of their rights. The claims are not assignable, the liens are. This one is a personal right which the statute gives to the laborer for his protection, and, when asserted, becomes a fixed and determinable lien. That is the laborer's right, and the statute is made for his, and not for the protection of another." 

In re Engle, 1 N. P. 110.

Sec. 642 

 need to realize prompt payment of his claim.98 The law should encourage the purchasing of such claims by persons who can afford to buy them, and to take their chances on reimbursement out of the funds in the hands of the assignee. To restrict their assignment is to defeat the very beneficent purposes of the act, for few laborers can afford to await the long delays that usually attend the distribution of an insolvent debtor's estate, and fewer can afford to employ counsel to properly protect their interests in the presentation of such claims in court. 

The modern trend of decisions is to extend the class of cases in which the right of subrogation obtains, with much liberality.99 The Legislature has likewise evinced this wholesome doctrine by permitting the assignment of all mechanics' liens or claims for mechanics liens.100 

In accordance with this view, it has been held that where one, not a mere volunteer, advances unpaid wages, prior to an assignment of an employer, with an honest purpose of relieving wage earners, and not for personal gain, he is entitled to be subrogated to the rights of such wage earners to assert a preference for such claims in the assets of the insolvent employer.101

Sec. 429.

Historical. (a) In General (b) Priority of Mortgage

Over Claims of Labor ers and Materialmen

In the first general statute on the subject of mechanics liens, passed in 1843,¹ a contractor was given a lien upon certain structures and upon the land on which they stood. 

In the same class of cases, middlemen, by notice to the owner, could intercept funds due the contractor from the owner for the payment of their claims. In this statute, however, a railroad was not listed as one of the structures upon which a lien could be had. This law was amended in 1871,2 and the right of the middleman was extended far beyond the right of the head contractor, as to the class of structures. Among other types of improvements, it now gave to the mechanic or other person the right to stop payments due the head contractor for work or materials furnished in the construction, alteration or repair of a railroad. This gave to the middleman a lien on funds due from a railroad, in express terms, but still no lien existed in favor of the head contractor. 

With the act of 1877,3 however, the whole lien law was revised and recodified. On account of the fact that the Legislature had on March 31, 1874,4 passed an act "to secure pay to persons performing labor or furnishing materials in constructing railroads," the act of 1877 omitted any reference to that class of construction. From 

1874 to 1877, middlemen had, therefore, a double pro- 

1. 41 Oh. Laws 66. 

2. 68 Oh. Laws 107. 

3. 74 Oh. Laws 168. 

4. 71 Oh. Laws 51.

Sec. 429

Liens upon Railroads vision for them; first, by the general mechanics lien law; and second, by the special act relating to railroads. 

After the enactment of the law of 1877, a mechanics lien, under the general act relating to mechanics liens, could no longer be had upon a railroad,5 although, curiously enough, such a lien could be had upon a railroad bridge for the construction thereof, and the sale of the whole railroad could be decreed to pay it.6 

We come, now, to the special legislation referring to mechanics liens upon railroads. The first act was passed 

March 31, 1874.7 It was entitled, “An act, to secure pay to persons performing labor or furnishing materials in constructing railroads." This law made no provision for a lien in favor of persons performing labor or furnishing materials for the construction of a railroad. In substance, it provided for the liability of a contractor, or, under certain circumstances, 7a of a railroad company to those who performed labor or furnished material under a contract, for or to any contractor or subcontractor on the work contracted for by the railroad company, and pointed out how that liability was to be created and enforced, but it did not grant a right to a lien on the property of the railroad itself.

In 1883,8 the whole law was amended and revised.

This law, while not imposing a direct liability on the railroad company to persons furnishing labor or materials to any contractor or subcontractor working under a contract with such railroad company, did, however, provide that the railroad company should make provision, in its contract for the construction of the railroad, for the manner or priority in which payments of the contract price should be made; i. e. first, to laborers and materialmen; second, to subcontractors; third, the balance, if any, to the principal contractor. It also provided, for the first time, that persons furnishing labor or materials, or furnishing boarding for laborers, in such work, should have a lien upon the railroad for the payment of their claims, and pointed out also the manner in which such lien should be perfected and enforced. In addition to this, the act was extended so as to include, besides laborers, materialmen and persons furnishing boarding for laborers, "any person who furnishes grain, hay, merchandise, tools or implements, or who repairs any tools or implements ***." Thus, although retaining some of the principal features of the earlier law, the whole law was considerably revised, and broadened in its scope, operation and effect. Except for a change in the numbers and classification of its sections, and some minor changes in its phraseology, the law of 1883, together with the interpretive amendment, which will next be referred to, is substantially the law of today as found in G. C. 8343 to 8352, inclusive. 

Up to and including the revision of 1883, however, no provision had yet been made for a lien on a railroad in favor of the original contractor, although the right was clearly granted to all materialmen and those who performed labor or furnished boarding, when furnished

Sec. 429

Liens upon Railroads under an agreement with the contractor or a subcontractor. These provisions were broad enough, moreover, to include a subcontractor himself as one entitled to such a lien.

For the purpose, therefore, of extending the benefits of this law to the original contractor who had so far been omitted from its operation, the Legislature in 1884,9 passed an act "to declare the true intent and meaning" of the act of 1883. In substance it provided, "that the true intent and meaning" of the act of 1883, "is hereby declared to be as follows: Any person or persons who perform labor, or furnish material or boarding, under contract, express or implied, with such railroad company, or any of its authorized agents, for the construction of such railroad, is entitled to a lien for the payment of the same upon such railroad ***" The only effect and purpose of this latter act was to give a lien under G. C. 

8345 as well to persons furnishing materials directly to or performing labor under contract with a railroad, as to those who dealt with contractors and subcontractors, who were already protected by the act.10

The word "owner" in the sections of this subdivision of this chapter, shall be held and considered as including any lessee, receiver, corporation, company, or persons owning, operating or managing any railroad with whom or in whose behalf such contracts are made.

Sec. 431

Liens upon Railroads Sec. 431. Constitutionality of the Statute. 

The railroad lien law has now been in effect for more than fifty years, and yet the Supreme Court of Ohio has never specifically declared it constitutional, notwithstanding the fact that it has passed upon several of its provisions many times.11 In a nisi prius case, however, the question was specifically raised.12 The law was assailed on the grounds: (1st), that although a law of a general nature, it was not uniform in its operation throughout the state; (2nd), that it impairs the obligation of contracts. 

With but brief discussion the court held both grounds untenable.13 In view of the many cases in which this law has been passed upon by the Supreme Court without any hint as to its unconstitutionality, it seems reasonable to assume that it cannot be successfully attacked on this ground. A Federal court, however, has held otherwise.14

 Sec. 432. Liberal Construction of the Statute. 

In line with the general principles of construction, the statute, being remedial in its character, should receive a liberal construction with the view to carrying out the purpose of the Legislature in its enactment.15 But this does not justify the relinquishment of a mandatory requirement of the law respecting the perfection of the lien. 

Such statutes confer an extraordinary right in derogation of the common law, and, though liberality with reference to errors in procedure is permissible, the steps prescribed by statute to perfect such lien must be followed, and in that respect the law is strictly construed and applied.16

The term "railroad" also "may include all the lands, depots, shops, buildings, structures, and appurtenances incidental to the operation of the road and the transaction of the business of the company;"19 but exclusive of its rolling stock or other personal property.20 

A review of the decisions in Ohio reveals the fact that the word "railroad" when used by the Legislature without any qualification as to the kind of road intended, will be limited to the class of railroads known as steam railroads; in other words, that the term "railroad" used in the statute is not generic, pertaining to all classes of railroads, but special, including only steam railroads.21

Under the statutes of Ohio, steam railroads and interurban or street railways are not recognized as belonging to the same class, and statutes relating to the former are not applicable to the latter, unless an intention clearly appears to the contrary.22

With these distinctions in mind it is clear that the Railroad Lien Law, G. C. 8343 to 8352, inclusive, applies only to steam railroads and not to street, interurban or suburban railways.23

 Sec. 434. To What "Construction" the Statute 

Applies.

By its express language, the Railroad Lien Law24 applies only in cases where a person performs labor or furnishes material "for or in the construction of any railroad, depot buildings, water tanks, or any part thereof. 

The term "construction" has been defined as "the process of bringing together or correlating a number of independent entities, constructing a definite entity, as distinguished from reconstruction, repairing an existing entity."25 It is doubtful that the Legislature intended to use the term in this limited sense, so as to provide a lien only in the case of the initial or original construction of a railroad. It is the history of all first class railroads that the processes of construction are almost endless; that cheaper and less efficient construction is constantly being replaced by better and more efficient construction; that it is the aim of every railroad to keep step with the ever-quickening march of progress and invention; all with the view to furnishing safer, faster and more economical means of transportation to the public whom they serve and upon whose continuing patronage depends their success or failure. 

It is not conceivable, therefore, that the Legislature intended to protect those persons only who laid or furnished the original rails, who graded the first roadbed, or constructed the first depot buildings, and then, to leave without remedy, for the payment of their claims, those persons who, at a later time, replaced the obsolete rails

So it has been held, under a statute similar to the Ohio statute, that a lien might attach for additional construction of side-tracks, filling up of holes, widening the right of way, etc., even though the original road construction had long been completed.26 And the removal of an old bridge and the construction of a new one was held to be such a construction of a part of the railroad company's road as to come within the meaning of such lien statute.27 So, too, the furnishing of gravel or dirt, in the maintenance and repair of a railroad, comes within the meaning of "construction" of a railroad.28 In thus using the term "construction" in its broader sense, it might properly be said to include the erection of offices, shops and roundhouses.29

Sec. 435. The Purpose of G. C. 8343 and 8344. 

These sections of the General Code were at one time embraced in one section (3207) of the Revised Statutes, and, in the main were the principle feature of the original act of 1874. They provide what contracts for railroad construction shall stipulate, and create a personal liability on the part of the contractor to each person performing labor or furnishing materials stipulated for in the contract with the owner of the road. But they make no provision for a lien upon the road,31 nor do they impose any liability on the railroad company for the labor so performed or the materials so furnished.32 Proceeding further (G. C. 8344), the act goes on to declare that a railroad company shall provide in its contract that payments thereunder shall be made in the following order of priority: first, to laborers, materialmen, or persons furnishing boarding, without preference among them; second, 30. Sec. 437. The Remedy Is in Equity. 

These sections make it mandatory upon the railroad company to provide in its construction contracts that its payment thereunder shall be made in the order of priority prescribed in the statute.36 The railroad company cannot evade this responsibility. A fund is thus created and held by the railroad company in which several classes of claimants are interested, many of whom the railroad company may have no knowledge of. "In such case the proper remedy is to invoke the aid of a court of equity to effect a distribution of the fund. Its orders and decrees for the bringing in of creditors, for distribution of the fund, and in certain cases of contribution among creditors, will protect the owner of the road and holder of the fund, and secure to creditors their dues, according to their respective rights. * * * Any creditor of the owner can commence such a proceeding."

Sec. 441. 

Priorities under G. C. 8343 and 8344.

By the express provisions of the statute,41 payments under a railroad construction contract must be made in the following order of priority: 

1st: to the persons performing labor, furnishing materials, or boarding, on the order of any contractor or subcontractor to persons employed by them, or either of them, in furnishing materials or labor for or in the construction of such railroad, without preference. 

2nd: to any subcontractor, any balance due under his contract after payment of his or their liabilities to persons performing labor or furnishing materials or boarding, under his or their contract. 

3rd: to any contractor,. or construction company, intervening between a subcontractor and the railroad company, in the order of such intervention from such subcontractor upward to the owner of the rail-

While the statute clearly defines the order of priority of payment as between the three classes of claimants, it does not, except in the case of the first class, establish any rule of priority as between persons of the same class. 

In the absence of any provision to the contrary, persons of the same class should have no priority among themselves; all should share pro rata in the funds available for their particular class. This is the spirit of laws relating to mechanics liens in general.42 

Sec. 442. No Extra-Territorial Effect. 

G. C. 8343 and 8344, which require a railroad company, contracting for construction work, to stipulate in its contract that it will pay out the contract price to persons in the order named in the statute, has no application to a contract made in another state for work to be done in such state.43

As has already been stated, the original act of 1874 made no provision for a lien in favor of persons engaged in the construction of a railroad. The revised act of 

1883, however, specifically grants such a lien upon a railroad. This right to a lien is in addition to the rights of a claimant under G. C. 8343 and 8344.44

Liens upon Railroads Sec. 444. Persons Entitled to a Lien. 

The persons entitled to a lien upon a railroad under the provisions of the act are- 1st: A person who performs labor or furnishes materials for or in construction of any railroad, depot buildings, water-tanks, or any part thereof.45 

2nd: A person who furnishes boarding on the order of any contractor or subcontractor, to persons employed by them or either of them ***.46 

3rd: A person who furnishes grain, hay, merchandise, tools or implements, or who repairs any tools or implements, on the order of any contractor or subcontractor *** (But the amount of such claim shall not exceed the wages of the person performing labor or furnishing materials, to whom furnished, or the amount found due such contractor, or subcontractor, under the provisions of this subdivision.) 47

It is clearly the intention of these sections, when read and construed together with G. C. 8343 and 8344, to protect all persons furnishing labor or materials for the construction of a railroad, when such labor and materials have been furnished either under a contract made directly with the railroad company, or by virtue of an agreement with another person who has himself contracted directly with the railroad company. 48

However, this is not alone the test. Not only must the labor and materials be furnished under some contract, or by virtue of some privity of contract, with the railroad; but these must be furnished for or in the construc-

Certainly there was no intention on the part of the Legislature to create a lien in favor of persons who might, either on their own initiative or that of another, perform labor or furnish materials for which the railroad had no use or which did not comply with the stipulations of its contract. 

A subcontractor engaged in stripping the surface soil of a tract of land for the purpose of preparing the ground to be used as a gravel pit, from which gravel is to be taken to be used as ballast in the construction and repair of railroad tracks, is engaged in furnishing labor and material for and in the construction of a railroad, and a person who rents a steam shovel to such subcontractor to be used in said work is a person who furnishes tools and implements on the order of a subcontractor for his use, and is entitled to a lien under the provisions of G. C. 8351.50

Sec. 445. . 

In the language of the statute the lien will attach to “such railroad", for which the persons designated therein have furnished their labor and materials. In the sense in which the term "railroad" is so used, it includes not only its real estate, right of way and tracks but also its depot buildings, water-tanks, round-houses, shops, signal towers and all other structures and appurtenances incidental to its operation.55 In other words a "railroad" is an entire thing and as such the whole railroad may be sold as a single entity to pay the claim of one who has acquired a lien thereon.56 But the rolling stock of a railroad does not constitute a part of its real estate,57 and a mechanics lien upon the railroad will not embrace such property,58 nor will it extend to its corporate franchise.59

Liens upon Railroads Sec. 446. Duration of the Lien. 

By perfecting the lien in the manner provided in the statute, it will operate as such on the railroad from the date of the filing of the affidavit as therein required,60 and will subsist for one year thereafter, except that, if an action is brought to enforce the lien within that time, it shall continue in force until finally adjudicated.61 

Sec. 447. How Lien Is Perfected. Filing the Affi davit. 

In order to perfect his right to such a lien, a person designated in the statute as one entitled thereto, must first prepare and, within forty days from the date he ceased performing labor, or furnishing materials, or boarding on or for the railroad, file with the recorder of the county an affidavit containing an itemized statement of his account.62

(2nd) the time when such materials were furnished, or labor performed. (3rd) the name of the contractor or subcontractor for whom the materials were furnished, or labor performed.

While it is a general rule of construction that laws relating to mechanics liens, being remedial in their nature, will be construed liberally, this does not justify the relinquishment of a mandatory requirement of the law respecting the perfection of the lien. Consequently, the preparation and filing of the affidavit, being one of the steps prescribed by statute to perfect such lien, must strictly meet the requirements of the statute relating thereto, and a failure so to do, resulting in deficiencies in the affidavit or the itemized statement contained therein, cannot be supplied by evidence or corrected by extraneous proof.65

The question often arises in the filing of a mechanics lien as to whether the contract under which it is to be filed is an entire or severable one. If it is an entire contract only one lien need be filed; if severable, a separate lien for each particular performance, whether it be for labor or the delivery of materials, must be filed. Thus, a contract to grade a section of a railroad is an entire contract, and a provision in it for payments from time to time, as the work progresses, will not make it a severable one. 

It is not the multiplicity of items, in a contract which determines its severable or non-severable character, but its object.67

Enforcement of the Lien.

Sec. 459

Liens upon Railroads 

As to all other liens "taken or to be taken" upon a railroad, the lien of a person performing labor or furnishing materials for the construction thereof will have preference. From this it would appear that it is immaterial when the performance of labor or furnishing of materials commenced, since the lien of the claimant is given precedence over any lien taken, regardless of when it was taken. If this conclusion is correct, then in this respect the lien granted under the railroad lien law differs from that granted under the general mechanics lien law, since the latter lien dates only from the commencement of the work and does not affect any bona fide liens which have been acquired upon the property of the owner prior to the commencement of such work.90 Persons acquiring liens upon railroad property, other than personal property, must be held, therefore, to have contracted with reference to the railroad lien law and to know that the priority of their liens may be lost or affected by the subsequent acquisition of liens in favor of those performing labor or furnishing materials for the construction of such railroad.91

Sec. 463 

Liens upon Railroads Sec. 462. Arbitration of Disputed Claims. 

In the event a claim cannot be adjusted between the parties interested, it may be submitted to the arbitration of three disinterested persons, one to be chosen by each of the parties, and one by the two thus chosen. Their de cision, or that of any two of them, in the absence of fraud or collusion shall be final and conclusive on the parties.95

Sec. 463. Suit upon Disputed Claims. 

If any claim be disputed and is not settled or submitted to arbitration, the claimant in such case must commence suit on his claim within forty days after notice that it has been disputed, and prosecute it to final judgment. The amount thus ascertained or found due in such adjudication shall then be paid by the railroad company or owner.96

This statute is not at all clear. It does not specify who is to furnish the notice to the claimant to commence suit on his claim. It is of equal interest to both the railroad and the contractor, that the disputed claim be adjudicated without delay; but as upon which of these the burden rests to notify the claimant, the statute is silent.

(a) In General.

To carry such reorganization into effect such company is vested with certain powers enumerated in G.

Sec. 684 

 (b) Priority of Mortgage or Deed of Trust Over Claims of Laborers and Materialmen. 

By the express provisions of G. C. 9085, the lien of the mortgages or deeds of trust authorized by G. C. 9083 are postponed to the lien of judgments recovered against the company, after its reorganization, for labor thereafter performed for it, or materials or supplies thereafter furnished to it, and certain other claims. Parties electing to reorganize under these statutes must therefore be presumed to have consented to the superiority of such claims for labor, materials and supplies performed for or furnished to such company after the taking effect of such mortgages or deeds of trust. "The purpose of the statute is obviously to secure to the road, in any event, the supplies necessary to the ordinary conduct of its business, so that in case of insolvency its running may not be suspended for want of credit, and that the natural equity inherent in the claims of persons under such circumstances furnishing it with articles necessary to its existence shall be protected.”102 

In the suit to establish the claims of such laborers or materialmen against the railroad company, the mortgagee is neither a necessary or proper party. Such claims are merely upon account and no defense could be offered by any mortgagee against any judgment that might be rendered thereon. It is only when the lien of a judgment so obtained is brought into conflict with the mortgagee's lien that the latter has a right to be heard. When a priority over such mortgage lien is asserted by such judgment creditors (i. e. laborers and materialmen) then the mort-

Sec. 466. The Statute. 

G. C. 8376. Any person who has performed common or mechanical labor upon, or furnished supplies to any railroad, street railroad, or railroad operated wholly or in part by electric motor power, turnpike, plank road, canal or on any public structure being erected, or on any abutment, pier, culvert or foundation therefor, or for any side track, embankment, excavation, or any public work, protection, ballasting, delivering or placing ties, or track-laying, whether the labor is performed for, or the supplies or materials are furnished to any company, corporation, contractor, or subcontractor, construction company, or any individual, shall have a first and absolute lien on the whole of the property on which such work is done, or to which such supplies were contributed, and on any fund arising from a sale thereof or any part thereof under an order of any court."

G. C. 8377.-Such person shall hold the railroad, street railroad or railroad operated wholly or in part by electric motor power, canal, turnpike, plank road, or structure, to the creation or construction of which such labor or supplies were contributed, or so much thereof as in whole or part have been created by such labor or supplies, to the exclusion of any such railroads, canal, turnpike, plank road, public work or structure, as to opera-

Sec. 467

Lien on Public Works tion, occupation or use, until the claim for such labor or supplies is properly adjusted and paid in full." 

Sec. 467. History of the Act. 

On March 20, 1889, the Legislature passed an act entitled "To fix responsibility and to protect labor and the rights of contractors and sub-contractors on all public works or work done for companies, corporations, contracting companies or individuals."1 On May 12, 1902, the Legislature passed an amendatory act, amending Section 1 of the act of March 20, 1889,2 by inserting the words "street railroad, or railroad operated wholly or in part by electric motor power."3 Prior to this amendment, it had been held that the act of March 20, 1889, did not permit of a mechanics lien being acquired upon the property of railroads operated by motive power other than steam. Electrically operated railroads or street railways not having been in existence at the time of the enactment of the act of March 20, 1889, it was held that the intention of the Legislature was to include only steam railroads within the operation of this act.4 The purpose of the amendatory act was obviously to correct this situation and to make the law applicable to both steam and electric railroads.

March 20, 1889, is represented now by sections 8376 and 8377 of the General Code. 

3. 95 Oh. Laws 609. 

4. Massillon Bridge Co. vs. 

Cambria Iron Co., 59 Oh. St. 179.

The Federal Court in Ohio, however, reached a contrary view holding that the original act applied to all railroads irrespective of whether their motor power was steam or electricity.

Sec. 688 

 Sec. 468. To Whom the Act Applies. 

It will be seen from a reading of the act (G. C. 8376) that a direct lien upon the property of the owner is granted to all persons who have performed "common or mechanical labor upon, or furnished supplies" for the purposes named therein, regardless of whether such labor or material was furnished to the owner, "contractor, or subcontractor, construction company, or any individual." 

Altho this act, as it now reads, bears the general title "Lien on Public Works", it must not be construed as authorizing a mechanics lien upon public property. No lien can be acquired by any person on public property.5 

Obviously, then, the act "does not apply to highways owned or constructed by public authorities, but only such as are owned or constructed by private corporations for profit."6 

Sec. 469.

Constitutionality of G. C. 8376 and 8377. 

Upon the authority of the case of Palmer vs. Tingle,7

Section 3231-1, Revised Statutes (now G. C. 8376 and 

8377) was held unconstitutional as being an infringement upon or abridgement of the freedom of contract secured and guaranteed to all persons, whether corporations or private individuals, by the Bill of Rights.8 For all pur- 

5. See Section 110, ante. 

6. In re Schilling, 251 F. 966, 970. 

The dictum of the court in 

Maryland Casualty Co. vs. Citizens National Bank, 18 Oh. App. 

193, 196 is an erroneous statement of the law as regards the right to a lien upon a public highway. 

7. 55 Oh. St. 423. 

8. Stewart vs. Gardner, 10 

C. C. (N.S.) 408. 

Aff. without op. 78 Oh. St. 451.

The Federal Courts have, upon the authority of Palmer vs. 

Tingle, 55 Oh. St. 423, adopted the same view. Geo. A. Shaw 

Co. vs. Cleveland, C., C., & St. 

L. Ry. Co., 173 F. 746.

Sec. 469

Lien on Public Works poses, therefor, the entire act as now embraced in G. C. 

8376-8380 inclusive, is void and of no effect, since, if the lien itself cannot be acquired, the remedies provided for its enforcement must also be denied.

While it is true that by the constitutional amendment adopted September 3, 1912,9 a direct lien may now be acquired upon property of the owner if the Legislature sees fit to enact laws to accomplish this purpose, such constitutional amendment has not of itself cured the unconstitutionality of the acts of March 20, 1889, and of May 12, 1902, (now Sections 8376-8380 inclusive). Such acts having been unconstitutional when they were enacted were therefore wholly void and of no effect.10 Such legislation in conflict with the constitution as it then existed when the act was passed "is not only illegal or voidable, but it is absolutely void. It is as if never enacted, and no subsequent change of the constitution removing the restriction could validate it or breathe into it the breath of life.11 No reenactment of these sections (G. C. 83768380 inclusive) having ever been made by the Legisla ture subsequent to the constitutional amendment of 1912, they are now therefor, void and of no effect and should be removed from the General Code.12 

9. Art. II-Section 33 of the 

Constitution of Ohio.

PART VI PENAL STATUTE Sec. 470. The Statute. 

G. C. 13180.-Wrongful use of material purchased by contractor.--"Whoever, being an owner, contractor or sub-contractor, with intent to defraud in purchasing materials on credit, represents that they are to be used in a designated building or other improvement, and thereafter uses or causes them to be used in the construction of a building or improvement other than that designated, without the written consent of the person of whom such materials were purchased, shall be fined not more than five hundred dollars."

There appears to be no adjudicated case in which the construction of this statute has been involved.

NOTE: The attention of Owners and Architects is called to the provisions of the above paragraph beginning, "and further". This clause gives direct right of suit against the Surety to all Subcontractors and Materialmen having direct contracts with the Contractor, and will generally involve the Owner in an added premium.
